title: Test: Mock tmux client for testing
description:
## Purpose
End-to-end integration test script for the complete swarm orchestration workflow, from scanning to agent launch to limit detection and respawn.

## Test Script Structure

```bash
#\!/bin/bash
# scripts/test_swarm_e2e.sh
# End-to-end test for weighted multi-project agent swarm orchestration
#
# Prerequisites:
# - ntm binary built and in PATH
# - tmux installed
# - br (beads_rust) installed
# - Test project directories set up

set -euo pipefail

# ============================================================================
# Configuration
# ============================================================================
TEST_DIR="${TEST_DIR:-/tmp/ntm_e2e_test_$$}"
LOG_FILE="${TEST_DIR}/e2e_test.log"
VERBOSE="${VERBOSE:-1}"

# Colors for output
RED="\033[0;31m"
GREEN="\033[0;32m"
YELLOW="\033[1;33m"
NC="\033[0m" # No Color

# ============================================================================
# Logging Functions
# ============================================================================
log() {
    local level=$1
    shift
    local msg="$*"
    local timestamp=$(date "+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%3N")
    echo -e "[$timestamp] [$level] $msg" | tee -a "$LOG_FILE"
}

log_info()  { log "INFO " "$@"; }
log_warn()  { log "WARN " "${YELLOW}$*${NC}"; }
log_error() { log "ERROR" "${RED}$*${NC}"; }
log_pass()  { log "PASS " "${GREEN}$*${NC}"; }
log_fail()  { log "FAIL " "${RED}$*${NC}"; }

log_section() {
    echo "" | tee -a "$LOG_FILE"
    echo "============================================================" | tee -a "$LOG_FILE"
    echo "  $1" | tee -a "$LOG_FILE"
    echo "============================================================" | tee -a "$LOG_FILE"
}

# ============================================================================
# Setup Functions
# ============================================================================
setup_test_environment() {
    log_section "Setting up test environment"
    
    mkdir -p "$TEST_DIR"
    log_info "Test directory: $TEST_DIR"
    log_info "Log file: $LOG_FILE"
    
    # Create test projects with different bead counts
    log_info "Creating test projects..."
    
    # Tier 1 project (400+ beads)
    create_test_project "tier1-project" 450
    
    # Tier 2 project (100-399 beads)
    create_test_project "tier2-project" 200
    
    # Tier 3 project (<100 beads)
    create_test_project "tier3-project" 50
    
    # Project without beads (should be skipped)
    mkdir -p "$TEST_DIR/no-beads-project"
    log_info "Created no-beads-project (should be skipped)"
    
    log_pass "Test environment setup complete"
}

create_test_project() {
    local name=$1
    local bead_count=$2
    local project_dir="$TEST_DIR/$name"
    
    mkdir -p "$project_dir/.beads"
    
    # Create mock beads
    for i in $(seq 1 $bead_count); do
        echo "{\"id\":\"bd-$i\",\"status\":\"open\",\"title\":\"Test bead $i\"}" >> "$project_dir/.beads/issues.jsonl"
    done
    
    log_info "Created $name with $bead_count beads"
}

# ============================================================================
# Test Cases
# ============================================================================
test_dry_run() {
    log_section "Test: Dry Run Mode"
    
    log_info "Running: ntm swarm --scan-dir $TEST_DIR --dry-run"
    
    local output
    output=$(ntm swarm --scan-dir "$TEST_DIR" --dry-run 2>&1) || {
        log_fail "Dry run command failed"
        log_error "Output: $output"
        return 1
    }
    
    log_info "Dry run output:"
    echo "$output" | tee -a "$LOG_FILE"
    
    # Verify expected output
    if echo "$output" | grep -q "tier1-project"; then
        log_pass "Tier 1 project detected"
    else
        log_fail "Tier 1 project NOT detected"
        return 1
    fi
    
    if echo "$output" | grep -q "tier2-project"; then
        log_pass "Tier 2 project detected"
    else
        log_fail "Tier 2 project NOT detected"
        return 1
    fi
    
    if echo "$output" | grep -q "no-beads-project"; then
        log_fail "No-beads project should NOT appear"
        return 1
    else
        log_pass "No-beads project correctly excluded"
    fi
    
    if echo "$output" | grep -q "Dry-run complete"; then
        log_pass "Dry run completed without execution"
    else
        log_fail "Dry run indicator not found"
        return 1
    fi
    
    log_pass "Dry run test PASSED"
}

test_plan_output() {
    log_section "Test: Plan JSON Output"
    
    local plan_file="$TEST_DIR/swarm_plan.json"
    
    log_info "Running: ntm swarm --scan-dir $TEST_DIR --dry-run --output $plan_file"
    
    ntm swarm --scan-dir "$TEST_DIR" --dry-run --output "$plan_file" 2>&1 | tee -a "$LOG_FILE"
    
    if [[ \! -f "$plan_file" ]]; then
        log_fail "Plan file not created"
        return 1
    fi
    
    log_info "Plan file created: $plan_file"
    log_info "Plan contents:"
    cat "$plan_file" | tee -a "$LOG_FILE"
    
    # Validate JSON structure
    if \! jq -e . "$plan_file" > /dev/null 2>&1; then
        log_fail "Plan file is not valid JSON"
        return 1
    fi
    log_pass "Plan file is valid JSON"
    
    # Check required fields
    local total_agents
    total_agents=$(jq -r ".total_agents" "$plan_file")
    log_info "Total agents in plan: $total_agents"
    
    if [[ "$total_agents" -gt 0 ]]; then
        log_pass "Plan contains agent allocations"
    else
        log_fail "Plan has no agent allocations"
        return 1
    fi
    
    log_pass "Plan output test PASSED"
}

test_session_creation() {
    log_section "Test: Session Creation (requires tmux)"
    
    # Skip if tmux not available
    if \! command -v tmux &> /dev/null; then
        log_warn "tmux not available, skipping session creation test"
        return 0
    fi
    
    # Clean up any existing test sessions
    tmux kill-session -t "cc_agents_1" 2>/dev/null || true
    
    log_info "Running swarm with single session for test..."
    log_info "ntm swarm --scan-dir $TEST_DIR --sessions-per-type 1 --dry-run"
    
    # For actual execution (commented out for safety):
    # ntm swarm --scan-dir "$TEST_DIR" --sessions-per-type 1
    
    # Verify sessions would be created
    local plan_file="$TEST_DIR/session_test_plan.json"
    ntm swarm --scan-dir "$TEST_DIR" --sessions-per-type 1 --dry-run --output "$plan_file"
    
    local session_count
    session_count=$(jq -r ".sessions | length" "$plan_file")
    log_info "Sessions in plan: $session_count"
    
    if [[ "$session_count" -ge 3 ]]; then
        log_pass "Plan includes expected session count (3 types)"
    else
        log_fail "Unexpected session count: $session_count"
        return 1
    fi
    
    # Check session naming
    local cc_session
    cc_session=$(jq -r ".sessions[] | select(.agent_type==\"cc\") | .name" "$plan_file" | head -1)
    log_info "CC session name: $cc_session"
    
    if [[ "$cc_session" == "cc_agents_1" ]]; then
        log_pass "Session naming is correct"
    else
        log_fail "Session naming mismatch: expected cc_agents_1, got $cc_session"
        return 1
    fi
    
    log_pass "Session creation test PASSED"
}

test_allocation_tiers() {
    log_section "Test: Allocation Tier Calculations"
    
    local plan_file="$TEST_DIR/tier_test_plan.json"
    ntm swarm --scan-dir "$TEST_DIR" --dry-run --output "$plan_file"
    
    # Check tier 1 allocation
    local tier1_cc
    tier1_cc=$(jq -r ".allocations[] | select(.project.name==\"tier1-project\") | .cc_agents" "$plan_file")
    log_info "Tier 1 (450 beads) CC allocation: $tier1_cc"
    
    # Check tier 2 allocation  
    local tier2_cc
    tier2_cc=$(jq -r ".allocations[] | select(.project.name==\"tier2-project\") | .cc_agents" "$plan_file")
    log_info "Tier 2 (200 beads) CC allocation: $tier2_cc"
    
    # Check tier 3 allocation
    local tier3_cc
    tier3_cc=$(jq -r ".allocations[] | select(.project.name==\"tier3-project\") | .cc_agents" "$plan_file")
    log_info "Tier 3 (50 beads) CC allocation: $tier3_cc"
    
    # Verify tier hierarchy
    if [[ "$tier1_cc" -gt "$tier2_cc" ]] && [[ "$tier2_cc" -ge "$tier3_cc" ]]; then
        log_pass "Tier allocation hierarchy is correct"
    else
        log_fail "Tier allocation hierarchy violated: T1=$tier1_cc, T2=$tier2_cc, T3=$tier3_cc"
        return 1
    fi
    
    log_pass "Allocation tier test PASSED"
}

# ============================================================================
# Cleanup
# ============================================================================
cleanup() {
    log_section "Cleanup"
    
    # Kill any test tmux sessions
    tmux kill-session -t "cc_agents_1" 2>/dev/null || true
    tmux kill-session -t "cod_agents_1" 2>/dev/null || true
    tmux kill-session -t "gmi_agents_1" 2>/dev/null || true
    
    if [[ "${KEEP_TEST_DIR:-0}" == "0" ]]; then
        log_info "Removing test directory: $TEST_DIR"
        rm -rf "$TEST_DIR"
    else
        log_info "Keeping test directory: $TEST_DIR"
    fi
    
    log_info "Cleanup complete"
}

# ============================================================================
# Main
# ============================================================================
main() {
    log_section "NTM Swarm E2E Test Suite"
    log_info "Starting at $(date)"
    log_info "Test directory: $TEST_DIR"
    
    trap cleanup EXIT
    
    local failed=0
    
    setup_test_environment
    
    test_dry_run || ((failed++))
    test_plan_output || ((failed++))
    test_allocation_tiers || ((failed++))
    test_session_creation || ((failed++))
    
    log_section "Test Summary"
    if [[ $failed -eq 0 ]]; then
        log_pass "All tests PASSED"
        exit 0
    else
        log_fail "$failed test(s) FAILED"
        exit 1
    fi
}

main "$@"
```

title: [LOW] OnSuccess silently doesn't fire for top-level Parallel/Loop/Branch/Foreach/BeadQuery steps
description:
## Summary

bd-w6nth.7 (61f21316) introduced \`Step.OnSuccess\` runtime support and plumbed \`runOnSuccessSteps\` into the executeStep success path. bd-0fkcn (99913657) extended it to foreach body steps. But the dispatch in \`executeStep\` (internal/pipeline/executor.go:752) early-returns for compound step kinds before reaching the runOnSuccessSteps call:

\`\`\`go
// Handle parallel steps
if len(step.Parallel.Steps) > 0 {
    return e.executeParallel(ctx, step, workflow)   // <-- never reaches runOnSuccessSteps
}

// Handle loop steps
if step.Loop != nil {
    return e.executeLoop(ctx, step, workflow)        // <-- same gap
}

// ... later ...

if step.Branch != \"\" {
    return e.executeBranch(ctx, step, workflow)      // <-- same gap
}

if step.BeadQuery != nil {
    return e.executeBeadQuery(ctx, step, workflow)   // <-- same gap
}

if step.Foreach != nil || step.ForeachPane != nil {
    return e.executeForeach(ctx, step, workflow)     // <-- same gap
}

// ...
// Only THIS path triggers OnSuccess (around line 847):
stepResult := e.executeStepOnce(ctx, step, workflow)
if stepResult.Status == StatusCompleted {
    ...
    e.runOnSuccessSteps(ctx, step, workflow)
    return result
}
\`\`\`

A workflow author writing:

\`\`\`yaml
- id: parallel_thing
  parallel:
    steps: [...]
  on_success:
    - id: notify
      command: echo "fanout done"
\`\`\`

…expects \`notify\` to fire when the parallel group reaches StatusCompleted. It silently does not. The same gap applies to top-level Loop/Branch/Foreach/BeadQuery steps. (Branch/Parallel inside a foreach body get OnSuccess via the foreach.go:905 path — only the top-level dispatch is broken.)

## Severity

P3 (LOW). Schema-allowed configuration that silently no-ops. Discovered by review of bd-w6nth.7's plumbing; no live workflow is known to depend on this, but the documented feature surface contradicts the runtime behavior.

## Why no test catches it

\`grep -n \"Parallel.*OnSuccess\\\\|TestParallel.*OnSuccess\" internal/pipeline/*_test.go\` is empty. \`TestOnSuccessStepsRunOnParentSuccess\` and siblings cover only command-step parents, and bd-0fkcn's \`TestOnSuccessExplicitIDsInsideForeachAreNamespaced\` covers the foreach-body case (which goes through executeForeachNestedStep, not executeStep). The compound-step gap is uncovered.

## Suggested approach

Two reasonable shapes:

### Option A — runOnSuccessSteps after every successful executeStep return

Wrap each compound dispatch in a helper that runs OnSuccess if the result is StatusCompleted. Concretely:

\`\`\`go
if len(step.Parallel.Steps) > 0 {
    result = e.executeParallel(ctx, step, workflow)
    if result.Status == StatusCompleted {
        e.runOnSuccessSteps(ctx, step, workflow)
    }
    return result
}
\`\`\`

…repeated for Loop / Branch / Foreach / BeadQuery, OR factored into a single \`dispatchAndMaybeRunOnSuccess\` wrapper that takes the dispatcher func.

### Option B — funnel all dispatches through one post-success hook

Restructure executeStep so the dispatch returns a result, then a single tail block applies the post-success hook. Cleaner but bigger diff.

Option A is the minimum-viable fix. Option B is the right shape for the larger \"unify on-success / on-failure / on-skip hooks\" follow-up if that's ever scoped.

## Acceptance

- New test \`TestOnSuccessFiresForParallelParent\`: top-level parallel step with on_success children, after parallel completes assert state.Steps has the namespaced on_success child entries.
- Same shape for Loop, Branch, Foreach, BeadQuery.
- Existing tests for command-step OnSuccess still pass unchanged.

title: Sub-epic: Canonical context window registry consolidation
description:
PROBLEM: Context window limits for AI models are duplicated in 4+ separate maps across the codebase, each using different Go types (int vs int64), different key naming conventions ('claude-opus-4' vs 'opus' vs 'opus-4'), and slightly different model coverage. When model providers update context windows (which happens regularly), ALL of these must be updated manually and kept in sync — a process that is fragile and has already led to drift.

LOCATIONS OF DUPLICATION:
  1. internal/context/monitor.go:21-56 — ContextLimits map[string]int64 (most complete, includes dated models)
  2. internal/tokens/tokens.go:102-129 — ContextLimits map[string]int (simpler aliases like 'opus', 'sonnet')
  3. internal/robot/robot.go:9288-9303 — getContextLimit() switch statement (yet another copy)
  4. internal/context/pack.go:18-23 — TokenBudgets map (per-agent-type, not per-model, but derived from model limits)
  5. internal/agents/profiles.go:84,123 — Context budgets embedded in profile definitions

GOAL: Create a single canonical registry module that all consumers import. The registry should:
  - Support exact match and fuzzy/prefix match for model names
  - Handle date-suffix stripping (e.g., claude-opus-4-20260101 → claude-opus-4)
  - Support alias resolution (opus → claude-opus-4)
  - Be overridable via TOML config for users who need custom limits
  - Use a consistent Go type (int, not int64 — no model has >2B token context)

WHY THIS MATTERS: Incorrect context limits cause NTM to either (a) rotate agents too early (wasting context), or (b) not rotate them soon enough (causing context overflow and degraded agent performance). Both failure modes are silent and hard to diagnose.
close_reason: All 7 children completed: registry created, 5 consumers migrated, config override added

title: Design and implement single-source-of-truth context limit registry

title: Implement semantic similarity matching in ensemble pipeline
description:
PROBLEM: internal/ensemble/pipeline.go:367 — 'A more sophisticated approach would use semantic similarity'. Currently the ensemble pipeline uses simple string/keyword matching to correlate findings across agents. This misses semantically similar findings phrased differently.

CURRENT BEHAVIOR: Findings from different agents are correlated using exact or fuzzy string matching (check the actual implementation around line 367).

DESIRED BEHAVIOR: Use embedding-based semantic similarity to cluster related findings. This would:
  - Catch when Agent A says 'null pointer risk in auth handler' and Agent B says 'potential nil dereference in authentication middleware' — these are the same finding
  - Improve synthesis quality by properly deduplicating semantic duplicates
  - Reduce noise in ensemble output

IMPLEMENTATION OPTIONS:
  a) Call an embedding API (e.g., via NTM's AI gateway integration) to embed each finding and cluster by cosine similarity
  b) Use a local lightweight embedding model
  c) Use TF-IDF or BM25 as a middle ground (no API call, better than string matching)

RECOMMENDATION: Start with option (c) — TF-IDF similarity is fast, local, and significantly better than string matching. Graduate to embeddings if precision matters.
close_reason: Deferred: Semantic similarity matching in ensemble is a major feature (embedding integration or TF-IDF). Current string matching works for MVP. Recommend TF-IDF as first step when prioritized.

  3. Parse the structured output into the existing synthesis format
  4. Respect the token budget from config (ensemble.budget.synthesis = 8000 per config.go:1074)

DEPENDENCY: Requires a configured AI provider (API key or gateway). Should gracefully fall back to mechanical merging if no AI is available.

title: Implement attention feed work-vs-abandonment distinction
description:
PROBLEM: internal/robot/attention_contract.go:956 — The attention feed 'conflates legitimate long-running work with abandonment'. The comment at line 968+ describes what would need to change.

CURRENT BEHAVIOR: When an agent has been idle (no output) for a threshold period, the attention system treats it the same regardless of whether the agent is:
  a) Doing genuine long-running work (e.g., large compilation, complex reasoning)
  b) Actually stuck or abandoned

DESIRED BEHAVIOR: Distinguish between these states using signals:
  1. CPU/process activity — if the agent process is consuming CPU, it's working
  2. Last input timing — if we recently sent it a prompt, it may still be processing
  3. Historical pattern — agents that typically take long on similar tasks
  4. Agent type — Gemini tends to be slower, Codex tends to be faster

IMPLEMENTATION: Read the attention_contract.go comment block (lines 956-973) for the author's own notes on what would need to change. The key insight is that idleness should be interpreted relative to the agent's expected behavior pattern, not absolute thresholds.

The conclusion is architecturally sound: require Agent Mail 'explicit abandon' messages before emitting bead_orphaned. No code change needed — the design is correct.

title: Sub-epic: Unify inconsistent retry policies across subsystems
description:

  - internal/config/webhooks.go:137 — MaxAttempts = 5

title: Design unified RetryPolicy config struct with TOML support
description:
Create a shared RetryPolicy type in internal/config that provides consistent retry behavior across all subsystems.

DESIGN:
  type RetryPolicy struct {
      MaxAttempts   int           // Default: 3
      InitialDelay  time.Duration // Default: 1s
      MaxDelay      time.Duration // Default: 30s
      BackoffFactor float64       // Default: 2.0 (exponential)
      Jitter        bool          // Default: true
  }

TOML MAPPING:
  [retry]
  max_attempts = 3
  initial_delay_ms = 1000
  max_delay_ms = 30000
  backoff_factor = 2.0
  jitter = true

  # Subsystem overrides (optional, inherit from global)
  [retry.webhook]
  max_attempts = 5

  [retry.alerts]
  max_attempts = 3

  [retry.scheduler]
  max_attempts = 5

IMPLEMENTATION:
1. Add RetryPolicy struct and defaults to internal/config/config.go
2. Add [retry] section to Config struct
3. Add RetryPolicyFor(subsystem string) method that checks subsystem-specific override first, then returns global default
4. Add DefaultRetryPolicy() function
5. Add the section to config init template

EXISTING BEHAVIOR TO PRESERVE: The current default values differ by subsystem (webhooks=5, alerts=3, scheduler=5, etc.). The subsystem overrides handle this — set sensible per-subsystem defaults that match current behavior so this is not a behavior change.

title: [HIGH] nested foreach aliases bleed across parallel outer iterations
description:
Review of aad0cbae found a real concurrency bug in nested foreach alias scoping. The commit uses the shared executor variable map for materializing nested foreach aliases: pushForeachVars sets e.state.Variables[varName] and loop.* under varMu, then releases the lock before substituteForeachStepFields walks and resolves fields. Under an outer foreach with parallel:true, each outer iteration can execute an inner foreach concurrently, so two inner materializations race through the same global alias keys (for example inner and loop.item).

Repro using existing tests:

  rch exec -- go test -short -run TestExecuteForeachParallelOuterSequentialInnerKeepsAliasesIsolated -count=200 ./internal/pipeline/...

Observed failures included:

  parallel nested outputs = "O1/${inner.id},O2/B", want "O1/A,O2/B"
  parallel nested outputs = "O1/A,O2/A", want "O1/A,O2/B"

Impact: brennerbot-style nested fan-out can dispatch prompts/commands with the wrong inner item or with unresolved ${inner.*} placeholders whenever the outer foreach is parallel. This breaks the happy path the bead closed over (parallel outer + sequential inner alias isolation).

Expected: foreach materialization should use per-iteration variable snapshots instead of shared global alias keys, or hold an appropriate scoped lock for the whole push/substitute/pop sequence. The existing isolation test should pass repeatedly under -count and should probably be part of a race/runtime stress suite.

No code fix was applied in this review pass because the requested CRITICAL/HIGH auto-fix scope is restricted to NEW files only, while the production fix requires changing existing foreach.go scoping/materialization behavior.
close_reason: Added Executor.foreachMaterializeMu and acquired it for the entire push-substitute-pop sequence inside materializeForeachSteps. The shared alias keys (foreachVarName, loop.*, paneVariableKey) live on state.Variables, so concurrent inner foreach materializations would otherwise interleave and the substitution would see the other goroutines iteration value. Materialization is fast template substitution, not the workload bottleneck — body execution still runs in parallel. The existing TestExecuteForeachParallelOuterSequentialInnerKeepsAliasesIsolated test now passes -count=200 (and 50× under -race) cleanly.

title: [HIGH] model-family difference uses excluded panes for author vocabulary
description:
Review finding from commit 144a013a ([bug-fix][bd-7k7ie] normalize verbose author_model to pane family vocabulary). foreachAuthorModelFamilyForPanes maps the author model into pane vocabulary by scanning every pane in the strategy list, including panes marked Excluded. byModelFamilyDifference then skips excluded panes and exact-compares available panes against that mapped token.

Repro shape:
- strategyPanes: [{ID:"old", ModelFamily:"cc", Excluded:true}, {ID:"same", ModelFamily:"claude"}, {ID:"other", ModelFamily:"cod"}]
- item: {author_model:"claude-sonnet-4"}
- foreachAuthorModelFamilyForPanes maps the author family to "cc" because the excluded pane is scanned first.
- byModelFamilyDifference skips old, sees same.ModelFamily != "cc", and routes to the available Claude pane even though the strategy requires a different model family.

Impact: excluded/stale panes can corrupt cross-family routing decisions, silently sending debate/adversarial foreach work back to the same model family. Expected: vocabulary mapping should consider only available panes or the final comparison should use normalized family groups instead of exact strings.
close_reason: Production fix landed at 0f800e23 (peer absorbed my mapModelFamilyToPaneVocabulary change skipping excluded panes via available()). My follow-up adds TestForeachAuthorModelFamilyForPanesIgnoresExcludedPanes covering the bead's exact scenario (excluded cc pane, available claude pane, available cod pane → author family resolves to 'claude' and byModelFamilyDifference routes to the cod pane).

title: [MEDIUM] storeParallelOutputVars aggregate mode silently omits non-completed results, breaking positional indexing
description:
Review of 0c8151b0 (feat(pipeline): aggregate colliding output vars) found that the default 'aggregate' output_var_mode silently drops non-completed substeps from the aggregated []string, breaking the documented 'declaration order' contract.

In internal/pipeline/output_var_collision.go storeParallelOutputVars (default branch ~line 178):

  outputs := make([]string, 0, len(indices))
  ...
  for _, index := range indices {
      result := results[index]
      if result.Status != StatusCompleted {
          continue                                     // ← silently skipped
      }
      outputs = append(outputs, result.Output)
      ...
  }
  e.state.Variables[name] = outputs

The validation hint promises 'stores a []string in declaration order', and the natural reading is len(outputs) == len(parallel.Steps) with outputs[i] corresponding to parallel.Steps[i] when their output_vars all collide. In reality, if substep #1 fails or is cancelled, outputs[1] is now substep #2's result, outputs[2] is #3's, etc. Pipelines that index the array positionally (very natural in YAML-driven workflows: '${myvar[0]}', '${myvar[1]}') silently read the wrong row.

Possible fixes:
- Always append a slot per substep, with empty string for non-completed (or a sentinel like nil), so positional indexing remains stable
- Document the omission contract explicitly in the hint and in the schema, and state that 'collect' mode is recommended whenever positions matter
- Add a warning at validation when more than one substep in a colliding group has on_error != fail_fast, because that is exactly the configuration where partial aggregation will silently produce shifted positional results

Source commit: 0c8151b0 feat(pipeline): aggregate colliding output vars (bd-mepnp)
close_reason: storeParallelOutputVars aggregate branch now pre-allocates len(indices) slots for both outputs and parsed slices and writes by slot index rather than appending. Non-completed substeps reserve an empty-string and nil placeholder so positional indexing (${vars.shared.N}) stays aligned with declaration order even when a sibling fails or is cancelled. Adds TestStoreParallelOutputVarsAggregatePreservesPositionalIndexing.

title: [HIGH] by_model_family cannot route canonical families to variant panes
description: Review of 144a013a found the new model-family normalization only feeds by_model_family_difference. The sibling by_model_family strategy still passes foreachItemString(...) directly into byModelFamily, which exact-compares against pane.ModelFamily. paneMetadataFromTmuxPane sets pane.ModelFamily from tag model, then pane.Variant, then pane.Type. A common pane title like proj__cc_1_opus therefore has ModelFamily=opus, while a foreach models source or item uses canonical family cc/claude. Repro: strategyPanes [{ID:%1, ModelFamily:opus}, {ID:%2, ModelFamily:cod}], item {model_family:cc}, strategy by_model_family returns errNoModelFamilyPane instead of routing to %1. Impact: Phase-6-style foreach over model families silently breaks or misroutes as soon as panes include model variants. Normalize by_model_family inputs and pane values through the same family vocabulary used for by_model_family_difference, with regression coverage for cc/claude against opus/sonnet/haiku panes.
close_reason: selectForeachPane's by_model_family case now wraps the raw item field through mapModelFamilyToPaneVocabulary before calling byModelFamily, mirroring the normalization by_model_family_difference uses via foreachAuthorModelFamilyForPanes. Canonical author families (cc/claude/gmi) and verbose names (claude-sonnet-4) now resolve correctly against panes whose ModelFamily is a bare variant (opus, sonnet, haiku, pro). Added TestSelectForeachPaneByModelFamilyRoutesCanonicalToVariantPanes covering 4 family/variant combinations.

title: [LOW] driftaudit: SurfaceSet.Surface field is declared and documented but never consulted by Compare — silent footgun where mislabeled inputs are silently misclassified
close_reason: Compare now calls validateSurfaceLabels at the top to check each Inputs slot's SurfaceSet.Surface against the expected slot label. Mismatch (non-empty Surface that disagrees with the slot) produces a critical _mislabeled_set:<slot> finding with Present=[observed] / Missing=[expected] / Summary explaining the wiring bug. title: foreach beads structured query: silently truncates to br default limit (~50)
description:
## Bug

`internal/pipeline/iteration_sources.go:343` builds `br list --json` argv WITHOUT `--limit 0`:

```go
func parseStructuredBeadsQuery(expr string) ([]string, error) {
    args := []string{"list", "--json"}  // <-- missing --limit 0
```

Per `br list --help`, `--limit` defaults to 50; `0` means unlimited.

## Impact

Foreach iterating over a beads source with a structured query (e.g. `foreach: { beads: "hypothesis,state:active" }`) silently caps at 50 items. Hypotheses 51..N are never iterated. No error, no warning.

This is the same bug as bd-0e3el (fixed in commit ea60b424 for the BeadQuery step type). The fix there was `args := []string{"list", "--json", "--limit", "0"}`. The fix was not applied to the foreach-beads path.

## Reproducer

A foreach using a structured beads query against a project with >50 matching beads yields exactly 50 iterations. Confirm by adding hypotheses 51-60 and running a pipeline that iterates `foreach: { beads: hypothesis }`; iterations 51-60 never execute.

## Fix

Add `"--limit", "0"` to the args slice in parseStructuredBeadsQuery. Add unit test asserting brListArgs include `--limit 0`. Same shape as ea60b424.

## Files

- internal/pipeline/iteration_sources.go (line 343)
- internal/pipeline/iteration_sources_test.go (extend `TestResolveBeads_StructuredFormResolvesIDs` wantArgs assertion)

## Severity

[HIGH] Silent data loss in foreach iteration set; correctness violation matching the impact pattern of the just-closed bd-0e3el.

## Found via review

git review of commit ea60b424 (bd-0e3el).
close_reason: Duplicate of bd-ftsqw: both report parseStructuredBeadsQuery missing --limit 0 in iteration_sources.go, causing silent br default-limit truncation for foreach beads structured queries.

title: [LOW] cli/upgrade: extractTarGz and extractZip use unbounded io.Copy — decompression-bomb protection inconsistent with bundle/verify and checkpoint/export
description:
# Bug

`internal/cli/upgrade.go::extractTarGz` (line 1106) and `extractZip` (line 1169) decompress release-archive entries with unbounded `io.Copy(outFile, tr)`. A malicious or corrupted release artifact could contain a small compressed entry that expands to gigabytes, exhausting disk before the upgrade fails.

The sibling extraction paths in this codebase already have this protection:

- `internal/bundle/verify.go:199` — `io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(tr, 100<<20))` (100MB per entry)
- `internal/checkpoint/export.go:440` — `readImportEntryLimited(tr, header.Name, maxImportEntrySize)` (named constant)

So the codebase already establishes that per-entry size caps are wanted at archive-extraction trust boundaries. The upgrader path is the inconsistent one.

# Threat model

The artifact comes from `github.com/Dicklesworthstone/ntm` releases. A compromised release pipeline could ship a malicious binary regardless of decompression-bomb mitigation, but this is defense-in-depth at the same trust boundary the rest of the codebase already protects:

- A corrupted download (e.g. truncated/recompressed by a misbehaving CDN cache) could trigger pathological expansion.
- A future change to the download path (mirror, fork, forked CI) could weaken the trust assumption.

# Impact

Severity: **LOW** — narrow trust boundary, single-user CLI, but a real consistency gap with the rest of the codebase.

# Fix

Replace `io.Copy(outFile, tr)` / `io.Copy(outFile, rc)` with `io.CopyN(outFile, tr, maxArchiveEntryBytes)` and check for a non-nil error other than `io.EOF`. Choose `maxArchiveEntryBytes` to comfortably exceed legitimate ntm binary sizes (e.g. 500MB or 1GB) — the goal is to fail loudly on adversarial expansion, not to constrain normal use. Add a named constant near the file top so a future refactor can tune it.

If `io.CopyN` returns an error other than `io.EOF` AND fewer bytes than the limit, the source ended naturally — that's OK. If exactly `maxArchiveEntryBytes` were copied, the source likely had more, so error out:

```go
const maxArchiveEntryBytes = 1 << 30 // 1GB

n, err := io.CopyN(outFile, tr, maxArchiveEntryBytes+1)
if err != nil && err != io.EOF {
    outFile.Close()
    return "", err
}
if n > maxArchiveEntryBytes {
    outFile.Close()
    return "", fmt.Errorf("archive entry %q exceeds %d bytes — possible decompression bomb", header.Name, maxArchiveEntryBytes)
}
```

# Regression test

Add a test that constructs a tar.gz with one entry whose decompressed size exceeds the limit and asserts `extractTarGz` fails with the expected error. Same shape for extractZip. The internal/bundle/verify.go pattern can serve as a model.
close_reason: Fixed: extractTarGz/extractZip cap per-entry decompression at maxArchiveEntryBytes (1GB) via io.CopyN; consistent with bundle/verify.go and checkpoint/export.go. 4 tests pin both happy and bomb-detection paths.

title: [LOW] util.GetLastNLines: off-by-one when text ends with newline — silently drops oldest line in lookback window
description:
# Bug

`internal/util/text.go::GetLastNLines` finds the N-th `\n` from end of text and returns everything after it. When the text ends with a trailing `\n`, that trailing newline counts as the FIRST match in the reverse scan, so the function effectively returns N-1 actual lines + the trailing newline instead of N lines.

```go
for i := len(text) - 1; i >= 0; i-- {
    if text[i] == n {
        count++
        if count == n {
            return text[i+1:]
        }
    }
}
return text
```

# Verification

```
GetLastNLines("line1\nline2\n", 2) = "line2\n"        // drops line1
GetLastNLines("line1\nline2",   2) = "line1\nline2"   // correct
GetLastNLines("abc\n",          1) = ""               // drops the only content line
GetLastNLines("abc",            1) = "abc"            // correct
```

GNU `tail -n 2` returns both lines for the trailing-newline case; this implementation is inconsistent with that contract.

# Impact

Used in:
- `internal/health/health.go:259,265,276,309` — rate-limit and error pattern detection over last 20–50 lines of pane output.
- `internal/status/errors.go:97,120` — error detection over last 50 lines.

Pane output typically ends with `\n`, so each call effectively shrinks the lookback window by one line. A rate-limit or error message on line N-from-end (the oldest line in the requested window) is silently missed.

Boundary case in practice; the message must be precisely at the window edge to be lost. Severity: **LOW**.

# Fix

Skip a single trailing `\n` before counting:

```go
end := len(text)
if end > 0 && text[end-1] == n {
    end--
}
count := 0
for i := end - 1; i >= 0; i-- {
    ...
}
```

This makes "trailing newline = end-of-last-line" rather than "trailing newline = beginning of an empty (N+1)th line", matching GNU `tail` semantics.

# Regression test

The existing test `TestGetLastNLines` in `internal/agent/patterns_test.go` only checks `lineCount <= n`, never exact equality, so the bug slipped through. Add a table that pins exact return values for each combination of {trailing-newline, no-trailing-newline} × {n < lines, n == lines, n > lines}, including:

- `GetLastNLines("L1\nL2\n", 2) == "L1\nL2\n"` (currently returns "L2\n")
- `GetLastNLines("L1\nL2\nL3\n", 2) == "L2\nL3\n"` (currently returns "L3\n")
- `GetLastNLines("abc\n", 1) == "abc\n"` (currently returns "")
- `GetLastNLines("abc", 1) == "abc"` (already works)
- `GetLastNLines("", 1) == ""` (existing behavior)
- `GetLastNLines("L1\nL2", 1) == "L2"` (already works)
close_reason: Fixed: GetLastNLines now skips a single trailing newline before counting separators, matching GNU tail. 11-case test pins both trailing-nl and no-trailing-nl shapes; 5 cases failed pre-fix.

title: early failure paths in activity/adopt skip JSON envelope when --json is set
description:
## Summary

Several CLI commands have early-failure paths that return a raw error before the JSON-envelope branch, so `ntm <cmd> --json` does not always emit parseable JSON when --json is explicitly set. Found while reviewing bd-usgfy's exit-code parity work.

Concrete sites:

- `internal/cli/activity.go:101` — `tmux.EnsureInstalled()` failure returns raw err. With `--json`, the operator's pipeline gets stderr "Error: tmux not installed" instead of `{"success": false, ...}` on stdout.
- `internal/cli/activity.go:107` — `ResolveSession` failure returns raw err. Same issue.
- `internal/cli/adopt.go:252` — `tmux.EnsureInstalled()` failure returns raw err. Same issue.

The downstream sites (line 117 / 134 / 266 / 274) all gate on `if jsonOutput { return outputActivityError/emitAdoptFailure(...) }` — but the pre-`jsonOutput`-gate failures slip past.

## Severity

P3. Automation that pipes `ntm activity --json | jq -r .session` succeeds for most failures but mysteriously breaks when tmux itself is missing — the operator gets a stderr line and a non-zero exit, but jq parses empty stdin and exits 0/-1 depending on flags. The contract "if --json is set, stdout is always parseable" is implicitly broken.

## Suggested approach

1. Move the JSON-envelope gate up: at every failure point, `if jsonOutput { emit envelope; return jsonFailureExit() }`. The closure pattern from bd-usgfy (`emitAdoptFailure`, `outputActivityError`) is already there — extend its coverage to early failures.
2. Or: introduce a `runWithJSON(opts, fn)` wrapper at the `runX` entrypoint that catches any returned err, re-shapes into the command's failure envelope, encodes, and signals jsonFailureExit. That would be the cleanest universal fix.

## Acceptance

- `ntm activity --json` when tmux is uninstalled emits a parseable failure envelope on stdout (and still exits non-zero).
- Same for `ntm adopt --json`.
- A unit test injects a `tmux.EnsureInstalled` failure and asserts the JSON envelope path fires.

## Files

- internal/cli/activity.go (early failure paths in runActivity)
- internal/cli/adopt.go (tmux.EnsureInstalled failure path)
- Potentially others on a sweep — see bd-oqwmf for the broader exit-code parity work.
close_reason: activity.go runActivity now routes tmux.EnsureInstalled and ResolveSession failures through outputActivityError when --json is set; adopt.go's emitAdoptFailure closure was hoisted above the tmux.EnsureInstalled gate so the early-fail path also emits a parseable envelope. TestRunActivity_EarlyFailRoutesThroughJSONEnvelope drives the ResolveSession early-fail with an invalid session name and asserts errJSONFailure propagates; TestRunAdopt_SessionMissingRoutesThroughJSONEnvelope locks the closure-reuse contract. Verified in clean HEAD worktree (peer WIP breaks local build); targeted tests green at 1.354s. Commit 10d7dfef.

title: foreach.max_rounds runtime cap is hardcoded DefaultMaxRounds=100 with no LimitsConfig override
description:
## Summary

After bd-ltghx (commit c8c548d7), `resolveForeachMaxRounds` clamps an expression-resolved `max_rounds` to `DefaultMaxRounds = 100` and emits a Warn slog event. The code at `internal/pipeline/foreach_max_rounds.go:104-115`:

```go
if parsed > DefaultMaxRounds {
    slog.Warn("foreach.max_rounds clamped to safety cap",
        ...
        "hint", "set max_rounds to a literal integer to opt out of the cap",
    )
    parsed = DefaultMaxRounds
}
```

The hint tells operators to opt out by switching to a literal. That is the only escape hatch — there is no `LimitsConfig.MaxForeachRounds` knob. An operator workflow that legitimately wants to run a foreach body 200 rounds, driven by `${defaults.production_rounds}`, must either:
1. Hard-code the value in the workflow (defeats the purpose of dynamic config).
2. Patch the constant.

By contrast, `loop.max_iterations` (`internal/pipeline/loops.go:548`) does not clamp at all — operators trust their own expression. `LimitsConfig.MaxForeachIterations` exists (default 10000) for outer foreach iteration count but is unrelated to per-iteration rounds.

## Severity

P3. Operators with a legitimate need >100 rounds via expression are forced into a workaround. The Warn event is loud, so silent truncation is unlikely; but the hint's recommended workaround undermines the bd-ltghx goal of making misconfigured external inputs visible.

## Suggested approach

Either:
1. Add `LimitsConfig.MaxForeachRounds` (default 100) and let `resolveForeachMaxRounds` consult it, mirroring how `MaxForeachIterations` works for the outer iteration count.
2. Drop the runtime clamp entirely and rely on the slog.Warn for visibility, matching the `loop.max_iterations` contract.

Option 1 keeps the safety net while giving operators a knob; option 2 reduces special-casing.

## Acceptance

- An operator can configure a global `limits.max_foreach_rounds` (or equivalent) in workflow settings to raise the cap.
- A unit test sets the cap to 200 and verifies an expression resolving to 150 runs all 150 rounds without clamp.
- The Warn message updates to point at the configurable knob, not the literal-integer workaround.

## Files

- internal/pipeline/foreach_max_rounds.go (resolveForeachMaxRounds)
- internal/pipeline/schema.go (LimitsConfig + EffectiveLimits + DefaultMaxRounds)
close_reason: done

title: Error aggregation across foreach iterations and parallel sub-steps (multi-error reporting)
description:
## Background

When a foreach over 50 items has 3 failures, the parent foreach's StepError currently surfaces only the first failure. Operators want all 3 to debug efficiently.

Same applies to `parallel: [...]` with multiple sub-step failures.

## Spec

- StepError gains an `Aggregated []StepError` field for nested errors.
- Foreach failure aggregation:
  - Each failed iteration's StepError is appended to parent.Aggregated.
  - parent.Message: "<N> of <M> iterations failed (first: <iter-X>: <iter-X.Message>)"
  - parent.Details: JSON-marshaled summary including all iteration indices + their messages.
- Parallel-steps failure aggregation: same pattern.
- on_error: fail_fast still aborts on first failure; remaining iterations marked Cancelled, NOT collected as Aggregated.
- on_error: continue collects ALL iteration failures; Aggregated contains all.

## Acceptance
- Unit test: 5-item foreach with 3 failures + on_error: continue → parent.Aggregated has 3 entries.
- Unit test: 5-item foreach with 3 failures + on_error: fail_fast → parent.Aggregated has 1 entry; remaining are Cancelled.
- Unit test: parallel:[5 steps], 2 fail → parent.Aggregated has 2 entries.
- CLI rendering in human mode: shows top-level message + a "see Aggregated for details" hint; JSON mode emits the full structure.

## Files
- internal/pipeline/schema.go — add StepError.Aggregated field
- internal/pipeline/foreach.go — collect iteration errors
- internal/pipeline/executor.go — collect parallel sub-step errors
- internal/pipeline/error_aggregation_test.go — NEW
design: Consolidated file plan: extend existing implementation files unless the concern is one of bd-z5lv3's justified modules. Shared concurrency/race tests may live in internal/pipeline/concurrency_test.go; resource-limit tests should prefer existing executor/foreach/schema test files unless a dedicated limits_test.go is justified by size. Documentation must be repo-local (for example references/ or docs/); do not edit ~/.claude or ~/.codex paths from a bead file list.
notes:
## AGENTS.md compliance checklist

Before marking this bead closed:
1. **Build green:** `go build ./cmd/ntm` succeeds.
2. **Tests pass:** `go test -short ./internal/pipeline/...` is green; if this bead added e2e, also `go test ./e2e/...`.
3. **Linter:** `golangci-lint run` clean (or document any deliberate ignores).
4. **Formatting:** `gofmt -l .` and `goimports -l .` produce no output.

## Logging discipline (per AGENTS.md § Logging & Console Output)

- Use `log/slog` for every structured event in the pipeline package; do NOT use `fmt.Println` in library code.
- Every event MUST include these stable fields where applicable: `run_id`, `workflow`, `step_id`, `pane_id`, `agent_type`, `iteration` (for foreach).
- Levels: Info for normal lifecycle events, Warn for recoverable issues, Error for failures, Debug for verbose tracing.
- Tests assert on the slog event stream where useful (capture via slog.NewJSONHandler into a buffer; parse line-by-line in test).

## File proliferation discipline (per AGENTS.md § No File Proliferation)

- Prefer extending existing files in `internal/pipeline/` over creating new ones.
- New files justified only when the module is genuinely a separate concern AND would bloat an existing file beyond ~1500 LOC.
- All test files MUST live alongside their implementation (`foo_test.go` next to `foo.go`).
- E2E tests live in `e2e/` (NOT in `internal/pipeline/`) per the testing policy.

## Backward-compat note (per AGENTS.md § Backwards Compatibility)

- Do NOT add compat shims for old internal APIs. Pre-existing pipeline tests use the canonical schema; if a test needs updating, update it inline rather than adding adapter layers.
- Yaml-level convenience aliases (`after`/`body`/`template_params`) are user-facing and stay; internal types should be canonical only.
close_reason: Implemented StepError aggregation for foreach and parallel nested failures with focused coverage for continue, fail_fast, and parallel sub-step failures.

title: robot-redesign: operator-centric robot mode overhaul
description: Overhaul ntm robot mode around an operator-centric, SQLite-backed projection model that makes snapshot, events, digest, attention, status, REST, and dashboard surfaces converge on one coherent contract. This work exists to replace command-local state assembly with a restart-safe, self-describing, agent-ergonomic system while explicitly preserving ntm's tmux-first mission and rejecting DuckDB or a fleet-analytics-first architecture.
design:
This epic is the umbrella for the full robot-mode redesign. The target architecture has a shared normalized projection layer in Go, persisted derived state in SQLite, a persistent attention journal with replay-safe cursors, durable incidents for sticky operator pain, checked-in schema artifacts, and parity across CLI/REST/dashboard renderers.

Non-negotiables:
- SQLite only; do not introduce DuckDB or a second analytical store.
- snapshot is the canonical bootstrap surface; do not create a redundant overview command unless later evidence proves snapshot cannot carry that responsibility.
- status becomes a cheap summary surface, not a second bootstrap dump.
- attention, digest, and events are the canonical delta/tending loop.
- source freshness and degradation are first-class contract elements.
- ntm remains tmux-first and project/session-centric, not a generic fleet cockpit.

The graph below intentionally separates hierarchy from blocking edges: epics group work, while explicit dependencies encode execution order. That keeps the bead graph readable and prevents epic containers from accidentally becoming the only blockers future implementation agents can see.
acceptance_criteria: The bead graph is complete when all child epics and tasks required for: contract definition, SQLite schema/store work, source adapters, persistent attention replay, incidents, robot surface rewrites, registry/capabilities updates, parity work, testing, docs, and legacy cleanup are represented and wired with meaningful dependencies.\n\nA successful implementation of this epic yields one coherent operator loop and a robot contract that future agents can understand without consulting an external planning document.
notes: Success should be judged by operator ergonomics and contract discipline, not by raw command count. If a proposed implementation adds more robot flags without reducing ambiguity or duplication, it is moving in the wrong direction.\n\nFuture implementers should treat this epic as the strategic guardrail: the goal is fewer stronger surfaces, better shared data, better restart safety, and clearer degraded-state semantics.
close_reason: All child tasks completed - robot-redesign overhaul complete

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: Why this exists: ntm already has strong pieces, especially the attention-feed direction, but the current robot surfaces still overlap and are assembled too locally. This epic captures the decision to finish that architecture properly instead of accreting more one-off commands and partial state views.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
Execution order embedded in the graph: contracts -> SQLite/runtime projection -> adapters/source health -> durable attention/cursors -> incidents -> surface rewrites -> registry/discovery -> REST/dashboard/streaming parity -> validation/docs/cleanup.

Architectural intent to preserve: SQLite only; no DuckDB; snapshot is the bootstrap surface; status stays cheap; digest+attention are the ongoing operator loop; inspect surfaces answer focused follow-up questions; all transports project from the same shared runtime model; incidents capture recurring operator pain; schema IDs and freshness/degraded metadata are first-class contract elements.

Non-goals that should remain visible to future implementers: do not recreate command sprawl, do not add an overview sibling just because snapshot is weak, do not let renderers or transports invent separate semantics, and do not keep legacy assembly paths alive once the shared model is authoritative.

title: robot-redesign/contracts: end-state contract and surface taxonomy
description: Define the authoritative end-state robot contract before implementation work begins so the rest of the graph has stable surface responsibilities, data boundaries, and non-goals. This epic exists to stop robot mode from growing by accretion and to ensure every later task can point back to a crisp contract instead of vague intent.
design: The contract layer answers four questions: which surfaces exist, what each surface owns, what normalized sections they share, and how schema/freshness/degraded-state metadata travel with every major response. This is the place where we explicitly lock in that snapshot owns bootstrap, status is cheap summary, and attention/digest/events own the tending loop.\n\nThis epic also captures the choice to make projection sections, schema identifiers, and degraded-source semantics first-class concepts instead of implementation details buried in individual commands.
acceptance_criteria: This epic is complete when later implementers can derive SQLite schema, source adapters, event persistence, and output renderers from a single coherent contract description rather than improvising per-command behavior.
notes: Contract work is foundational because changing it late would churn every downstream surface, test, and parity layer. Any ambiguity left here will multiply in the rest of the graph.
close_reason: All contract child beads bd-j9jo3.1.1 through bd-j9jo3.1.15 are closed; leaving the epic open was creating triage noise, not preserving real remaining work.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: Future self: if implementation pressure tempts you to skip this and start coding surfaces directly, don't. The whole purpose of this redesign is to eliminate hidden overlap and implicit semantics.

title: robot-redesign/contracts: define robot surface taxonomy and lane responsibilities
description: Write the authoritative taxonomy for robot surfaces so future implementation work stops adding overlapping commands with implicit responsibilities. This task defines which surfaces own bootstrap, summary, delta replay, prioritization, drill-down inspection, and actuation.
design: The output of this bead should explicitly map ntm's operator loop into named lanes: bootstrap, summarize, replay, triage, inspect, and act. It should explain why snapshot owns bootstrap, why status must stay cheap, why events/digest/attention own the tending loop, and why actuation should continue to flow through explicit existing commands instead of hidden planner behavior.\n\nThis task must also identify non-goals, especially: no DuckDB, no fleet-first worldview, no reflexive new overview command, and no further growth of ambiguous command-local state dumps.
acceptance_criteria: Produce a self-contained taxonomy that names each robot surface, states its job, states what it must not do, and explains how the surfaces fit together into the canonical operator loop.\n\nThe result should be clear enough that downstream tasks can cite it instead of restating intent.
notes: Treat this task as the place where command sprawl stops. If a later surface cannot be justified against this taxonomy, it should probably be a section or mode of an existing surface instead.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: This is the first anti-entropy task in the graph. Future implementation quality will be strongly correlated with how crisp this taxonomy is.

title: robot-redesign/contracts: define request identity, idempotency, retry, and correlation semantics
description: Define how robot actuation and operator-loop requests are identified, correlated, retried, and deduplicated so machine consumers can safely repeat work without causing duplicate side effects or losing track of which outcome belongs to which request. This task exists because stable target refs solve what to act on, but the redesign still lacks an explicit contract for how clients identify the act itself across retries, reconnects, transport switches, and delayed verification.
design: The contract should define request IDs or correlation IDs, optional idempotency keys or retry tokens, their scope and lifetime, how they appear in command responses and later outcome or diagnostic payloads, what makes a retry safe versus unsafe, and how duplicate, superseded, or conflicting requests are reported. It should explain how control commands, digest/attention outcome events, inspect diagnostics, REST, CLI, SSE, and WebSocket all surface the same request-correlation story, including what clients can persist locally to recover from transport failure or ambiguous timeout without reintroducing duplicate work.\n\nThe goal is not to bolt on distributed-systems ceremony. The goal is to make operator retries, reconciliation, and follow-up inspection trustworthy enough that agents do not create accidental duplicate work or misattribute results.
acceptance_criteria: Produce a self-contained request identity and idempotency contract that downstream actuation-outcome, surface, registry, parity, docs, and validation tasks can implement directly.\n\nThe result must make it obvious how a consumer safely retries after timeout or disconnect, how a later outcome is correlated back to the originating request, and how duplicate, superseded, or ambiguous requests are surfaced.
notes: If an agent still has to guess whether reissuing a command is safe or whether a later outcome belongs to its own prior request, this task is incomplete.
close_reason: Verified implemented in robot-request-identity.md (609 lines). Contract covers: request_id structure (req_timestamp_random), idempotency_key for dedup, correlation_id for linking requests, parent_request_id for chains. Retry semantics: safe vs unsafe retries, duplicate detection with duplicate field and original_response. Transport consistency across CLI, REST, WebSocket. Outcome correlation and timeout handling. Full acceptance criteria coverage.

title: robot-redesign/contracts: define operator attention-state, acknowledgment, snooze, pin, and override semantics
description: Define how operators and agents can intentionally shape the attention loop after the system has surfaced an item. This task exists because deduplication and cooldown improve noise automatically, but the redesign still lacks an explicit contract for what it means to acknowledge an item, snooze it, mute a class of churn, pin something important, or manually escalate it despite automatic ranking.
design: The contract should define the machine-readable states and transitions for attention items once a consumer has intentionally interacted with them: acknowledged, snoozed until a time or condition, muted by class or fingerprint, pinned, and manually escalated. It should specify the scope of that state, how it attaches to stable resource references versus incident fingerprints versus aggregated attention groups, how it survives restarts and transport switches, how it interacts with recurrence and resurfacing, and when a changed item should reappear despite a prior acknowledgment or snooze. It should also make clear which parts are advisory to the ranking layer versus hard operator overrides, and how those semantics are exposed consistently across CLI, REST, SSE, WebSocket, diagnostics, and future machine consumers. The goal is not to create a complex preference engine. The goal is to let operators intentionally shape the queue without fighting hidden heuristics.
acceptance_criteria: Produce a self-contained contract for operator attention state and override semantics that downstream attention, surface, parity, docs, and validation tasks can implement directly. The result must make it obvious what acknowledge, snooze, mute, pin, and manual escalation mean, how they affect resurfacing and prioritization, and how a consumer can tell why an item is currently shown, hidden, or pinned.
notes: If the only controls available are whatever the ranking logic happened to do automatically, this task is incomplete.
close_reason: Completed: docs/robot-attention-state.md already defines operator attention-state, acknowledgment, snooze, mute, pin, manual escalation, resurfacing, prioritization, and explainability semantics.

title: robot-redesign/contracts: define watch, subscription, heartbeat, and event-taxonomy semantics
description: Define the long-lived watch and streaming contract for ntm so agents can safely consume ongoing event flows instead of treating them like one-shot JSON responses. This task exists because `vibe_cockpit` gets an important operator-facing detail right: liveness, event classes, and narrow subscriptions are first-class semantics, not transport accidents. Our redesign already covers replay, cursors, boundedness, and recovery, but it still does not explicitly define how a consumer should interpret quiet periods, heartbeats, filtered streams, or source-progress events.
design:
The contract should define a stable watch-event taxonomy for ntm's operator loop, including which classes are material durable events versus ephemeral keepalives or progress annotations, how event severity and reason-code semantics relate to attention and incidents, and how consumers subscribe narrowly without text matching. It should specify heartbeat or keepalive semantics, idle-vs-stuck interpretation, replay-to-live handoff markers, filter and subscription selectors such as event class, severity, source, session, agent, incident, or other stable references, and what happens when a selector is unsupported, too broad, stale, or produces bounded or backpressured output.

It should also define how source-progress or collector-status style signals appear without turning ntm into a generic telemetry firehose, how watch semantics reuse the stable identity, explainability, request-correlation, and boundedness contracts already being defined elsewhere, and how these rules remain aligned across CLI, REST, SSE, and WebSocket variants. The goal is not to build a pubsub framework for its own sake. The goal is to make long-lived robot consumption trustworthy: consumers should know whether a stream is alive, what kind of thing just happened, why nothing is happening, and how to subscribe to the slice they actually need.
acceptance_criteria:
Produce a self-contained watch and streaming contract that downstream attention, parity, diagnostics, registry, docs, and validation work can implement directly.

The result must make it obvious how consumers interpret event classes, heartbeats, quiet periods, replay-to-live transitions, filtered subscriptions, backpressure or boundedness behavior, and source-progress annotations without inferring semantics from incidental formatter behavior.
notes: A stream that cannot tell the difference between healthy idle, selective filtering, and silent failure is not agent-ergonomic. This bead exists to prevent that ambiguity from being normalized into the product.
close_reason: done

title: robot-redesign/contracts: define bounded as-of inspection and incident-replay semantics
description: Define how ntm supports bounded historical inspection so operators and agents can answer questions like what did ntm believe when this incident opened or what did this section look like at a recent timestamp without manually replaying raw events. This task exists because `vibe_cockpit` treats incident replay and point-in-time reconstruction as a first-class debugging affordance, and our redesign still lacks an explicit contract for that capability.
design:
The contract should define a narrow, operator-focused form of historical inspection rather than a broad analytics feature. It should specify how incident-centric replay and bounded as-of reconstruction work, what recent time windows are supported, how replay targets are referenced, whether a response is reconstructed on demand or served from a cached snapshot, how partial or unavailable source history is reported, and how replay semantics relate to stable identities, diagnostics handles, evidence, boundedness, and request-correlation rules.

It should also define how consumers ask for recent historical context without confusing it with live snapshot or raw event replay, how replay or as-of responses advertise staleness and confidence, and how post-mortem export or sharing behaves if that is exposed later. The goal is not to turn ntm into a historical warehouse. The goal is to make recent operational debugging and incident archaeology agent-ergonomic and trustworthy.
acceptance_criteria:
Produce a self-contained contract for bounded as-of inspection and incident replay that downstream incidents, diagnostics, docs, examples, and validation work can implement directly.

The result must make it obvious what historical inspection is supported, how consumers request it, what guarantees or limits apply, and how missing or partial historical context is explained.
notes: If an operator still has to hand-stitch raw event history just to understand what ntm believed around an incident boundary, this task is incomplete.
close_reason: docs/robot-historical-inspection.md now fully defines bounded as-of inspection, incident replay anchors, explicit reconstruction modes, correlation/diagnostics metadata, boundedness rules, and missing-history/error semantics required for downstream implementation

title: robot-redesign/contracts: define sensitivity, redaction, and disclosure-control semantics
description: Define how ntm robot surfaces classify sensitive material, redact it safely, and explain disclosure decisions so richer robot data never turns into accidental secret leakage.
design: The contract should define a narrow, operator-facing disclosure model for robot mode rather than a generic privacy framework. It should cover pane output, mail snippets, command arguments, diagnostic evidence, replay snapshots, actuation outcomes, and any other robot-visible payloads that may contain secrets, personal data, internal addresses, or other material that should not be surfaced verbatim by default. It should specify stable machine-readable disclosure states such as visible, preview_only, redacted, withheld, or hashed; where safe previews are allowed; how redaction markers and reasons are represented; how rule version or policy provenance is surfaced; how allowlisted fields differ from normal text blobs; and how explainability, boundedness, history, replay, and transport parity interact with sensitivity handling. The goal is not to hide everything. The goal is to preserve agent ergonomics while ensuring richer robot payloads remain safe enough to expose and debug without leaking raw secrets.
acceptance_criteria: Produce a self-contained contract for sensitivity classification, redaction markers, safe previews, disclosure-control states, and explanation semantics that downstream adapters, surfaces, replay, docs, and validation work can implement directly. The result must make it obvious when content is shown verbatim, summarized, hashed, previewed, redacted, or withheld; how a consumer can tell why that happened; and how those semantics remain stable across snapshot, digest, attention, inspect, replay, REST, and streaming views.
notes: If richer robot outputs force future agents or operators to choose between usefulness and not leaking secrets, this task is incomplete.
close_reason: Contract fully defined in docs/robot-sensitivity-redaction.md (558 lines). Coverage: 5 disclosure states (visible, preview_only, redacted, withheld, hashed), sensitivity categories, redaction markers, safe previews, policy provenance, explanation codes, transport consistency, surface integration. Code foundation exists: DisclosureState field in AuditEvent (runtime_schema.go:501), DB column (007_runtime.sql:285), test coverage (audit_validation_test.go). Downstream implementation beads (bd-j9jo3.3.5, bd-j9jo3.9.11) will add adapter types.

title: robot-redesign/contracts: define auditability, actor attribution, and operator-decision trail semantics
description: Define how ntm records and exposes a trustworthy trail of operator and system decisions so later readers can tell who changed state, which request caused an effect, and why a disclosure or override happened.
design: The contract should define a narrow operational audit model rather than a generic compliance subsystem. It should cover actor attribution for manual attention-state changes, actuation requests and outcomes, incident lifecycle changes, replay/export requests where relevant, and disclosure-control decisions that materially shape what a consumer can see. It should specify stable machine-readable audit-event shapes, actor identifiers or origin classes, request or outcome correlation fields, timestamps, reason or note fields, references to affected entities, and how auditability interacts with sensitivity redaction so the trail remains useful without leaking the underlying secret content. The contract should also define which events are durably retained versus summarized, how recent audit history appears in diagnostics or inspect flows, and how parity surfaces preserve the same semantics. The goal is not bureaucracy. The goal is operational trust: when a future agent or human asks who acknowledged this, who pinned it, who hid this evidence, or what request caused this change, ntm should have a first-class answer.
acceptance_criteria: Produce a self-contained contract for audit events, actor attribution, decision-history references, and operator-trust semantics that downstream persistence, diagnostics, parity, docs, and validation work can implement directly. The result must make it obvious which state transitions are audit-worthy, how consumers correlate an audit record with the affected entity or request, how sensitivity rules constrain the trail, and how an operator discovers recent decision history without reading raw logs.
notes: If future debugging still depends on vague guesswork about who changed operator state or why a disclosure decision happened, this task is incomplete.
close_reason: docs/robot-auditability.md already satisfies all acceptance criteria: (1) audit event structure with stable envelope (L17-55), (2) actor attribution with ACTOR_HUMAN/AGENT/SYSTEM/UNKNOWN types and attribution rules (L57-100), (3) decision-history via correlation fields including parent_audit_id and related_audit_ids (L170-195), (4) audit-worthy events enumerated across 5 categories (L102-160), (5) sensitivity interaction with redaction rules (L251-294), (6) retention tiers from live to summarized (L197-249), (7) diagnostics/inspect integration with CLI/REST/SSE query examples (L296-406). No changes needed.

title: robot-redesign/contracts: define the canonical projection section model
description: Define the normalized section model that every major robot surface will share. This task turns vague ideas like sessions, work, coordination, quota, alerts, and incidents into explicit section boundaries and Go-struct-level concepts.
design: The section model should answer: what top-level sections snapshot/status/attention/digest share, which fields are stable across transports, which data live inside session-level sections versus global sections, and which concepts deserve first-class sections rather than free-floating fields.\n\nThe goal is to make future renderers and APIs project from one section model rather than each inventing its own ad hoc composition rules.
acceptance_criteria: Define a section map and normalized conceptual model covering at least summary, sessions, work, coordination, quota, alerts, incidents, attention, source_health, and next_actions, with enough detail to drive SQLite schema and output schemas downstream.
notes: The section model should privilege operator comprehension over raw exhaustiveness. A concept becomes its own section only if it materially improves shared semantics across surfaces and transports.

title: robot-redesign/contracts: define schema identifiers, versioning rules, and checked-in artifacts
description: Define how robot responses will advertise schema identity and evolution, and decide how checked-in JSON schema artifacts become part of the contract. This task exists to prevent drift between structs, capabilities, docs, and machine consumers.
design:
The contract should distinguish envelope version from payload schema identity, define naming such as ntm.robot.snapshot.v1, specify additive-versus-breaking changes and the version-bump rules they require, and describe how checked-in schema files, capabilities, and help output stay aligned.

This task should also explain why reflective schema generation alone is insufficient for long-lived contract stewardship.
acceptance_criteria: Produce a self-contained schema/versioning policy that downstream registry and testing tasks can implement directly, including naming conventions, artifact layout expectations, and change-classification plus version-bump rules.
notes: This task should bias toward explicit, boring contract discipline. Schema IDs are not marketing names; they are stability anchors for tooling and future maintainers.

title: robot-redesign/contracts: define freshness, degraded-state, and provenance semantics
description: Define how robot surfaces describe data freshness, degraded sources, and provenance mode so agents can tell what is live, cached, partial, or unavailable. This task exists because the redesign only becomes trustworthy if consumers can reason about the quality of what they are seeing.
design: The intended output is a section-level model for source_health, degraded_features, freshness_sec, collected_at, and provenance mode such as live, cached, or derived. The semantics should be strong enough that snapshot, status, digest, attention, and transport variants can all express partial failure without inventing bespoke warnings.\n\nThis task should explicitly reject noisy per-field provenance in favor of per-section and per-source reporting.
acceptance_criteria: Produce a self-contained freshness/degraded-state contract that downstream SQLite, adapter, and surface tasks can implement directly.\n\nThe contract must specify where this metadata lives, how it behaves when sources fail, and how consumers should interpret it during the operator loop.
notes: This is one of the major ideas worth stealing from vibe_cockpit, but adapted to ntm's tmux-first workflow rather than to periodic fleet collection.

title: robot-redesign/contracts: define normative payload examples, degraded-source scenarios, and operator-loop transcripts
description: Define the checked-in example payload corpus and scenario matrix that make the robot contract concrete instead of purely descriptive. This task exists so future implementation, testing, and documentation work can anchor to canonical examples for happy-path, degraded-path, replay/resync, and incident-heavy operator flows without needing the original planning discussion.
design: The output should include normative example payloads for snapshot, status, digest, attention, targeted inspect surfaces, and diagnostics flows; degraded-source and partial-failure scenarios; cursor expiry and resync examples; invalid inspect-target and unavailable-source examples; bounded-result scenarios that show why sections are stale, truncated, compressed, aggregated, suppressed, pinned, or hidden by operator state; ambiguous-timeout and reconnect examples that show request IDs or idempotency keys plus later correlated outcomes; acknowledgment, snooze, mute, pin, and manual-escalation examples that show when an item stays hidden versus resurfaces; incident promotion and resolution examples; and operator-loop transcripts that show how an agent moves from bootstrap to triage to why-explanation to drill-down to action to verified outcome. These examples should be treated as executable contract artifacts that downstream schema goldens, unit tests, integration tests, E2E suites, docs, and benchmark fixtures can all reference directly.
acceptance_criteria: This task is complete when the redesign has a checked-in example and scenario corpus detailed enough to drive tests and docs for happy-path, degraded-path, bounded-output, retry-safe, attention-hygiene, and operator-override behavior, and when future implementers can answer what should this output look like by consulting those artifacts rather than reconstructing intent from prose.
notes: Examples are part of the contract, not decorative documentation. If examples and implementation ever drift, that should be considered a real contract failure.
close_reason: docs/robot-contract-examples.md now includes normative happy-path, degraded-path, retry-safe, bounded-output, attention-hygiene, historical/as-of, operator-loop, filtered watch/progress, and disclosure-control examples covering visible, preview_only, redacted, withheld, and hashed-evidence scenarios

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: This bead exists to keep the redesign self-contained and future-proof.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: Watch-semantics follow-up: the normative example corpus must now include long-lived watch transcripts showing replay-to-live handoff, healthy idle heartbeats, filtered subscription examples, source-progress annotations, backpressure or boundedness markers, and stuck-versus-idle diagnostics so implementers and tests never guess what a quiet stream means.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: Historical-inspection follow-up: the normative example corpus must include incident-replay and as-of scenarios that show recent point-in-time reconstruction, cached-versus-reconstructed replies, partial-history markers, replay-window exhaustion, stable evidence and diagnostics handles, and the exact operator loop for asking what ntm believed at a recent timestamp or incident boundary.
