title: [MEDIUM] foreach.max_rounds lacks parse validation; negative/zero silently default to 1
description:
## Severity: [MEDIUM]

Commit 20dfc963 added `foreach.max_rounds` (bd-2ubxp.14) but did not add the corresponding parser validation that already exists for `loop.max_iterations`.

## Existing validation for loop (parser.go:652)

```go
if step.Loop.MaxIterations.Value < 0 {
    result.addError(ParseError{
        Field:   stepField + ".loop.max_iterations",
        Message: "max_iterations cannot be negative",
    })
}
```

## Missing for foreach.max_rounds

`grep -rn MaxRounds internal/pipeline/parser.go internal/pipeline/validation.go` returns nothing. The runtime resolver silently treats invalid values:

```go
// foreach_max_rounds.go
if mr.Expr == "" && mr.Value <= 0 {
    return 1, nil   // silently defaults to single round
}
```

This means:
- `max_rounds: 0` → 1 round (the user-typed zero is invisible)
- `max_rounds: -5` → 1 round (no error surfaced)
- `max_rounds: 1000000` → 1M rounds (no upper cap; loops with max_iterations have DefaultMaxIterations = 100)

## Why this matters

1. Footgun: an author who types `max_rounds: 0` expects "no rounds"; gets one round and no diagnostic. Compare to `loop.max_iterations: 0` which surfaces a parse error today.
2. Resource exhaustion: there is no analogue to `DefaultMaxIterations = 100` for max_rounds. A misconfigured workflow with `max_rounds: ${vars.from_external}` resolving to a huge number runs unbounded.
3. Inconsistency: foreach loops are the closer cousin of for-loops; their per-iteration cap should follow the same validation contract as while/until loops.

## Fix sketch

In parser.go alongside the existing loop validation:

```go
for _, fc := range []*ForeachConfig{step.Foreach, step.ForeachPane} {
    if fc == nil { continue }
    if fc.MaxRounds.Expr == "" && fc.MaxRounds.Value < 0 {
        result.addError(ParseError{
            Field:   stepField + ".foreach.max_rounds",
            Message: "max_rounds cannot be negative",
        })
    }
}
```

Plus an upper-bound cap in resolveForeachMaxRounds (for both literal and expression forms). Pick a sensible default — e.g., a new `DefaultMaxRounds = 100` constant — and clamp with a slog.Warn when exceeded so misuse is loud rather than silent.

## Acceptance

- Workflow with `max_rounds: -1` fails parse with a clear error pointing at the field.
- Workflow with `max_rounds: 0` either fails parse or surfaces a slog.Warn at runtime so the author knows they are not getting iterated rounds.
- A configurable upper cap exists (parity with DefaultMaxIterations for loops).

## Files
- internal/pipeline/parser.go (add validation)
- internal/pipeline/foreach_max_rounds.go (add cap)
- internal/pipeline/foreach_max_rounds_test.go (negative/zero/over-cap cases)
close_reason: Fix landed in c8c548d7: parser.go now rejects negative literal max_rounds with a clear ParseError pointing at the field (mirrors loop.max_iterations validation). Added DefaultMaxRounds=100 in schema.go. resolveForeachMaxRounds clamps expression-resolved values above the cap with a Warn slog event so misuse is loud. Zero is left alone because IntOrExpr has no IsSet flag (default value indistinguishable from explicit). Two new tests: TestForeachMaxRounds_NegativeLiteralRejectedAtParse and TestForeachMaxRounds_ExprResolvedAboveCapClampsToDefault.

title: bd-ypo73 sibling: resolveBranch + resolveItems + on_failure recovery still use non-ctx substitute, drop foreach max_rounds round overlay
description:
## Summary

bd-ypo73 (4f60e1f4) closed the loop-dispatcher gap in bd-2ubxp.20's ctx-threading migration: `executeStep`'s when condition, `loop.while`, and `loopControlAppliesForStep` all switched to `evaluateConditionCtx`. A grep for the remaining non-ctx `substituteVariables` / `substituteVariablesStrict` callers turns up three more sites in production code paths that can run inside a foreach max_rounds body and silently drop the round overlay:

### Site 1: `internal/pipeline/control_flow.go:21` — `resolveBranch`

```go
func (e *Executor) resolveBranch(ctx context.Context, step *Step) (string, error) {
    expr := e.substituteVariables(step.Branch)
    ...
}
```

`step.Branch` substitution discards `ctx`. A workflow author who writes:

```yaml
foreach:
  items: ["x"]
  max_rounds: 3
  steps:
    - id: route_by_round
      branch: "round_${round}"
      branches:
        round_1: { ... }
        round_2: { ... }
        round_3: { ... }
```

…cannot resolve `${round}` against the round overlay attached to ctx by `withRoundOverrides`. The substitution falls back to `state.Variables["round"]` (which post-bd-2ubxp.20 is no longer populated) and surfaces "round not set: foreach max_rounds binding only available inside an iteration body".

### Site 2: `internal/pipeline/loops.go:739` — `resolveItems`

```go
func (le *LoopExecutor) resolveItems(expr string) ([]interface{}, error) {
    resolved := le.executor.substituteVariables(expr)
    ...
}
```

`resolveItems` is called from `executeForEach` (line 100) which already has `ctx`. A loop nested inside a max_rounds body whose `loop.items` references `${round}` (e.g. `${vars.batches_${round}}`) cannot resolve. Less common than the branch case but mechanically the same gap.

### Site 3: `internal/pipeline/control_flow.go:521, 535, 568, 603` — `recoveryStepFromFallback` + `recoveryPaneSpec` + `recoveryParams`

```go
template = e.substituteVariables(template)
wait = WaitCondition(e.substituteVariables(rawWait))
resolved := strings.TrimSpace(e.substituteVariables(v))
return e.substituteVariables(v)
```

`executeOnFailureRecovery` (control_flow.go:248) takes `ctx` and dispatches a recovery template; the recovery step's pane/template/params/wait substitutions all run through the non-ctx variant. If the failing step lives in a max_rounds body and its on_failure recovery template references `${round}` (e.g. for round-tagged audit logs), the round overlay is dropped.

## Severity

P3. Same severity as bd-ypo73 — these are siblings of the same migration gap. Real-world impact is bounded by how often branch/loop.items/on_failure references reach `${round}`, but the silent failure mode (substitution error far from the foreach declaration) is hard to debug.

## Suggested approach

Each site has access to a `ctx context.Context` already. Switch each call to `e.substituteVariablesStrictCtx(ctx, …)` (or capture and discard the err if the historical contract was lossy):

1. `resolveBranch` already takes ctx — wire it.
2. `resolveItems` — change signature to accept ctx, update the single caller.
3. Recovery helpers (`recoveryStepFromFallback`, `recoveryPaneSpec`, `recoveryParams`) — thread ctx from `executeOnFailureRecovery` (line 248) down into each helper.

Same audit pattern bd-ypo73 used: `grep -n 'substituteVariables\b' internal/pipeline/*.go internal/pipeline/control_flow.go | grep -v _test.go | grep -v 'Ctx\b'` should be empty for any line whose enclosing function holds a `ctx context.Context` parameter and dispatches body steps.

## Acceptance

- A regression test mirroring `TestForeachMaxRounds_NestedLoopWhenResolvesRoundOverlay` (4f60e1f4) for each site:
  - Branch case: foreach max_rounds=2, body has `branch: "round_${round}"` with branches keyed `round_1` / `round_2`; assert each round routes correctly.
  - resolveItems case: foreach max_rounds=2, body has `loop` with `items: "${vars.items_${round}}"` and asserts each round's loop iterates the round-specific list.
  - Recovery case: foreach max_rounds=2, body's failing command triggers an on_failure recovery whose template references `${round}`; assert the recovery substitution succeeds.
- Audit pattern above shows no remaining gap.

## Files

- internal/pipeline/control_flow.go (resolveBranch, recoveryStepFromFallback, recoveryPaneSpec, recoveryParams)
- internal/pipeline/loops.go (resolveItems + executeForEach call site)

## Related

- bd-ypo73 (4f60e1f4) — original migration sweep; this is the parity follow-up.
- bd-2ubxp.20 (5edbb6e6) — root of the ctx-overlay migration.
close_reason: Threaded ctx through resolveBranch (control_flow.go:24→substituteVariablesCtx), resolveItems (loops.go:745 ctx parameter + SetLocalOverrides on the manual Substitutor), and the on_failure recovery chain (recoveryStepFromFallback + recoveryPaneSpec + recoveryParams + recoveryParamValue all gain ctx and use substituteVariablesCtx). Added substituteVariablesCtx as the non-strict ctx wrapper around substituteVariablesStrictCtx. Regression TestForeachMaxRounds_BranchPredicateResolvesRoundOverlay constructs max_rounds=3 + branch on '${round}' + three keyed branches and asserts no 'round not set' errors. Pipeline -race -short green. Commit 098e7141.

title: [CRITICAL] scheduler queue Enqueue update-existing-ID path drifts stats.ByPriority/ByType + sessionCounts/batchCounts
description:
## Bug

`internal/scheduler/queue.go::Enqueue` (line 74-101) handles a same-ID re-enqueue by calling `updateJobLocked` and returning early at line 78-82:

\`\`\`go
if _, exists := q.byID[job.ID]; exists {
    q.updateJobLocked(job)
    return  // <-- skips ALL counter updates
}
\`\`\`

`updateJobLocked` only replaces the heap entry and refreshes `byID`. It does NOT adjust:

- `q.stats.ByPriority[old]` / `[new]`
- `q.stats.ByType[old]` / `[new]`
- `q.sessionCounts[old SessionName]` / `[new]`
- `q.batchCounts[old BatchID]` / `[new]`

If the updated job has a different Priority, Type, SessionName, or BatchID than the original, every one of those tracking maps drifts.

This is the same family as bd-o35sn (Stats() drift on Dequeue/Cancel) and bd-s8sex (cross-axis drift on Cancel), but for the Update path.

## Confirmed repro

\`\`\`
job1: ID="j1", Priority=Normal
q.Enqueue(job1)
job1updated: ID="j1", Priority=Urgent  // same ID, Priority changed
q.Enqueue(job1updated)
stats := q.Stats()
// ACTUAL: stats.ByPriority = {Normal: 1}    ← drift
// EXPECTED: stats.ByPriority = {Urgent: 1}
\`\`\`

This is exercised by an EXISTING test (`pure_test.go:625` — `Enqueue same ID with different priority should update`) that checks the heap is updated but does NOT check the stats map. The heap order updates correctly via `heap.Fix`; only the stats are wrong.

## Fix shape

Inside `updateJobLocked` (or in Enqueue before calling it), capture the OLD job's indexed fields, then after the swap decrement the old buckets and increment the new ones — same delete-when-zero pattern the bd-o35sn/bd-s8sex fixes use elsewhere.

\`\`\`go
old, exists := q.byID[job.ID]
if exists {
    // decrement old, then update, then increment new
    q.stats.ByPriority[old.Priority]--
    if q.stats.ByPriority[old.Priority] <= 0 {
        delete(q.stats.ByPriority, old.Priority)
    }
    // ... same for ByType, sessionCounts, batchCounts
    q.updateJobLocked(job)
    q.stats.ByPriority[job.Priority]++
    q.stats.ByType[job.Type]++
    q.sessionCounts[job.SessionName]++
    if job.BatchID != "" {
        q.batchCounts[job.BatchID]++
    }
    return
}
\`\`\`

## Regression test

A new test that re-enqueues a job with changed Priority and asserts:
- `Stats().ByPriority[old]` is gone (deleted when zero) or 0
- `Stats().ByPriority[new]` is 1
- Same shape for ByType / SessionName / BatchID changes
- `CurrentSize` stays 1
- `TotalEnqueued` stays 1 (this is the same job, not a new one)
close_reason: Fixed in internal/scheduler/queue.go::Enqueue: when re-enqueuing an existing job ID, capture the old job's Priority/Type/SessionName/BatchID and re-bucket all four tracking maps (stats.ByPriority, stats.ByType, sessionCounts, batchCounts) using the same delete-when-zero discipline as the bd-o35sn / bd-s8sex fixes. Pre-fix, the early-return through updateJobLocked skipped every counter update, so Stats() reported the wrong distribution and CountBySession/CountByBatch returned phantom counts whenever an indexed field changed across the update. Regression test TestJobQueue_Enqueue_Update_RebucketsStats covers priority/type/session/batch field changes and the no-change-update happy path; verified 4 of 5 sub-tests fail pre-fix and all pass post-fix.

title: ntm pipeline run --start-from=<step-id> (resume from arbitrary step for iteration)
description:
## Background

Authoring a 30-step pipeline + iterating: a syntax error at step 28 means the operator re-runs steps 1-27 every time. Slow. Need a way to start from a specific step.

Distinct from Resume (which continues a previous run); --start-from begins a NEW run that simulates state for prior steps.

## Spec

### CLI

`ntm pipeline run <file> --start-from=<step-id> [--from-state=<run-id>]`

Behavior:
- Without `--from-state`: skip step IDs that come dependency-wise BEFORE step-id; their state.Steps[] entries are populated with synthetic Status=Skipped + SkipReason="--start-from skipped".
- With `--from-state=<prior-run-id>`: load prior state's outputs for skipped steps so `${steps.X.output}` references work.

### Validation

- Refuse if `<step-id>` is inside a foreach/parallel/loop body (would orphan iterations). Operator must start from the parent step.
- Surface clear error for unknown step IDs.

### Skip transitivity

If --start-from=phase_4_loop and phase_4_loop depends on phase_3_complete_flag, phase_3_complete_flag is skipped (not run). Same for transitive deps. Document this clearly.

## Acceptance

- Unit test: --start-from=step3 in a 5-step linear pipeline → steps 1, 2 are Skipped; 3, 4, 5 run.
- Unit test: --from-state with prior outputs → step 3 can reference ${steps.step1.output}.
- Unit test: --start-from inside foreach body → clear error, won't run.

## Files
- internal/cli/pipeline.go — flag parsing
- internal/pipeline/executor.go — start-from logic in Run() init
- internal/pipeline/start_from_test.go — NEW (or extend executor_test.go)

- Use `log/slog` for every structured event in the pipeline package; do NOT use `fmt.Println` in library code.
- Every event MUST include these stable fields where applicable: `run_id`, `workflow`, `step_id`, `pane_id`, `agent_type`, `iteration` (for foreach).
- Levels: Info for normal lifecycle events, Warn for recoverable issues, Error for failures, Debug for verbose tracing.

title: [HIGH] nested body dependencies can be satisfied before their parent runs
description: Review of 7304d410 found that executeWorkflow now auto-marks any ready nested step as executed instead of running it, but DependencyGraph still registers parallel/loop body step IDs as ordinary graph nodes with no implicit dependency on their parent container. That means a top-level step can depend_on a nested body step ID and become unblocked before the parent loop/parallel step has executed the body at all. Repro shape: step prep; step group depends_on prep and contains loop/parallel body step inner; top-level step after depends_on inner. At startup, inner is ready independently of group, so executeWorkflow marks inner executed, then after can become ready and run before group executes. Even when group later runs, after may have already consumed missing or stale steps.inner.output. Expected: nested body IDs should not satisfy top-level dependencies independently; either reject top-level depends_on references to nested body steps, or add implicit graph edges so nested body nodes cannot be marked executed before their parent container runs and stores the actual result. Impact: resume/control-flow graphs can silently run downstream steps out of order and with missing/stale nested outputs. The production fix requires dependency graph/schema changes, so no code fix is applied under the review-only NEW-file fix restriction.
close_reason: DependencyGraph now tracks each step container parent at construction (parallel/loop bodies). Validate emits a new nested_body_dep error when an edge crosses container boundaries except for the always-allowed targets: top-level steps and same-container siblings. Operators get a clear diagnostic naming the misrouted nested step plus its container. Three regression tests cover the rejection, sibling allow, and nested-on-top-level allow paths.

title: output_var collision policy in parallel + foreach (aggregate / last / collect modes)
description:
## Background

If a foreach with parallel:true has 100 iterations, each writing to `output_var: result`, the workflow.Variables[result] map entry is concurrently written. Last writer wins is racy AND probably not what the author intended.

Same issue for parallel:[step1, step2] where both have `output_var: result`.

## Spec

Two modes; configurable per-step (default = aggregate):

### Mode: aggregate (default)
- output_var inside foreach captures a SLICE of per-iteration outputs (in iteration order).
- workflow.Variables[result] = []string{iter0_output, iter1_output, ...}
- Authors who want a specific iteration's output use `${steps.<step-id>.iter.<N>.output}`.

### Mode: last
- output_var captures the LAST iteration's output (current Phase A semantics for sequential foreach).
- For parallel, "last" means "last by completion time" — explicitly racy; require opt-in via `output_var_mode: last`.

### Mode: collect
- Foreach option `output_var_mode: collect` populates a structured map `{[iter.id]: output}` keyed by item.id when iterating beads / pairs / debates.

### Validator rule
- output_var on a step inside `parallel:[]` (the inline parallel-list form, not parallel:true on a foreach) — the inner step's output_var collides with siblings if same name. Validator emits warning suggesting per-step output_var.

## Acceptance

- Unit test: foreach over 5 items each emitting "iter-N" → output_var holds ["iter-0","iter-1",...,"iter-4"].
- Unit test: output_var_mode: collect over beads → output_var holds {"H-001":"out1","H-002":"out2",...}.
- Unit test: parallel:[2 steps] both with output_var:result → validation warning.
- Unit test: output_var_mode: last on parallel foreach → still works but a Debug-level "non-deterministic" warning is logged.

## Files
- internal/pipeline/schema.go — add Step.OutputVarMode + ForeachConfig.OutputVarMode
- internal/pipeline/foreach.go — implement aggregation modes
- internal/pipeline/parser.go — validator warning
- internal/pipeline/foreach_test.go

Documentation must be repo-local (for example references/ or docs/); do not edit ~/.claude or ~/.codex paths from a bead file list.

title: [LOW] pressure/provider: readMemoryRatio reports 100% used when MemAvailable line is absent from /proc/meminfo
description:
In internal/pressure/provider.go readMemoryRatio (commit 7a3d732d, bd-fxj4f admission control feature), the function parses /proc/meminfo line-by-line and accepts a missing MemAvailable line as 'available=0', then computes:

  if totalKB <= 0 || availableKB < 0 {
    return 0, false
  }
  used := 1 - (availableKB / totalKB)

When MemAvailable is not present in /proc/meminfo, availableKB stays at the zero value (0). The validation gate uses strict less-than ("availableKB < 0"), so zero passes. The computation then yields used = 1 - (0/totalKB) = 1.0 — 100% memory usage — and the provider reports the host as fully memory-pressured.

This affects:
- Linux kernels older than 3.14 (where MemAvailable did not exist).
- Stripped /proc mounts in some containers, sandboxes, or CI runners.
- Custom-mounted /proc layers that filter out MemAvailable.

On those hosts the spawn-pressure admission path will deny work as if memory were saturated, even when the host is fine.

Suggested fix: track whether MemAvailable was actually observed and return (0, false) when it wasn't, e.g.

  var totalKB, availableKB float64
  haveAvailable := false
  for ... {
    switch strings.TrimSuffix(fields[0], ":") {
    case "MemTotal":
      totalKB = value
    case "MemAvailable":
      availableKB = value
      haveAvailable = true
    }
  }
  if totalKB <= 0 || !haveAvailable {
    return 0, false
  }

Or, conservatively, change the gate to '<=': availableKB <= 0 → return false. The 'haveAvailable' boolean is the cleaner signal because it preserves the 'no probe data' return shape the caller already special-cases (in checkMemory and elsewhere).

Severity LOW: modern Linux nearly always has MemAvailable. But the failure mode is silent and can manifest in CI / minimal container environments without warning.

Source: internal/pressure/provider.go readMemoryRatio (~line 119); commit 7a3d732d.
close_reason: Extracted parseMemoryRatio(raw string) (float64, bool) so the parser is unit-testable without touching /proc. Added a haveAvailable bool that is set only when the MemAvailable line is observed; the gate is now 'totalKB <= 0 || !haveAvailable' instead of the buggy 'availableKB < 0' which let absent-equals-zero through. readMemoryRatio is now a thin os.ReadFile wrapper. New provider_test.go covers seven cases: standard meminfo (0.25 used), missing MemAvailable returns (0,false), empty input, total=0, MemAvailable observed-zero (genuine full pressure, distinct from missing), available>total clamp, and malformed-line resilience. Commit: 20b3414b. rch exec -- go build ./cmd/ntm and rch exec -- go test -short ./internal/pressure/... both pass.

title: [HIGH] foreach iteration falsely marked completed when ctx cancels mid-iteration with partial successful nested steps
description:
Review of e440bb9b [bug-fix] pipeline: preserve completed foreach checkpoints after late cancel (bd-5ptsz) found that the new shouldCompleteForeachIteration helper cannot distinguish 'all nested steps ran successfully then ctx cancelled' from 'first nested step ran successfully then ctx cancelled before step 2'. Both cases have len(results) > 0 and iterationSucceeded == true under the new contract, so both cause markForeachIterationCompleted to fire, but only the former is actually complete. The latter writes a partial iteration to CompletedIterationIDs and resume silently skips the unfinished nested steps.

In internal/pipeline/state_resume.go (~line 427), the new helper:

  func shouldCompleteForeachIteration(ctx context.Context, results []StepResult, shouldBreak bool) bool {
      if !iterationSucceeded(results, shouldBreak) { return false }
      if ctx.Err() == nil { return true }
      return len(results) > 0
  }

iterationSucceeded only checks that every entry in results has Status==Completed; it does not know how many nested steps the iteration was supposed to contain.

In internal/pipeline/loops.go executeIteration (~line 517), the cancellation guard is at the top of each nested-step iteration:

  for _, nestedStep := range loop.Steps {
      select {
      case <-ctx.Done():
          return results, false, false   // can return PARTIAL results
      default:
      }
      ...
      result := le.executor.executeStep(...)
      results = append(results, result)
      ...
  }

So if loop.Steps has 3 nested steps and ctx cancels between step 1 (already appended as Completed) and step 2, executeIteration returns ([{Completed}], false, false). The outer loop in executeForEach then calls shouldCompleteForeachIteration(cancelledCtx, [Completed], false), which returns true via the len(results) > 0 branch, and markForeachIterationCompleted is called. persistState writes the iteration to CompletedIterationIDs, then the next outer for-loop tick observes ctx.Done() and returns Cancelled.

On resume, firstIncompleteIteration (state_resume.go ~line 337) treats this iteration as done and the unfinished nested steps 2..N are silently skipped. This is the same class of silent-resume-skip bug that the original bd-xreqm fix (the deleted comment cites it explicitly) was guarding against; the partial-results variant was simply latent before because the strict ctx.Err() == nil guard masked it.

Reproducer (conceptual):
  loop.Steps: [stepA, stepB]
  ctx cancels between stepA and stepB
  executeIteration returns ([{stepA: Completed}], shouldBreak=false, shouldContinue=false)
  shouldCompleteForeachIteration(cancelled, [{Completed}], false) == true
  CompletedIterationIDs gains the iteration. On resume, stepB is never re-executed.

Old behavior under the strict ctx.Err()==nil guard: this iteration was NOT marked completed, resume re-ran the iteration from scratch (idempotent re-run of stepA, then stepB). New behavior: silent loss of stepB.

Note: the new test in resume_helpers_test.go asserts shouldCompleteForeachIteration(cancelledCtx, [{Completed}], false) == true; that test codifies the buggy behavior and would need to be updated alongside the fix. The all-Completed-then-cancelled case (which the commit message intends to preserve) and the partial-Completed-then-cancelled case both look identical to the helper today.

Suggested fix: thread the expected nested-step count (or a 'cancelled-mid-iteration' flag returned by executeIteration) into the helper and only mark completed when len(results) covers every loop.Steps entry that was actually scheduled (i.e. the iteration ran to its natural end). For example, have executeIteration return a 'completedNaturally bool' that is true only when the for-loop exits without hitting the <-ctx.Done() select, and use that as the gate alongside iterationSucceeded.

Source commit: e440bb9b [bug-fix] pipeline: preserve completed foreach checkpoints after late cancel (bd-5ptsz)
close_reason: Duplicate of bd-vq8bc: both report the same foreach partial-cancel checkpointing bug in shouldCompleteForeachIteration (ctx cancelled + non-empty successful partial results marked complete, causing resume to skip remaining nested steps).

# Feature: Prompt Engine - Mode-specific preambles with schema enforcement

Each mode agent receives a structured prompt with three mandatory components:
1. Base instructions (tone, structure, constraints)
2. Mode preamble (the reasoning 'lens')
3. **Output schema contract** (mandatory structured output)

## Prompt Structure

### 1. Base Instructions
```
You are participating in a reasoning ensemble analyzing: {problem_statement}

Context Pack:
{context_pack}

Your role: Apply your assigned reasoning mode rigorously.

Constraints:
- Stay within your reasoning mode's strengths
- Be explicit about confidence levels (numeric or high|medium|low)
- Reference specific evidence (file:line)
- Flag your mode's known failure modes
- DO NOT exceed {token_cap} tokens
```

### 2. Mode Preamble (The Lens)
```
## Your Reasoning Mode: {mode_name}

{mode_description}

What you excel at:
{best_for}

How you differ from other modes:
{differentiator}

Common failure modes to avoid:
{failure_modes}
```

### 3. Output Schema Contract (MANDATORY)
```
## REQUIRED OUTPUT FORMAT

You MUST structure your response as valid YAML with these exact fields:

mode_id: {mode_id}           # optional; system will inject if missing
thesis: |
  Your one-sentence main insight
confidence: 0.0-1.0           # numeric or high|medium|low

top_findings:
  - finding: Description of finding
    impact: critical|high|medium|low
    confidence: 0.0-1.0        # numeric or high|medium|low
    evidence_pointer: path/to/file.go:142
    reasoning: How you reached this

risks:
  - risk: Description of risk
    impact: critical|high|medium|low
    likelihood: 0.0-1.0        # numeric or high|medium|low
    mitigation: Suggested mitigation
    affected_areas: [string]

recommendations:
  - recommendation: What to do
    priority: critical|high|medium|low
    effort: low|medium|high
    rationale: Why this helps
    related_findings: [int]    # indices into top_findings (0-based)

questions_for_user:
  - question: What needs clarification?
    context: Why this matters
    blocking: false
    suggested_answers: [string]

failure_modes_to_watch:
  - mode: Potential failure of my analysis
    description: What could go wrong
    indicators: [string]
    prevention: How to guard against it

NON-COMPLIANT OUTPUTS WILL BE REJECTED.
```

## Schema Validation

- Parse YAML structure
- Check required fields present
- Validate enum values (impact/priority/etc.)
- Accept numeric or qualitative likelihood/confidence values
- Ensure evidence_pointers are valid file references

title: [MEDIUM] runOnCancelSteps uses context.Background — cleanup steps cannot be interrupted, can hang the run forever
description:
Review of 78a9b16e (fix(pipeline): run cancellation cleanup contract) found that cleanup steps run under an uncancellable context, so a buggy or slow on_cancel step can hang the executor indefinitely.

In internal/pipeline/executor.go runOnCancelSteps:

  for i := range workflow.Settings.OnCancel {
      step := workflow.Settings.OnCancel[i]
      ...
      result := e.executeStep(context.Background(), &step, &cleanupWorkflow)
      ...
  }

The intent of context.Background() is correct: cleanup must run AFTER the main ctx is cancelled, so reusing the cancelled ctx would skip cleanup entirely (defeating the contract). But the swing to a non-cancellable Background ctx removes ALL deadlines, so a single misbehaving cleanup step (long sleep, infinite loop, network call to a dead host with no per-call timeout) blocks the executor forever and the user cannot abort.

Real-world failure modes:
- A cleanup step that does a recursive delete on a slow or hung NFS mount
- A cleanup step that posts to a Slack/webhook URL that is timing out
- A retry-policy cleanup step (RetryCount > 0, retry_delay 30s) blocking for RetryCount * retry_delay seconds
- A cleanup step that calls the agent or shell with no per-step timeout

Mitigations:
- Apply a separate cleanup_timeout (workflow.Settings.OnCancelTimeout, default e.g. 60 s) and use context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), cleanup_timeout) per step or for the whole cleanup phase
- Honor a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler on the executor that propagates cancellation to the cleanup ctx after a grace period (so 'second Ctrl-C' aborts cleanup)
- Document the contract explicitly: on_cancel steps run with no parent timeout; require an explicit per-step timeout

The included test TestExecutor_Run_GlobalTimeoutRunsOnCancelSteps verifies the happy path (cleanup writes a file). The hung-cleanup case has no coverage.

title: [LOW] dispatchplan: Required candidates bypass agent-type filter and source-disabled checks but the godoc only documents budget bypass
description:
In internal/dispatchplan/plan.go (commit 0606f7d3, bd-fxj4f.11), the Candidate.Required field documents only one bypass:

  Required          bool     // included before any budget check

And the package doc says:
  // Required headers bypass the budget check (agent identity always
  // lands); subsequent non-required candidates respect remaining budget.

But the Plan() body actually bypasses three additional gates for Required candidates:

  switch {
  case c.EstimatedTokens <= 0 && !c.Required:        // 1. empty-tokens
      dec.Reason = ReasonOmittedEmpty
  case sourceDisabled(disabled, c.Source) && !c.Required:  // 2. source-disabled
      dec.Reason = ReasonOmittedSourceOff
  case c.ID != "" && containsKey(seenIDs, c.ID):     // 3. dedupe (NOT bypassed)
      dec.Reason = ReasonOmittedDuplicate
  case !agentTypeAllowed(c.AgentTypeFilter, in.AgentType) && !c.Required:  // 4. agent-type
      dec.Reason = ReasonOmittedAgentType
  case c.Required:
      // includes here regardless of source/agent-type/empty
  case in.BudgetTokens > 0 && report.UsedTokens+c.EstimatedTokens > in.BudgetTokens:
      dec.Reason = ReasonOmittedBudget
  ...
  }

So a Required candidate is included even when:
  - its source is disabled (e.g., CASS off, mail off);
  - its AgentTypeFilter excludes the dispatching agent;
  - its EstimatedTokens is 0 or negative.

Only the duplicate-ID gate (case 3) actually applies to Required candidates.

Two failure modes:

  1. Operator reads the godoc + doc-comment and wires up a Required
     candidate WITH an AgentTypeFilter, expecting the filter to scope
     it to one agent type. Result: filter is silently ignored,
     candidate lands in every agent's prompt regardless.
  2. A consumer routing on Decision.Reason and counting "for each
     disabled source, all its candidates → ReasonOmittedSourceOff"
     undercounts because Required candidates from that source slip
     through with ReasonRequiredHeader.

Two reasonable fixes:

  (a) Tighten the docs to match the code. Update Candidate.Required
      and the package doc to spell out which gates Required bypasses
      (budget + source-disabled + agent-type-filter + empty-tokens)
      and which it still respects (duplicate-ID). Pin the contract
      with a small test that asserts each bypass.

  (b) Tighten the code to match the docs. Move case 5 (c.Required)
      AFTER cases 2 (source-disabled) and 4 (agent-type-filter),
      so Required only bypasses the budget gate. Rename
      ReasonRequiredHeader's meaning and add ReasonOmittedRequired*
      sub-codes for "Required but excluded by source/agent-type".

(a) is the smaller change and matches the code's evident design intent — Required IS meant to be "system header always lands, independent of every per-source/per-agent gate". (b) would change behavior for any caller who happens to set both Required AND a filter today.

Severity LOW: behavior is internally consistent; the gap is only documentation. But the package's stated mission is "every inclusion and every omission with a stable reason code" — operators reading the godoc to predict Reason on a Required candidate will get the wrong mental model.

Source: internal/dispatchplan/plan.go (Plan switch statement ~line 200, Candidate.Required godoc ~line 95, package doc ~line 12); commit 0606f7d3 (bd-fxj4f.11).
close_reason: Tightened the godoc to spell out the full bypass scope of Required: bypasses EstimatedTokens<=0, source-disabled, agent-type-filter, AND budget gates; respects the duplicate-ID gate. Updated both the package-level doc comment and Candidate.Required field doc. Added regression test TestPlan_RequiredBypassesEveryGateExceptDuplicateID that constructs a Required candidate hitting each bypassed gate (empty tokens, disabled source, mismatched agent-type filter, budget overflow) plus a duplicate Required candidate whose ID was already emitted, and asserts the documented Reason mapping. go test -short ./internal/dispatchplan/... green.

title: [MEDIUM] branches map without branch predicate passes validation but cannot execute
description:
Review of 9693c864 (feat(pipeline): add branch shell predicate evaluation + lookup) found a parser/executor mismatch for branch steps. validateWorkflowStep currently treats a step as having branch work when either step.Branch is non-empty OR len(step.Branches) > 0. That means a YAML/JSON step containing only branches: but no branch: predicate passes lint as a valid branch step.

At runtime, executeStepOnce only dispatches branch handling when step.Branch != "". A branches-only step therefore falls through to prompt resolution and fails with a generic missing prompt/prompt_file error instead of being rejected at parse time.

Relevant current code:
- internal/pipeline/parser.go: hasBranch := step.Branch != "" || len(step.Branches) > 0
- internal/pipeline/executor.go: if step.Branch != "" { return e.executeBranch(...) }
- internal/pipeline/schema.go documents Branch as the selector whose stdout chooses a Branches entry.

Reproducer shape:
  steps:
    - id: route
      branches:
        default:
          command: echo fallback

Current behavior: lint/validation accepts the step as having work; runtime does not dispatch branch handling.
Expected behavior: validation should reject branches without a non-empty branch predicate with an actionable error, or executor should intentionally define a default predicate.

Likely fix: in validateWorkflowStep, distinguish hasBranchPredicate from hasBranchesMap; require step.Branch when len(step.Branches) > 0, and require non-empty Branches when step.Branch is set. Add parser regression coverage for both half-configured branch shapes.

Impact: malformed branch workflows can pass lint and then fail later with an unrelated prompt error, making pipeline lint unreliable for branch control-flow configs.

Source commit: 9693c864 feat(pipeline): add branch shell predicate evaluation + lookup (bd-w6nth.1)
close_reason: validateWorkflowStep now distinguishes hasBranchPredicate from hasBranchesMap and rejects each half-configured shape (branches without branch, branch without branches) with an actionable error. Updated parser_test 'branch only is valid' to include a branches map and added two regression cases for the half-configured shapes.

title: Cancellation cleanup contract (Ctrl-C, timeout, kill child process tree)
description:
## Background

When the operator hits Ctrl-C or the global timeout fires, the executor's ctx.Cancel() propagates to step goroutines. But:
- Subprocess command steps may have child processes that ignore SIGINT.
- Foreach iterations may be mid-template-dispatch (tmux PasteKeys can block).
- File handles, locks, partial writes all leak unless explicitly cleaned up.

## Spec

Define cleanup contracts per step kind:

### Command steps
- On ctx.Done(): send SIGTERM to the child process. Wait up to 5s for graceful exit. If still running, SIGKILL the process group (use Setpgid + Kill(-pgid)).
- Capture whatever stdout/stderr was emitted before kill; mark Status=Cancelled with partial Output.
- Write to dispatch log: `pipeline.command.cancelled` event with elapsed_ms, bytes_captured, signal_sent.

### Template steps
- tmux PasteKeys is fast; cancellation is unlikely to interrupt mid-paste. But IF it does, mark Status=Cancelled and log `pipeline.template.cancelled`.
- Don't try to undo the partial paste (operator can see it in the pane and decide).

### Foreach iteration goroutines
- ctx.Done() propagates to each goroutine via its goroutine-local ctx.
- Goroutines abort their iteration's step; collect partial result; signal back via results channel.
- Parent foreach aggregates: completed iterations + cancelled iterations + skipped (not-yet-started).

### Parallel sub-step goroutines
- Same as foreach iteration goroutines; ctx.Done() fans out.

### Workflow-level cleanup
- Run any cleanup steps registered via `Workflow.Settings.OnCancel []Step` (NEW field).
- Persist final state (`status=cancelled`, `cancelled_at: ISO`) before returning.
- If `Workflow.Settings.OnCancel` is empty, just persist + return.

### File reservations
- IF Phase B integrates with Agent Mail file_reservation_paths (E10): release any reservations the workflow held.
- Document this requires E10 to land first.

## Acceptance

- Unit test: a 10s sleep command + Ctrl-C → process killed within 5s; Status=Cancelled.
- Unit test: process-group kill (start a parent that spawns children; verify children also die).
- Unit test: foreach with 5 in-flight iterations + Ctrl-C → all 5 marked Cancelled in state.Steps; partial outputs captured.
- Unit test: workflow.Settings.OnCancel runs after main pipeline cancellation.

## Files
- internal/pipeline/executor.go — extend executeCommand with Setpgid + signal handling
- internal/pipeline/schema.go — add WorkflowSettings.OnCancel
- internal/pipeline/cancellation_test.go — NEW
- internal/pipeline/foreach.go — propagate ctx-cancellation to iterations cleanly
design: Consolidated file plan: extend existing implementation files unless the concern is one of bd-z5lv3's justified modules. Shared concurrency/race tests may live in internal/pipeline/concurrency_test.go; resource-limit tests should prefer existing executor/foreach/schema test files unless a dedicated limits_test.go is justified by size. Documentation must be repo-local (for example references/ or docs/); do not edit ~/.claude or ~/.codex paths from a bead file list.
notes:
## AGENTS.md compliance checklist

Before marking this bead closed:
1. **Build green:** `go build ./cmd/ntm` succeeds.
2. **Tests pass:** `go test -short ./internal/pipeline/...` is green; if this bead added e2e, also `go test ./e2e/...`.
3. **Linter:** `golangci-lint run` clean (or document any deliberate ignores).
4. **Formatting:** `gofmt -l .` and `goimports -l .` produce no output.

## Logging discipline (per AGENTS.md § Logging & Console Output)

- Use `log/slog` for every structured event in the pipeline package; do NOT use `fmt.Println` in library code.
- Every event MUST include these stable fields where applicable: `run_id`, `workflow`, `step_id`, `pane_id`, `agent_type`, `iteration` (for foreach).
- Levels: Info for normal lifecycle events, Warn for recoverable issues, Error for failures, Debug for verbose tracing.
- Tests assert on the slog event stream where useful (capture via slog.NewJSONHandler into a buffer; parse line-by-line in test).

## File proliferation discipline (per AGENTS.md § No File Proliferation)

- Prefer extending existing files in `internal/pipeline/` over creating new ones.
- New files justified only when the module is genuinely a separate concern AND would bloat an existing file beyond ~1500 LOC.
- All test files MUST live alongside their implementation (`foo_test.go` next to `foo.go`).
- E2E tests live in `e2e/` (NOT in `internal/pipeline/`) per the testing policy.

## Backward-compat note (per AGENTS.md § Backwards Compatibility)

- Do NOT add compat shims for old internal APIs. Pre-existing pipeline tests use the canonical schema; if a test needs updating, update it inline rather than adding adapter layers.
- Yaml-level convenience aliases (`after`/`body`/`template_params`) are user-facing and stay; internal types should be canonical only.

title: [LOW] scheduler/queue: CancelSession/Batch/Clear/Remove leave stats.ByPriority and ByType stale (sibling of bd-s8sex)
description:
# Bug

bd-s8sex fixed `CancelSession`/`CancelBatch` to decrement the cross-axis `batchCounts`/`sessionCounts`. The same two methods, plus `Clear` and `Remove`, also drift `q.stats.ByPriority` and `q.stats.ByType` — the per-priority and per-type counts that `Stats()` exposes for dashboards.

Compare to `Dequeue` (queue.go:131-138), which is the canonical pattern:

```go
q.stats.ByPriority[job.Priority]--
if q.stats.ByPriority[job.Priority] <= 0 {
    delete(q.stats.ByPriority, job.Priority)
}
q.stats.ByType[job.Type]--
if q.stats.ByType[job.Type] <= 0 {
    delete(q.stats.ByType, job.Type)
}
```

The drift across methods:

| method          | ByPriority decrement | ByType decrement | delete-when-zero |
|-----------------|----------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Dequeue         | ✓                    | ✓                | ✓                |
| Remove          | ✓                    | ✓                | ✗ (leaves 0s)    |
| CancelSession   | ✗ (stale)            | ✗ (stale)        | n/a              |
| CancelBatch     | ✗ (stale)            | ✗ (stale)        | n/a              |
| Clear           | ✗ (stale)            | ✗ (stale)        | n/a              |

# Verification

After `CancelSession("foo")` cancels 3 jobs at priority=1 type="session", `Stats().ByPriority[1]` still reports 3 even though the queue has 0 jobs left. After `Clear()`, both maps still hold the pre-Clear counts even though `CurrentSize=0`. After many `Remove()` calls of jobs at the same priority, the count goes 3→2→1→0 but the entry stays in the map.

# Impact

Stats are observability-only (no scheduling decisions branch on them). But:
- Dashboards reading `Stats().ByPriority` see inflated counts after cancellations.
- An unbounded number of leftover zero-entries can accumulate in `Remove`s output if jobs cycle through many distinct priorities.
- After `Clear`, the maps lie outright (CurrentSize=0 but ByPriority sums positive).

Severity: **LOW** — observability gap, mirrors bd-s8sex's same-shape fix for batchCounts/sessionCounts.

# Fix

Apply the Dequeue pattern to all four sites:

- `Remove`: add the `if <= 0 delete` cleanup after the existing decrements.
- `CancelSession` / `CancelBatch`: in the post-fix loops that already touch `batchCounts`/`sessionCounts` (bd-s8sex), also decrement `q.stats.ByPriority[job.Priority]` and `q.stats.ByType[job.Type]` per cancelled job, with the delete-when-zero cleanup.
- `Clear`: reset `q.stats.ByPriority = make(map[JobPriority]int)` and `q.stats.ByType = make(map[JobType]int)` alongside the existing `q.stats.CurrentSize = 0`.

# Regression test

Add `TestJobQueue_CancelSession_AlsoDecrementsStatsByPriorityAndType` (and CancelBatch + Clear siblings) that checks `Stats().ByPriority` and `Stats().ByType` are correct after each operation. Same shape as the bd-s8sex tests already added in pure_test.go.
close_reason: Fixed: Remove now deletes-when-zero; CancelSession/CancelBatch decrement cross-axis stats per cancelled job; Clear resets ByPriority/ByType. 4 new tests pin every site.

title: [LOW] bead_query filter operator detection mis-parses clauses where != value contains ==
description:
Review of 01fbb230 found that matchBeadFilterClause prefers '==' over '!=' even when '!=' appears first in the clause, producing wrong field name and an 'unknown bead field' error.

In internal/pipeline/bead_query.go matchBeadFilterClause:

  op := '=='
  parts := strings.SplitN(clause, '==', 2)
  if len(parts) != 2 {
      op = '!='
      parts = strings.SplitN(clause, '!=', 2)
  }

The detection assumes that if the clause splits cleanly on '==' into two parts, the operator is '=='. That is wrong when the clause is shaped like 'field!=foo==bar': SplitN('==', 2) returns ['field!=foo', 'bar'] (length 2), so op is locked to '==' and the field is parsed as 'field!=foo' which fails the beadRecordField lookup with 'unknown bead field'.

Equivalent issue: 'field==a!=b' parses fine ('==' op, value 'a!=b'); but a value that legitimately contains '==' or '!=' (e.g. a description with comparison operators) gets misinterpreted.

Fix options:
- Detect operator by finding the FIRST occurrence of '==' or '!=', whichever appears earliest in the string
- Or only allow operators after a known field name (left-side parse first)

Severity: LOW — most realistic filters will not embed comparison operators inside values; clear error makes it diagnosable; documented workaround is to pick a different filter shape.

Source commit: 01fbb230 feat(pipeline): add bead_query step (bd-mzde6)
close_reason: matchBeadFilterClause now picks the operator by earliest occurrence of '==' or '!=' instead of preferring '==' regardless of position. A clause like 'priority!=1==broken' now correctly parses 'priority' as the field with op '!=' and '1==broken' as the value. Tests cover both operators with each ordering and the false case.

title: [CRITICAL] cli/upgrade extractTarGz/extractZip preserves setuid/setgid/sticky from archive entries
description:
## Bug

`internal/cli/upgrade.go::extractTarGz` and `extractZip` pass archive-supplied mode bits through to `os.OpenFile` without masking, preserving setuid (0o4000), setgid (0o2000), and sticky (0o1000) bits.

- `extractTarGz` line 1113: `os.OpenFile(target, ..., os.FileMode(header.Mode))`
- `extractZip` line 1177: `os.OpenFile(target, ..., f.Mode())`

## Threat model

The upgrade flow downloads a release tarball from GitHub, verifies its checksum against `checksums.txt` (also fetched from the same release), and extracts the binary to a temp dir before replacing the running executable.

If `ntm` is installed in `/usr/local/bin`, the upgrade runs with sudo. A malicious tarball with `header.Mode = 0o4755` ships a setuid binary; after extraction it replaces the root-owned `/usr/local/bin/ntm` and the rename preserves the file's setuid bit and root ownership. Any subsequent invocation of `ntm` by any user runs with effective UID = root.

Checksum verification offers no defense here because the same compromised release pipeline produces both the tarball and `checksums.txt`. They will hash-match each other; only an out-of-band signature would catch the substitution.

## Why it's worth fixing even though the attack requires release-pipeline compromise

Defense-in-depth. Recent supply-chain attacks (e.g., xz-utils CVE-2024-3094) demonstrate that release-pipeline compromise is no longer rare. An archive extractor should never grant elevated privileges that the source code didn't ask for, regardless of the trust placed in the publisher.

## Fix shape

Mask the supplied mode to drop setuid/setgid/sticky bits before passing to `os.OpenFile`:

```go
const archiveSafeModeMask = os.ModeSetuid | os.ModeSetgid | os.ModeSticky
// tar:
mode := os.FileMode(header.Mode) &^ archiveSafeModeMask
// zip:
mode := f.Mode() &^ archiveSafeModeMask
```

Alternatively `os.FileMode(...).Perm()` keeps only the lowest 9 bits, which is even stricter.

## Regression test

Build a tarball with one entry whose `Mode = 0o4755`, extract via `extractTarGz`, `os.Stat` the extracted file, and assert its mode has no setuid/setgid/sticky bits set. Same shape for zip with a `zip.FileHeader{Mode: 0o4755}`.

## Pre-fix verification

Verified by reading the touched lines: header.Mode flows directly through `os.FileMode(...)` and `f.Mode()` into `os.OpenFile`. The umask on most systems is 022 — it masks group/other-write but does NOT mask setuid/setgid, so bits set in the source are preserved on disk.
close_reason: Fixed in internal/cli/upgrade.go: archiveModeMask (ModeSetuid|ModeSetgid|ModeSticky) stripped during extraction in both extractTarGz and extractZip. Investigation revealed only the zip path was actively vulnerable: archive/zip's f.Mode() translates external_attr to os.FileMode with the Go-level Mode* bits set, which os.OpenFile honors via its syscall translation. The tar path was safe-by-accident: os.FileMode(int64(header.Mode)) is a uint32 cast that does not flip ModeSetuid/Setgid/Sticky in the high Go-level bits, so os.OpenFile already drops them. The mask was applied to the tar path defensively to guard against a future refactor to header.FileInfo().Mode() (which would translate properly and reintroduce the gap). Regression tests: TestExtractZip_StripsSetuidSetgidStickyBits verifies the zip fix and was confirmed to fail pre-fix; TestExtractTarGz_PreservesLowerPermBitsThroughMask pins that the mask preserves the executable bit. Test expectations and bead description were corrected mid-fix when the tar extraction was found to be safe-by-accident.

title: [MEDIUM] signalCommandProcessGroup SIGKILL fallback only kills leader, leaks children
description:
Review of a7abefe2 (fix(pipeline): clean up command process groups on cancel) found that the SIGKILL fallback path leaks descendant processes when the process-group kill fails for any reason other than ESRCH.

In internal/pipeline/process_group.go signalCommandProcessGroup:

  err := syscall.Kill(-cmd.Process.Pid, sig)
  if err == nil { return nil }
  if errors.Is(err, syscall.ESRCH) { return os.ErrProcessDone }
  if sig == syscall.SIGKILL {
      return cmd.Process.Kill()    // ← single-process fallback
  }
  return cmd.Process.Signal(sig)   // ← single-process fallback

Because configureCommandProcessGroup sets Setpgid=true, every child and grandchild of the launched /bin/sh inherits the same process group (pgid == shell pid). The intended cleanup is to send the signal to -pgid so the entire tree dies together.

If syscall.Kill(-pgid, SIGKILL) fails for any reason other than ESRCH (for example EPERM under unusual security policies, or any future container/sandbox surprise), the fallback kills only the shell leader. The kernel reparents the surviving children to init, where they continue running. The 'clean up command process groups on cancel' contract is broken in exactly the failure mode the fallback was supposed to handle.

Reproducer (synthetic): inject a kill error for -pgid while leaving cmd.Process.Kill() functional, observe that descendant processes survive the cancel.

Fix options:
- After cmd.Process.Kill() succeeds, also walk descendants explicitly (read /proc/<pid>/task/<tid>/children on Linux, ps -o pid --ppid on darwin) and SIGKILL each
- Or, accept process-group failure as a hard error rather than silently degrading: log warn + return the error so the caller surfaces a 'process tree may be leaked' status

The TestExecuteCommand_CancelKillsProcessGroupChild test only exercises the happy-path (group-kill succeeds); the fallback path has no test coverage.

Source commit: a7abefe2 fix(pipeline): clean up command process groups on cancel (bd-e2z38)
close_reason: signalCommandProcessGroup's SIGKILL fallback now also walks /proc looking for processes whose pgid matches the leader's pid and SIGKILLs each one before returning. Best-effort and silent on systems without /proc. Adds parseProcStatPGID that handles comm fields with spaces/parens by scanning back to the last ')' before splitting. Tests cover stat parsing edge cases (simple, embedded parens, malformed inputs) and confirm killProcessGroupDescendants is safe with bogus PIDs.

title: robot/causality: Agent Mail and pipeline loaders ignore since/until window
description: loadAgentMailCausalityEvents and loadPipelineCausalityEvents in internal/robot/causality.go (e0766e0b) accept the parsed since/until window only via filterCausalityEvents at output time. The mail loader hits client.ListReservations and client.FetchInbox(limit=200) regardless of the window — wasting a network round-trip and inbox token usage when the user asked for, say, the last 5 minutes. title: LimitsConfig.MaxCommandStderrBytes and MaxStepCountTotal are dead-code (never enforced)
description:
## Bug

Two `LimitsConfig` fields are declared, given defaults via `EffectiveLimits()`, but never consulted at runtime:

1. `MaxCommandStderrBytes` (`internal/pipeline/schema.go:228`, default 4 MB).
   - Only mention outside schema is the test file. Command stderr is captured in `executor.go:executeCommand` but no length check.
   - `MaxCommandStdoutBytes` IS enforced at `executor.go:1064`. Stderr is asymmetric.

2. `MaxStepCountTotal` (`internal/pipeline/schema.go:230`, default 100000).
   - Zero runtime references outside schema and tests. Workflow with millions of steps would parse and run unconstrained.

Verify:
```
grep -n "MaxStepCountTotal\|MaxCommandStderrBytes" internal/pipeline/*.go | grep -v _test.go | grep -v schema.go
# (no results)
```

## Impact

[MEDIUM] for MaxCommandStderrBytes — pipeline command runs that emit unbounded stderr (e.g. a verbose debug command in a tight loop) can balloon memory/log size. The CONFIG lets users set a guardrail but the guardrail does nothing.

[MEDIUM] for MaxStepCountTotal — defense-in-depth against malicious or malformed workflows is bypassed; users believe the limit applies.

Combined: this is a security-relevant gap (silent guardrail failure) and a documentation-vs-behavior mismatch.

## Reproducer

1. `limits: { max_command_stderr_bytes: 100 }` + a `command: yes 2>&1 1>/dev/null | head -c 1000000`. No truncation occurs in stderr capture.
2. `limits: { max_step_count_total: 5 }` + a workflow with 50 steps. Workflow runs all 50.

## Fix sketch

For stderr: mirror the stdout-truncation block in executor.go. For step count: total step count check at validate/normalize time (counting recursive expansion of foreach/parallel/loop bodies); error if exceeded.

Tests:
- stderr: command emits N bytes of stderr, limit M < N → truncated to M with `[TRUNCATED at M bytes]` marker.
- step count: workflow with declared K steps where K > limit → validation error.

## Files

- internal/pipeline/executor.go (stderr truncation)
- internal/pipeline/parser.go OR internal/pipeline/validate.go (step count walker)
- NEW *_test.go file for both

## Found via review

Audit of LimitsConfig fields against runtime usage; companion to bd-pzckw (MaxSubstitutionDepth not read).
close_reason: Duplicate of bd-g7cu9: both track missing enforcement of LimitsConfig MaxCommandStderrBytes and MaxStepCountTotal. Verified runtime still only enforces MaxCommandStdoutBytes in executor.go and has no MaxStepCountTotal gate.

title: [HIGH] loop_control-only foreach steps are rejected by YAML validation
description: Review of 92441a46 (feat(pipeline): honor loop control in foreach) and the follow-up loop-control body fix found that the runtime still supports control-only foreach body steps, but parsed workflows cannot use them. The commit tests construct steps like Step{LoopControl: LoopControlBreak, When: ...} programmatically, and current foreach.go has foreachControlOnlyStep/foreachLoopControlDecision for the same shape. Parser validation, however, does not count loop_control as executable work in the required step-kind check, so YAML with id: break_on_c, loop_control: break, and a when condition comparing ${item} to "c" fails with "step must have prompt, prompt_file, command, template, parallel, loop, foreach, branch, or bead_query". Impact: user-facing workflows cannot express a pure break/continue guard even though the executor has a dedicated path for it; authors must attach loop_control to an unrelated command/template or bypass YAML entirely. Expected: either treat loop_control break/continue as a first-class valid control-only step kind in parser validation, with a parsed-YAML regression, or remove the unreachable runtime path and document that loop_control must be attached to real work steps. No code fix applied in this review pass because the requested CRITICAL/HIGH auto-fix scope is restricted to NEW files only, while the production fix belongs in internal/pipeline/parser.go.
close_reason: Parser validation now accepts loop_control: break/continue as a first-class step kind, matching the runtime contract in foreachControlOnlyStep. Updated step-kind error message to advertise loop_control alongside the other kinds. Added TestParseString_YAML_LoopControlOnlyForeachBody covering the canonical YAML form and TestValidate_StepKindMutualExclusivityAndRequiredWork cases for both break and continue with a when guard.

title: [MEDIUM] more CLI commands still exit 0 on success:false JSON (#125 / bd-usgfy parity sweep)
description:
## Severity: [MEDIUM]

#125 fixed lock/unlock/locks; bd-usgfy fixed activity/adopt/context/rotate-context. A sweep `grep -n "Success.*false" internal/cli/*.go` shows the pattern still leaks into:

- `internal/cli/assign.go` — 8 sites, including `runClearAssignments` line 2574 (`return json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout).Encode(makeClearErrorEnvelope("INVALID_ARGS", err.Error()))`) — encode succeeds → exit 0 even though Success:false.
- `internal/cli/ensemble.go` — 9 sites in checkpoint-resume paths (lines 2798, 2809, 2820, 2942, 2952, 2963, 2981, 2992) all funnel through `renderCheckpointResumeOutput` which calls `output.WriteJSON(w, payload, true)` and returns its (success-path) nil. Same bug.
- `internal/cli/ensemble_spawn.go:603` — `Success: false` in a path that may not propagate err.
- `internal/cli/resume.go:179`
- `internal/cli/profile_switch.go:340-352` — actually OK because it returns the original err (re-check during fix).

Severity is MEDIUM rather than HIGH because these are less commonly piped in shell wrappers than `lock`/`unlock`, but they ARE used in agent orchestration (assign clear, ensemble resume, ensemble spawn) and the automation hazard is the same.

## Fix

Same pattern as bd-usgfy / #125:

```go
if encErr := encode(...); encErr != nil { return encErr }
return jsonFailureExit()
```

For paths that funnel through a renderer (`renderCheckpointResumeOutput`, etc.), thread the failure signal through: either pass an explicit `success bool` argument and have the renderer return `errJSONFailure` for failure JSON, or have the caller check `payload.Success` and add the `jsonFailureExit()` after a successful render.

## Acceptance

- `grep -n "Success.*false" internal/cli/*.go | grep -v _test.go` cross-referenced against return paths shows no remaining exit-0-on-failure JSON sites.
- One unit test per file asserts the failure envelope returns `errJSONFailure`.
- `go test -short -count=1 ./internal/cli/` passes (test file fixtures may need updating).

## Files
- internal/cli/assign.go
- internal/cli/ensemble.go (and renderCheckpointResumeOutput contract)
- internal/cli/ensemble_spawn.go
- internal/cli/resume.go
- internal/cli/profile_switch.go (sweep verification only)
close_reason: Parity sweep landed in e91ccee9 (assign/ensemble/ensemble_spawn/rebalance/resume/send/session_persist/support_bundle all route success:false envelopes through errJSONFailure via emitJSONFailureEnvelope/jsonFailureExit). Follow-up test alignment in b96c13b4 added errors.Is(errJSONFailure) tolerance to ensemble_compare_test.go so the structured-failure assertions still pass after the run* funcs began returning the sentinel.

title: [LOW] faultharness: ModeDeadlineExceeded spent calculation is dead code; Result.Latency overstates time when ctx fires early on RealClock
description:
In internal/faultharness/harness.go Apply (commit 0952acd1, bd-3v1gs.8), the ModeDeadlineExceeded branch's spent calculation is dead code:

  case ModeDeadlineExceeded:
    err := clock.Sleep(ctx, b.Latency)
    spent := b.Latency
    if err == context.Canceled || err == context.DeadlineExceeded {
      // ctx fired first; treat that as the actual spend.
      spent = b.Latency // FakeClock has already added Latency; for
                        // RealClock the deadline cut us short, but
                        // we don't have a way to read it back without
                        // more wiring. Keep it simple.
    }
    return Result{ Latency: spent, ... }

The if-body assigns the SAME value the outer line already assigned (spent = b.Latency), so the entire conditional is a no-op. The author's inline comment acknowledges the limitation but the resulting Result.Latency is misleading whenever a real ctx deadline cuts Sleep short:

  - FakeClock: Sleep adds the full Latency to NowTime regardless, so b.Latency is the truthful 'simulated spend'. Reporting it is correct.
  - RealClock: Sleep blocks at most until ctx fires; if ctx has a 100ms deadline and Latency is 5s, the real wait is 100ms. But the harness still reports Result.Latency = 5s.

A test that asserts 'on a 100ms ctx deadline the harness spent ~100ms before returning DeadlineExceeded' would observe 5s in Result.Latency and either fail or paper over the gap. The harness's own comment names the missing wiring ('we don't have a way to read it back') — this is a known shortcut left visible in the API.

Two reasonable fixes:

  (a) Measure the actual elapsed time around clock.Sleep:
        before := clock.Now()
        err := clock.Sleep(ctx, b.Latency)
        spent := clock.Now().Sub(before)
        if spent > b.Latency { spent = b.Latency }   // RealClock noise cap
      Works for both FakeClock (Sleep advances NowTime by Latency, so spent==Latency) and RealClock (real elapsed). The if-block becomes load-bearing instead of dead.

  (b) Drop the dead if-block and document Result.Latency as 'the requested budget, not the actual spend' for ModeDeadlineExceeded. Smaller change; preserves current reporting; honest documentation.

Either fix should ship with a test that asserts the documented contract. Pre-fix, no test can distinguish the two interpretations because the value is always b.Latency.

Severity LOW: only matters on the RealClock+short-ctx path, which production callers rarely take (the harness is a test fixture). But the reported value is wrong there, and the inline comment already telegraphs the gap.

Source: internal/faultharness/harness.go ModeDeadlineExceeded branch (~line 243-258); commit 0952acd1 (bd-3v1gs.8).
close_reason: Replaced the dead-code if-block with a clock.Now() bracket around clock.Sleep, so Result.Latency reports the actual elapsed time. Both clock implementations cooperate: FakeClock with healthy ctx advances NowTime by Latency (delta = b.Latency, preserving current behavior); FakeClock with pre-cancelled ctx early-returns without advancing NowTime (delta = 0, the truthful elapsed); RealClock.Sleep returns when ctx fires (delta is real wall-clock time). Defensive cap clamps spent to [0, b.Latency] so a misbehaving custom clock cannot emit a misleading value. Two regression tests pin the contract: TestApply_DeadlineExceededReportsActualSpentNotRequestedBudget (healthy ctx → 5s; pre-cancelled ctx → 0; pre-fix both reported 5s); TestApply_DeadlineExceededLatencyIsClampedToBudget uses a runawayClock that advances 1h per Sleep and confirms the clamp drops it to b.Latency=5s. Existing TestApply_DeadlineExceededIsAlwaysErr / HonorsCtxCancel stay green. Commit: 782b6ea2. rch exec -- go build ./cmd/ntm and rch exec -- go test -short ./internal/faultharness/... both pass.

title: [HIGH] Foreach resume skips gaps when current_iteration is ahead
description:
Review of c0fa944b (test(pipeline): cover resume bookkeeping helpers) found that the new TestResumeProgressBookkeepingHelpers locks in an unsafe resume behavior.

The test marks iterations 0 and 2 completed, then calls beginForeachState("fanout", 4). firstIncompleteIteration correctly returns 1 for the same completed set, but beginForeachState overwrites that with state.CurrentIteration when CurrentIteration is greater than the first gap:

  start := firstIncompleteIteration(state.CompletedIterationIDs, stepID, total)
  if state.CurrentIteration > start && state.CurrentIteration < total {
      start = state.CurrentIteration
  }

The test expects start == 3, which means iteration 1 is skipped even though it is absent from CompletedIterationIDs.

Impact: a persisted state with a gap in CompletedIterationIDs can silently drop an incomplete foreach iteration on resume. Gaps can arise after interrupted/partial writes, force-resume edge cases, or future parallel/out-of-order completion metadata. The durable completed set should be authoritative for work that is safe to skip; CurrentIteration is only a cursor and must not jump past an incomplete gap.

Likely fix: beginForeachState should start at firstIncompleteIteration whenever a gap exists. CurrentIteration can be used only when it is equal to the first incomplete iteration or when there are no earlier gaps. Update the test to expect 1 for completed [0,2], and add a second no-gap case where completed [0,1,2] with CurrentIteration 3 starts at 3.

No direct fix applied in this review pass because the requested CRITICAL/HIGH fix policy restricts fixes to NEW files only, while the production fix belongs in internal/pipeline/state_resume.go and the existing test expectation.
close_reason: Fixed beginForeachState to start at first incomplete iteration; CompletedIterationIDs is now authoritative — CurrentIteration cursor cannot jump past a gap. Test updated to expect start=1 for completed=[iter0,iter2]; added regression for contiguous-complete case (completed=[iter0,iter1,iter2] with CurrentIteration=3 starts at 3).

title: Feature: Robot API - JSON interface for ensemble automation
description:
# Feature: Robot API

## Purpose
Expose ensemble functionality through JSON API for AI-to-AI orchestration and automation pipelines. Follows existing NTM robot mode patterns.

## Scope

### Robot Commands

**--robot-ensemble=SESSION**
Get ensemble state for a session.
```json
{
  "success": true,
  "timestamp": "2026-01-23T10:30:00Z",
  "ensemble": {
    "session": "myproject",
    "question": "What architectural problems exist?",
    "preset": "architecture-review",
    "status": "active",
    "started_at": "2026-01-23T10:25:00Z",
    "modes": [
      {"id": "abductive", "code": "B13", "tier": "advanced", "pane": "myproject__cc_1", "agent_type": "claude", "status": "done"}
    ],
    "synthesis": {"strategy": "deliberative", "status": "not_started"}
  },
  "summary": {"total_modes": 5, "completed": 2, "working": 2, "pending": 1}
}
```

**--robot-ensemble-spawn=SESSION**
Create new ensemble session.
```bash
ntm --robot-ensemble-spawn=myproject \
  --preset=architecture-review \
  --question='What problems exist?' \
  --agents=cc=3,cod=2

ntm --robot-ensemble-spawn=myproject \
  --modes=A1,B13,F43 \
  --allow-advanced=true \
  --question='...'
```

**--robot-ensemble-synthesize=SESSION**
Trigger synthesis.
```bash
ntm --robot-ensemble-synthesize=myproject \
  --strategy=deliberative \
  --format=markdown
```
Returns synthesis output metadata or status.

**--robot-ensemble-modes**
List available modes.
```json
{
  "success": true,
  "modes": [
    {"id": "abductive", "code": "B13", "tier": "advanced", "name": "Abductive Reasoning", "category": {"code": "B", "name": "Ampliative"}}
  ],
  "categories": [{"code": "A", "name": "Formal", "mode_count": 8}],
```

title: EPIC: Canonical Assignment Flow (ntm assign + spawn --assign)
description:
## Goal
Reduce user confusion by providing **one** canonical assignment flow and **one** convenience entry point.

## Decision
- **Keep**: `ntm assign` as the only assignment command.
- **Keep**: `ntm spawn --assign` as the only convenience entry (spawn + assign).
- **Expose**: `--strategy=balanced|speed|quality|dependency|round-robin` on `ntm assign`.
- **Drop/Merge**: `ntm swarm`, `ntm send --distribute`, YAML swarm config, and from‑file assignments.

## Why
Multiple entry points doing the same thing (assign work to agents) multiplies docs, tests, and code paths and will confuse users. The project benefits from a single, well‑designed path.

## Scope
- Keep existing strategies (`balanced`, `speed`, `quality`, `dependency`) intact and documented.
- Add `round‑robin` as an **optional** additional strategy (no renaming of existing ones).
- Implement assignment tracking + reporting so `balanced` can be truly load‑aware.
- Implement `ntm spawn --assign` as a thin wrapper over `ntm assign`.
- Update docs/help to emphasize canonical flow.

## Non‑Goals
- No new orchestration commands outside `assign` + `spawn --assign`.
- No YAML swarm config or additional CLI entry points.

## Success Criteria
- `ntm assign` is the only path for distributing work.
- `ntm spawn --assign` works end‑to‑end with clear output.
- Redundant commands are closed/dropped.
- Strategy list in docs/help matches code.

title: [HIGH] foreach max_concurrent bypasses global concurrency cap
description:
Review of 8e132e6e found that foreachMaxConcurrent treats foreach.max_concurrent as an override rather than a value bounded by settings.limits.max_concurrent_foreach. The effective LimitsConfig defaults MaxConcurrentForeach as a resource cap, but this helper does:

  maxConcurrent := limits.MaxConcurrentForeach
  if config.MaxConcurrent > 0 {
      maxConcurrent = config.MaxConcurrent
  }

A workflow can therefore set settings.limits.max_concurrent_foreach: 4 for safety and then put max_concurrent: 10000 on a single foreach step, causing executeForeachIterationsParallel to spawn goroutines and shell/agent work far beyond the configured cap. That defeats the resource-limit contract added for runaway pipelines and can overload the local machine or remote panes.

Expected: per-step foreach.max_concurrent should be constrained by the global effective cap, for example min(config.MaxConcurrent, limits.MaxConcurrentForeach), or validation should reject any per-step value above the global cap. Add regression coverage for a workflow with global max_concurrent_foreach lower than step max_concurrent and assert execution uses the lower cap / validation fails.

No code fix was applied in this review pass because the requested CRITICAL/HIGH auto-fix scope is restricted to NEW files only, while the production fix requires changing internal/pipeline/foreach.go.
close_reason: foreachMaxConcurrent now clamps per-step config.MaxConcurrent down to the global limits.MaxConcurrentForeach when both are positive. A workflow that sets settings.limits.max_concurrent_foreach=4 plus a per-step max_concurrent=10000 now uses 4. Added TestForeachMaxConcurrentBoundedByGlobalCap (4 cases) plus TestForeachMaxConcurrentZeroGlobalAllowsPerStep (unbounded-global edge case).

title: LimitsConfig.MaxSubstitutionDepth is silently ignored — Substitute uses constant
description:
## Bug

`internal/pipeline/variables.go:352` hardcodes the recursion depth to the package constant `DefaultMaxSubstitutionDepth` (8), ignoring the user-configurable `LimitsConfig.MaxSubstitutionDepth` field.

```go
// variables.go:348
func (s *Substitutor) Substitute(template string) (string, error) {
    result := protectEscapedSubstitutions(template)
    var firstErr error
    for depth := 0; depth < DefaultMaxSubstitutionDepth; depth++ {  // <-- not configurable
        ...
    }
```

## Expected behavior

`schema.go:231` defines `MaxSubstitutionDepth int` with yaml tag `max_substitution_recursion`, and `EffectiveLimits()` (line 264-266) clamps it to the default when unset. The intent is clearly to allow workflow authors to configure the depth via `limits.max_substitution_recursion`.

## Impact

[HIGH] Users who configure `limits.max_substitution_recursion: 16` in their workflow yaml will silently see 8-deep substitution. No warning, no error. A workflow that relies on >8 levels of recursive substitution will fail with `substitution recursion depth exceeded after 8 passes` despite an explicit higher configured limit. Misleading bug report from the field would not point to the silent override.

## Reproducer

1. Author a workflow with `limits: { max_substitution_recursion: 12 }` and a chain that requires 10 substitution passes (e.g. `${a}` → `${b}` → ... → `${j}` → "value").
2. Run the workflow.
3. Observed: SubstitutionError "depth exceeded after 8 passes".
4. Expected: substitution succeeds (limit 12 should accommodate 10 passes).

## Fix sketch

Plumb LimitsConfig (or just MaxSubstitutionDepth int) into Substitutor:
- Add `maxDepth int` field to Substitutor.
- Update NewSubstitutor signature OR add a setter `Substitutor.SetMaxDepth(int)`.
- Caller (Executor) reads workflow.Limits.EffectiveLimits().MaxSubstitutionDepth and propagates.
- Replace `DefaultMaxSubstitutionDepth` in the loop with `s.maxDepth` (fall back to default when zero).
- Update the error message to use the actual limit.
- Add test: configure 16, run a 10-deep chain → succeeds. Configure 4, same chain → fails with `depth exceeded after 4 passes`.

## Files

- internal/pipeline/variables.go (Substitutor struct, NewSubstitutor, Substitute loop, error message)
- internal/pipeline/executor.go (plumb limits when constructing Substitutor)
- NEW test file or extend existing substitution_recursion_test.go

## Found via review

git review of commit a702aac4 (bd-6lkqr.7 — recursive substitutions). The schema field MaxSubstitutionDepth exists and EffectiveLimits clamps it, but Substitute does not consult it.
close_reason: Duplicate of bd-yowuf; both track Substitute ignoring LimitsConfig.MaxSubstitutionDepth / max_substitution_recursion and hardcoding DefaultMaxSubstitutionDepth.

title: [HIGH] rotate_adjudicator strategy ignores adjudicator history at runtime
description: Review of c3637dfa found rotateAdjudicator accepts an adjudicatorHistory slice and correctly chooses the longest gap, but the runtime integration in selectForeachPane calls rotateAdjudicator(..., nil). That means foreach pane_assignment_strategy: rotate_adjudicator always behaves like first available non-champion and never avoids the most-recent prior adjudicator or balances by adjudication history. The bd-2ubxp.9 spec requires excluding/de-prioritizing prior adjudicators using workflow run state or session logs. Expected behavior: pass real adjudicator history from run state/session logs and update it as adjudication assignments are made; add an integration test with multiple debate items where the prior adjudicator is not a current champion.
close_reason: Added Executor.adjudicatorHistory state (snapshot/record/reset) and selectForeachPaneWithState wrapper that threads live history into rotateAdjudicator for the rotate_adjudicator strategy. prepareForeachIterations calls the wrapper; Run() resets history per run. The longest-gap rebalancing logic is now reachable: across successive debate items the strategy avoids the most-recent prior adjudicator. Added TestSelectForeachPaneWithStateRotatesAdjudicatorAcrossDebates (3-debate sequence with rotating champions) and TestSelectForeachPaneWithStateNonRotateUnaffected (non-rotate strategies unchanged).

title: [MEDIUM] handoff/generator: enrichWithCASS uses hardcoded 15s default timeout, blocks every handoff
description: internal/handoff/generator.go enrichWithCASS (added in 9955a927) constructs the default CASS client as cass.NewClient(cass.WithTimeout(15 * time.Second)). Every GenerateHandoff call without a pre-configured CASSClient and with IncludeCASS unset (or true) blocks for up to 15 seconds when CASS is slow or hung. For automated agent handoff flows that run in tight loops or as part of every pane action, this is way too high — even one slow CASS query stalls the handoff, which may be on a critical path (auto-handoff at compaction). Fix: (1) add CASSTimeout option to GenerateHandoffOptions; (2) lower the unset default to 3s, since CASS is local-only and a healthy lookup is sub-second; (3) document the budget in GenerateHandoffOptions doc-comment.
