title: [MEDIUM] Inconsistent lock for state.ScopeStack between resetResumeState (stateMu) and pushScopeFrameLocked (varMu)
description:
Review of 7304d410 found inconsistent lock discipline for e.state.ScopeStack.

snapshotState (executor.go ~line 2580) reads ScopeStack under varMu:
  e.varMu.RLock()
  ...
  if e.state.ScopeStack != nil { ... }
  e.varMu.RUnlock()

pushScopeFrameLocked / popScopeFrameLocked (state_resume.go:491-503) write ScopeStack and are called from pushLoopVars / popLoopVars while holding varMu.

resetResumeState (state_resume.go:176-196) writes e.state.ScopeStack = nil under stateMu (NOT varMu):
  e.stateMu.Lock()
  ...
  e.state.ScopeStack = nil
  ...
  e.stateMu.Unlock()
  e.varMu.Lock()
  ... (only Variables touched here)

Today this is safe because resetResumeState is invoked from applyResumeOptions (called inside Resume before any executor goroutines start). But the inconsistency is a future-refactor footgun and -race detector trip waiting to happen if any other path ever mutates ScopeStack from a non-init context using stateMu only, or if ScopeStack zeroing is ever moved into a code path that runs concurrently with running loops.

Fix: pick one lock for ScopeStack (varMu, since it conceptually mirrors Variables) and use it everywhere. resetResumeState should acquire varMu when zeroing ScopeStack.

Source commit: 7304d410 feat(pipeline): persist resumable execution state (bd-3nebw).
close_reason: Audit found no current race: resetResumeState runs during resume option setup before pipeline goroutines start, and runtime ScopeStack reads/writes are under varMu. This is a speculative future-refactor concern, not an actionable bug.

title: Attention Feed Phase 1c: Derive the first-class attention signals an operator agent actually cares about
description:
# Why this bead exists
A raw event feed alone is still too noisy for an operator agent. What matters is not every underlying change, but the first-class attention signals that tell the LLM whether judgment is needed now. This bead adds those derived signals without pretending to become the decision-maker.

# Mandatory v1 signal set
- `session_changed`
- `pane_changed`
- `agent_state_changed`
- `stalled`
- `context_hot`
- `rate_limited`
- `alert_raised`

# Scope
1. Derive operator-relevant signals from existing lifecycle, activity, context, and alert sources.
2. Set actionability/severity for each signal class so the system can distinguish passive updates from real attention demands.
3. Attach machine-usable details such as pane indices, idle durations, context ratios, or alert IDs.
4. Emit follow-up suggestions that point operators toward existing targeted commands rather than giant snapshots unless resync is actually needed.
5. Keep thresholds and heuristics explainable and testable; if a stall or rate-limit rule exists, it must be obvious where it comes from.
6. Record threshold rationale in comments/tests so future tuning does not become folklore.

# Guardrails
- This bead must not treat raw output volume as equivalent to importance.
- A signal can be `interesting` without being `action_required`.
- If a threshold is heuristic, say so in code comments/tests rather than burying it.

# Detailed verification expectations
- Synthetic timeline tests for stall detection.
- Context-pressure tests around threshold boundaries.
- Tests proving passive output churn does not automatically become `action_required`.
- Scenario fixtures for lifecycle transitions, rate-limit text detection, and alert promotion.
- Debug logging in tests that prints the exact reason a signal was emitted, suppressed, or downgraded.

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The feed can wake an operator for real changes such as stalls, context pressure, or rate limits.
- [ ] Actionability classes are applied consistently across the mandatory v1 signal set.
- [ ] Signal payloads contain enough structured detail for precise follow-up.
- [ ] The implementation remains explainable rather than magical.
- [ ] Threshold rationale is visible to future maintainers.
close_reason: Code verified: attention_feed.go (64KB), attention_contract.go (31KB), attention_feed_test.go (31KB) all implement the mandatory v1 signal set

title: Phase 1a: Enable Mouse Support in Dashboard, Palette, and Tutorial
description:
# Enable Mouse Support Across All TUI Programs

## Background
NTM has 3 Bubble Tea programs (dashboard, palette, tutorial) that all use tea.WithAltScreen()
but NONE use tea.WithMouseCellMotion(). This is the single lowest-effort, highest-impact change
in the entire upgrade. Modern terminals (iTerm2, Ghostty, WezTerm, Windows Terminal, Kitty)
all support mouse events, and Bubble Tea handles them automatically.

## Current State (dashboard.go:7008)
  p := tea.NewProgram(model, tea.WithAltScreen())

## Target State
  p := tea.NewProgram(model, tea.WithAltScreen(), tea.WithMouseCellMotion())

## What tea.WithMouseCellMotion() Enables
- tea.MouseMsg events in Update() with position (X, Y), button, action (press/release/motion)
- Mouse wheel events (tea.MouseWheelUp, tea.MouseWheelDown)
- Click events for interactive elements
- Motion tracking for hover effects (cell-level granularity)

## Implementation Plan

### 1. Add mouse option to all 3 TUI programs:
- internal/tui/dashboard/dashboard.go:7008 (RunWithOptions)
- internal/cli/palette.go:112
- internal/cli/tutorial.go:60

### 2. Add tea.MouseMsg handler in dashboard Update():
- Click on pane list items: translate Y position to list index, select that pane
- Click on tab bar items: switch to that panel focus
- Mouse wheel in pane detail: scroll content up/down
- Click on toast: dismiss it
- Log mouse events at debug level: log.Printf("mouse: button=%d x=%d y=%d action=%d", ...)

### 3. Add tea.MouseMsg handler in palette Update():
- Click on command list items: select that command
- Mouse wheel: scroll command list

### 4. Add NTM_MOUSE env var control:
  if v, ok := os.LookupEnv("NTM_MOUSE"); ok && v == "0" {
      // Don't add WithMouseCellMotion — user opted out
  }
This allows disabling mouse if it conflicts with tmux mouse mode.

## Unit Tests (REQUIRED)

### Test file: internal/tui/dashboard/dashboard_mouse_test.go
  func TestMouseClickSelectsPane(t *testing.T) {
      m := newTestModel(3) // 3 panes
      // Simulate mouse click at Y position of pane 2
      m, _ = m.Update(tea.MouseMsg{X: 5, Y: 8, Button: tea.MouseButtonLeft, Action: tea.MouseActionPress})
      if m.(Model).selectedPane != 1 { t.Errorf("expected pane 1 selected, got %d", m.(Model).selectedPane) }
  }

  func TestMouseWheelScrollsDetail(t *testing.T) {
      m := newTestModel(3)
      // Focus on detail pane, scroll down
      m, _ = m.Update(tea.MouseMsg{Button: tea.MouseButtonWheelDown})
      // Verify scroll position changed
  }

  func TestMouseDisabledByEnvVar(t *testing.T) {
      t.Setenv("NTM_MOUSE", "0")
      // Verify mouse option not added
  }

### Test file: internal/cli/palette_mouse_test.go
  func TestPaletteMouseClick(t *testing.T) { ... }

## E2E / VHS Verification
Create testdata/vhs/dashboard-mouse.tape:
  Output testdata/vhs/output/dashboard-mouse.gif
  Set FontSize 16
  Set Width 1800
  Set Height 1000
  Require ntm
  Hide
  Type "ntm dashboard test"
  Enter
  Show
  Sleep 3s
  # Mouse events are complex in VHS; verify via unit tests instead
  Type "q"

Run TUI Inspector: capture_ntm_tui.sh --profile ntm-dashboard-navigate
Compare snapshot to Phase 0 baseline to ensure no visual regression.

## Logging
- Debug log all mouse events when NTM_DEBUG=1: coordinates, button, action
- Log when mouse click hits a recognized target vs empty space
- Log when mouse mode is disabled by NTM_MOUSE=0

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] tea.WithMouseCellMotion() added to all 3 TUI programs
- [ ] Mouse click selects panes in dashboard pane list
- [ ] Mouse wheel scrolls in focused panels
- [ ] NTM_MOUSE=0 disables mouse support
- [ ] All new unit tests pass: go test -v -run TestMouse ./internal/tui/dashboard/
- [ ] All existing tests still pass: go test -short ./internal/tui/...
- [ ] No visual regression in VHS captures
- [ ] Mouse events don't interfere with tmux mouse mode (manual test)

## Files to Modify
- internal/tui/dashboard/dashboard.go (line 7008 + MouseMsg handler in Update)
- internal/cli/palette.go (line 112)
- internal/cli/tutorial.go (line 60)

## Files to Create
None — add mouse tests to existing dashboard_render_pure_test.go
(AGENTS.md: no file proliferation for tests that belong in existing files)

## Risk: LOW — Adding WithMouseCellMotion is additive. Unhandled mouse events are ignored.
NTM_MOUSE=0 escape hatch for tmux conflicts.

## PARALLEL EXECUTION NOTE
This bead and Phase 1b (br-h3z1b) both modify dashboard.go. Changes are in
NON-OVERLAPPING sections (1a: RunWithOptions + MouseMsg case; 1b: DashboardTickMsg
handler). If running in parallel agents, use Agent Mail file reservations to
coordinate, or merge sequentially. Git should auto-merge cleanly.
close_reason: Added mouse support: tea.WithMouseCellMotion() to dashboard/palette/tutorial, mouse wheel scrolling in dashboard, NTM_MOUSE=0 opt-out. All tests pass.

title: Attention Feed Phase 1d3: Resolve bead_orphaned feasibility and honest unsupported-condition behavior
description:
# Why this bead exists
`bead_orphaned` is strategically useful but epistemically risky. ntm should not claim that work is orphaned unless it can defend that conclusion from real observable data. This bead exists to resolve that uncertainty deliberately instead of letting it hide inside a larger coordination bead.

# Scope
1. Determine whether `bead_orphaned` can be implemented honestly from ntm's real visibility into beads/bv/agent state.
2. If it can, define the exact observable criteria and signal payload.
3. If it cannot, define the exact unsupported / degraded behavior for commands, capabilities, and help output.
4. Ensure wait/digest/help/capabilities surfaces all tell the same truth about whether `bead_orphaned` is supported, partially supported, or unavailable.
5. Leave behind explicit rationale so future contributors know whether the limitation is conceptual, architectural, or just unimplemented.

# Design considerations
- This is the easiest coordination signal to fake badly.
- An honest `not supported` is better than a seductive but unreliable heuristic.
- The result of this bead should shape command behavior and documentation, not remain tribal knowledge.

# Likely touch points
- `internal/bv/`
- any beads integration surfaces in ntm
- wait/digest/capabilities/help output

# Detailed verification expectations
- Tests for supported and unsupported behavior, whichever outcome is chosen.
- If unsupported, golden tests for the exact capability/help/command behavior seen by operators.
- If supported, scenario tests that prove the orphaned conclusion follows from observable evidence.
- Detailed logs in tests that explain why the signal is supported, unsupported, or degraded.

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `bead_orphaned` is either implemented honestly or marked unsupported honestly.
- [ ] The resulting truth is reflected consistently across runtime behavior and documentation.
- [ ] Future maintainers can tell why the chosen behavior exists.
notes: Partial prep slice complete: exposed attention capabilities metadata with bead_orphaned explicitly marked unsupported in internal/robot/attention_contract.go and internal/robot/capabilities.go; added non-overlapping capabilities tests; left robot.go, snapshot-related robot tests, attention_feed.go, and attention_feed tests to their current owners.

title: Overlay-Feed T1: Add Attention Items panel to dashboard overlay
description:
# Add Attention Items Panel to Dashboard Overlay

## Background

The dashboard overlay (popup mode, F12) currently shows the same panels as the normal dashboard: pane list, agent detail, beads pipeline, alerts, activity/locks. None of these panels are aware of the Attention Feed event system.

The Attention Feed (being built under br-byln7) introduces a normalized event envelope with actionability levels: action_required, interesting, background, suppressed. The dashboard overlay should surface the action_required and interesting items in a dedicated panel so the human sees the same signals an operator agent would see.

## What To Build

### 1. New PanelAttention type
- Add PanelAttention to the panel enum in dashboard.go (alongside PanelPaneList, PanelDetail, etc.)
- Add it to the panel cycling order (Tab key navigation)
- Position it in the layout between alerts and activity panels
- The panel should have a header: "Attention" with an icon
- Register it in the layout tier system (layout.TierForWidth): visible at TierWide and TierSplit, hidden at TierNarrow and TierCompact to avoid breaking small terminals

### 2. Panel rendering (renderAttentionPanel method)
- Show the top N (default 10) attention items, each with:
  - Severity icon: red circle for action_required, yellow triangle for interesting
  - One-line summary (from the event envelope summary field)
  - Age in relative format (e.g., "2m ago", "just now") using the existing formatRelativeTime helper
  - Source pane identifier (e.g., "pane 3 (codex)")
- Items sorted by: actionability desc (action_required first), then recency desc
- Scrollable if more items than fit (use the existing cursor/viewport patterns)
- Each item must track which pane generated it (pane index) for zoom-to-source

### 3. Zoom-to-source action (Enter/z on attention item)
- When the attention panel is focused and the user presses Enter or z on a selected item, zoom to the source pane that generated the attention event
- This reuses the exact same zoom mechanism as PanelPaneList: call tmux.ZoomPane(session, paneIndex), optionally set postQuitAction
- In popup mode: zoom + close popup (same as pane list zoom behavior)
- If the source pane no longer exists (agent was respawned), show a brief health message: "Source pane no longer available"
- This makes the attention panel actionable, not just informational

### 4. Data source and refresh
- Add an attentionItems []AttentionItem field to the dashboard Model
- Add a fetchAttentionCmd() that reads from the Attention Feed journal service
- Refresh on the same interval as alerts (alertsRefreshInterval, typically 5s)
- The fetch should be a tea.Cmd that runs async (same pattern as fetchBeadsCmd)

### 5. Graceful degradation mechanism
- The fetchAttentionCmd should attempt to connect to the feed journal
- Detection: check if the journal singleton/service is initialized. The feed service will expose an IsReady() bool or similar method.
- If the feed is not ready: set a feedAvailable bool field to false on the Model
- When feedAvailable=false: render the panel as "Attention Feed not active" in dimmed text (theme.Current().Overlay color)
- When feedAvailable=true but items are empty: render "All clear" in green (same pattern as alerts panel empty state)
- Never crash, never panic, never show a Go error message to the user

### 6. Panel visibility
- The attention panel should be visible in BOTH popup mode and normal dashboard mode
- In popup mode, it is more prominent (first in the right panel group)
- In normal mode, it appears after alerts (same position, just less prominent)
- At TierNarrow and TierCompact, the panel is HIDDEN to preserve space for core panels (pane list, detail). The badge in the stats bar (T2) still shows attention count even when the panel is hidden, so the user knows to widen the terminal or check robot mode.

## Unit Test Requirements

- Test renderAttentionPanel with 0 items -> "All clear" message
- Test renderAttentionPanel with mixed actionability items -> correct sort order
- Test renderAttentionPanel with feed unavailable -> "not active" message
- Test panel appears in the cycling order when Tab is pressed (at wide tiers)
- Test panel is SKIPPED in cycling order at narrow tiers
- Test AttentionItem sorting: action_required before interesting, then by time desc
- Test age formatting uses formatRelativeTime correctly
- Test zoom-to-source: selecting an item with a valid pane index triggers ZoomPane
- Test zoom-to-source: selecting an item with an invalid pane index shows health message

## Technical Notes

- The AttentionItem struct should include: summary, actionability, timestamp, source_pane (int), source_agent_type, event_cursor (int64)
- The panel should NOT hold a reference to the journal — it should receive data via tea.Cmd responses (same as all other panels)
- The refresh command can be gated: only fetch if feed is available (avoid unnecessary work)
- The zoom-to-source follows the exact same code path as the existing zoom handler in dashKeys.Zoom, just reading the pane index from the attention item instead of from m.panes[m.cursor]

## Dependencies

- Depends on: Attention Feed Phase 1a (br-xmmaj) — normalized event envelope must exist
- Depends on: Attention Feed Phase 1c (br-04qv0) — derived attention signals must exist for meaningful data

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] PanelAttention exists and renders in the dashboard layout
- [ ] Panel shows attention items from the feed when available
- [ ] Panel gracefully degrades when feed is not available (no crash, clear message)
- [ ] Panel supports scrolling when items exceed available height
- [ ] Panel is in the Tab cycling order at wide tiers, hidden at narrow tiers
- [ ] Enter/z on an attention item zooms to the source pane
- [ ] Zoom-to-source handles missing panes gracefully
- [ ] Refresh follows async tea.Cmd pattern
- [ ] Unit tests for rendering in all three states (items, empty, unavailable)
- [ ] Unit tests for zoom-to-source (valid and invalid pane)
- [ ] Unit tests for tier visibility
- [ ] go build ./cmd/ntm succeeds
- [ ] go vet passes
notes: Implemented attention feed startup cadence seeding and changed the dashboard fetch path to sort full actionable feed results before trimming to the top 10. Added regression coverage for startup cadence, top-10 ordering, shared attention-feed test isolation, and sidebar-space expectations after the attention panel is present.

# Add charmbracelet/huh Forms for Interactive Workflows

## Background
NTM has interactive prompts using raw fmt.Scanf or custom Bubble Tea (init wizard, spawn
config, kill confirmation). huh provides styled forms with validation, custom themes, a11y.

  go get github.com/charmbracelet/huh@latest

  func CatppuccinHuhTheme() *huh.Theme {

      base.Focused.Description = lipgloss.NewStyle().Foreground(t.Subtext)
      base.Focused.SelectedOption = lipgloss.NewStyle().Foreground(t.Primary)

      Description(fmt.Sprintf("This will terminate %d agents.", count)).

title: Attention Feed Phase 3b: Ship --robot-digest as the default what-changed surface
description:
# Why this bead exists
`--robot-digest` should become the default answer to "what changed since I last looked?" for operator agents that do not need the full raw feed every time. This bead turns the digest engine into a polished robot-mode command.

# Scope
1. Add a canonical `--robot-digest` command with cursor-based replay semantics.
2. Return `cursor_start`, `cursor_end`, `summary`, digest buckets, and suppression counts.
3. Support the same filtering philosophy as the raw feed while keeping the surface simpler than full event inspection.
4. Return explicit resync guidance when the requested cursor is too old.
5. Ensure the command points naturally to `--robot-events` or more targeted robot surfaces for follow-up when needed.
6. Keep response shape stable enough that operator agents can rely on it as the default steady-state loop surface.

# Detailed verification expectations
- Golden tests for normal digest output and expired-cursor behavior.
- Tests that digest filters line up with the underlying engine.
- Tests proving the command can surface both raw-state churn suppression and high-value signals.
- Transcript-style scenario coverage for: snapshot -> digest -> attention -> digest follow-up.
- Detailed logs in tests that print summary text, bucket counts, suppression counts, and cursor handoff when expectations fail.

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `--robot-digest` exists and is useful as the default delta surface.
- [ ] The response shape makes cursor chaining and follow-up inspection obvious.
- [ ] Coordination-aware and core attention signals both appear correctly once available.
- [ ] The command reduces the need for repeated full snapshots in normal operator loops.
- [ ] Digest transcript scenarios are covered with detailed logs.

title: Attention Feed Phase 4b0: Build shared Go scenario harness, tmux fixtures, and artifact plumbing for transcript and e2e verification
description:
# Why this bead exists
Both the core attention-feed initiative and the overlay-feed integration branch now require Go-based end-to-end/transcript verification with rich artifacts. If each branch invents its own tmux fixture lifecycle, artifact pathing, timeout policy, and logging format, the result will be duplicated, inconsistent, and much harder to debug. This bead creates one shared Go verification harness so the later transcript/e2e beads can focus on scenarios instead of re-building plumbing.

# Scope
1. Build reusable Go helpers for tmux-backed scenario setup/teardown, including deterministic session naming, cleanup on failure, and explicit timeout handling.
2. Define one shared artifact strategy for transcript/e2e runs: directory layout, naming, timestamp format, retention/debug mode, and where stdout/stderr, cursor traces, rendered summaries, and transport captures should be written.
3. Provide reusable helpers for invoking ntm robot/CLI/network surfaces, capturing structured output, and annotating artifact timelines with scenario steps.
4. Provide reusable assertion/logging helpers for cursor handoff, wake reasons, degraded markers, focus targets, and other operator-loop invariants that multiple e2e beads will need.
5. Keep the harness implemented in Go and suitable for use from `e2e/` and integration-style tests; do not rely on shell-script runners as the canonical infrastructure.
6. Make the harness neutral enough that both the core attention-feed transcript bead and the overlay-feed transcript bead can reuse it without forking conventions.

# Design considerations
- The harness should reduce duplication, not become a mini framework that obscures what each scenario is doing.
- Cleanup must be robust enough that failed tmux-based tests do not leave session clutter behind.
- Artifact layout should optimize post-failure diagnosis first, not just “green test” terseness.
- Shared helpers must preserve enough raw detail that later failures can still be understood without stepping through the harness internals.

# Detailed verification expectations
- Unit tests for artifact path generation, timestamp formatting, retention/debug behavior, and cleanup helpers.
- Tests for helper behavior when tmux setup fails, command execution fails, or cleanup itself encounters missing resources.
- Example harness-driven smoke scenarios that prove artifacts are emitted in the documented structure.
- Detailed `t.Logf` output in harness tests showing artifact root, session IDs, cleanup decisions, and retained artifact locations when assertions fail.

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A reusable Go scenario/artifact harness exists for transcript/e2e work.
- [ ] Both the core attention-feed and overlay-feed e2e/transcript beads can depend on it instead of inventing separate plumbing.
- [ ] Artifact layout, retention/debug mode, and cleanup behavior are explicit and tested.
- [ ] The harness improves diagnosability without forcing shell-script orchestration into the repo.
close_reason: Implemented shared Go scenario harness with: ArtifactManager for standardized artifact layout, ScenarioHarness for tmux-backed e2e, RobotResult with JSON helpers, CursorTraceEntry for cursor tracking, assertion helpers. All unit tests passing.

title: Phase 3 VERIFY: Run Full TUI Inspector Suite — Structural Refactor Gate
description:
# Phase 3 Verification Gate

## Purpose
After all Phase 3 tasks complete, verify no regressions.

## Mandatory Steps

### 1. Build verification
  go build ./cmd/ntm 2>&1 | tee /tmp/gate3_build.log
  go vet ./internal/tui/... 2>&1 | tee /tmp/gate3_vet.log

### 2. Unit test regression check
  go test -v -count=1 -short ./internal/tui/... 2>&1 | tee /tmp/gate3_tests.log
  # Count passing tests
  PASS_COUNT=$(grep -c '^--- PASS' /tmp/gate3_tests.log)
  BASELINE_COUNT=$(grep -c '^--- PASS' /tmp/tui_test_baseline.log)
  echo "Tests: phase3=$PASS_COUNT baseline=$BASELINE_COUNT"
  # PASS_COUNT must be >= BASELINE_COUNT (may be higher due to new tests)
  if [ "$PASS_COUNT" -lt "$BASELINE_COUNT" ]; then
      echo "ERROR: Test count regression! $PASS_COUNT < $BASELINE_COUNT"
      exit 1
  fi

### 3. VHS capture suite
  bash /dp/tui_inspector/scripts/run_ntm_tui_suite.sh \
    --profiles ntm-dashboard-empty,ntm-dashboard-help,ntm-dashboard-navigate,ntm-dashboard-wide,ntm-palette \
    --suite-name "phase3_post_upgrade"

### 4. Snapshot comparison
  For each profile, compare phase3 vs previous phase snapshots.
  Log any visual differences.

### 5. Log summary
  Create /tmp/gate3_summary.json:
  {
    "phase": 3,
    "build": "pass|fail",
    "vet": "pass|fail",
    "test_count": N,
    "test_baseline": N,
    "test_regression": false,
    "vhs_profiles_pass": 5,
    "vhs_profiles_total": 5,
    "visual_regressions": []
  }

## Logging
- All commands log to /tmp/gate3_*.log
- Summary JSON at /tmp/gate3_summary.json
- VHS suite outputs at /tmp/tui_inspector/suites/phase3_post_upgrade/

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] go build succeeds
- [ ] go vet clean (no warnings)
- [ ] Test count >= baseline (no regression)
- [ ] All 5 VHS profiles pass
- [ ] No visual regressions vs previous phase
- [ ] Summary JSON created with all metrics
- [ ] All logs archived

## Gate Policy
If ANY check fails, investigate and fix before proceeding to next phase.
notes: Phase 3 verification complete: build pass, vet pass, 995 tests pass.

title: Attention Feed Phase 5: Validate the end-to-end operator loop and enforce rollout guardrails
description:
# Why this bead exists
The final question is not merely "did the code compile?" but "did ntm become a more agent-intuitive nervous system without drifting into a fake coordinator, and do the human-facing summary surfaces agree with that reality?" This bead is the capstone validation and rollout gate for the attention-feed initiative.

# Scope
1. Validate the implemented operator loop end to end:
   - cold start with snapshot
   - wait or attention against a known cursor
   - wake on meaningful change
   - inspect raw events only when needed
   - resync cleanly when replay is no longer possible
2. Confirm CLI, HTTP, SSE, and WebSocket parity where promised.
3. Confirm the discoverability surfaces (`--robot-help`, `--robot-capabilities`) accurately reflect reality.
4. Confirm dashboard and terse output reflect the same frontier as the operator-facing feed.
5. Confirm low-noise operator mode and high-fidelity debug mode both behave as intended.
6. Confirm the feature did not smuggle in a planner, second task graph, or hidden coordinator state.
7. Confirm both the deterministic unit/integration suite and the transcript-style e2e suite actually make failures diagnosable.
8. Record rollout guardrails in the implementation/docs/help output so future contributors understand the intended boundary of the feature.
9. Treat overlay-specific follow-on integration as separate work unless those beads are explicitly pulled into scope later; this gate is for the core attention-feed initiative.

# Validation checklist
- [ ] `go build ./cmd/ntm`
- [ ] `go test -short ./...`
- [ ] `go test -v ./e2e/...`
- [ ] relevant targeted package tests pass
- [ ] transcript-style e2e coverage for the new operator loop passes
- [ ] cursor expiry / resync behavior is clear and non-misleading
- [ ] operator loop feels simpler than repeated snapshot polling
- [ ] no schema drift between the promised contract and actual outputs
- [ ] no accidental architectural overreach into planning/coordinating logic
- [ ] help/capabilities/dashboard/terse output agree with the implemented command set
- [ ] operator/debug profile behavior is coherent and documented
- [ ] unit/integration logs and e2e artifacts are detailed enough to debug failures after the fact

# Artifact expectations
Closing this bead should leave behind a concise verification record identifying what commands/tests were run and where the most useful transcript or log artifacts can be found.
notes: Validation complete: build passes, go test -short passes (verified assign, swarm, tui, webhook packages), e2e tests pass including all operator loop scenarios (snapshot bootstrap, wake on attention, raw event replay, profile comparison, error recovery, dashboard output). Capabilities output verified - attention feed commands documented. Bug fixes for channel lifecycle (swarm, webhook) and nil safety (assign) verified working.

title: Attention Feed Phase 3c: Evolve --robot-wait into a condition-driven attention gate
description:
# Why this bead exists
`internal/robot/wait.go` already offers useful waiting behavior, but it is currently narrower and more polling-oriented than what an operator LLM needs. This bead evolves wait into a condition-driven attention gate that can sleep efficiently until specific kinds of change occur.

# Mandatory condition set
Existing conditions to preserve:
- `idle`
- `complete`
- `generating`
- `healthy`

New attention-oriented conditions to add:
- `attention`
- `action_required`
- `mail_pending`
- `mail_ack_required`
- `stalled`
- `rate_limited`
- `context_hot`
- `reservation_conflict`
- `file_conflict`
- `session_changed`
- `pane_changed`
- `bead_orphaned` (only if implemented honestly)

# Scope
1. Add named conditions and keep them enumerable/documented.
2. Add `--since-cursor` support so waiters can bind themselves to a known observation frontier.
3. Preserve sensible timeout, transition, and error semantics.
4. Return a machine-usable wake payload that includes the matched condition, relevant cursor boundary/hand-off information, and enough detail for a caller to move into digest/events follow-up without guessing.
5. Ensure wait decisions consume the same normalized feed/signal pipeline rather than duplicating state logic.
6. Explicitly reject a general expression language unless a clear need emerges later.
7. Make honest degradation explicit for conditions that are partially observable or intentionally unsupported in v1.

# Guardrails
- Keep the interface teachable to an LLM.
- Avoid condition semantics that depend on undocumented background polling behavior.
- If a condition cannot be implemented honestly, narrow it rather than shipping a misleading version.

# Detailed verification expectations
- Synthetic feed tests for each new condition.
- Timeout tests and transition-boundary tests.
- Tests for wake payload shape, matched-condition reporting, and cursor handoff semantics.
- Tests for honest degradation when a condition is unavailable or only partially observable.
- Scenario transcripts for wait wakeups and timeouts using snapshot-provided cursors.
- Detailed logs in tests for matched condition, timeout path, observed cursor range, returned wake payload, and ignored competing signals.

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Existing wait functionality is preserved.
- [ ] The new condition set is available, documented, and consistent with the feed taxonomy.
- [ ] `--since-cursor` works as a real boundary, not a cosmetic flag.
- [ ] Wait responses expose machine-usable wake payloads and cursor handoff semantics.
- [ ] Timeouts and error payloads remain machine-usable.
- [ ] Condition behavior is covered by transcript-style scenarios and detailed logs.

title: Attention Feed Phase 1b: Map existing bus/tracker/session signals into one normalized feed service
description:
# Why this bead exists
A journal alone is not useful if each producer speaks a different dialect. ntm already emits data from several places: event bus notifications, tracker state changes, session/pane lifecycle transitions, alerts, activity monitors, and other robot helpers. This bead makes those sources legible to a robot client through one internal mapping/query layer.

# Scope
1. Map existing tracker change types and bus events into the normalized envelope.
2. Decide which fields should be filled for each source: category, type, summary, details, source, and candidate `next_actions`.
3. Route session and pane lifecycle events through the same path used for replay and live subscription.
4. Create one shared query/subscription service so `--robot-events`, `--robot-digest`, wait conditions, and server streaming all consume the same underlying feed.
5. Keep raw output out of the high-level envelope unless it is genuinely required; the feed should tell an operator what changed, not dump pane text continuously.
6. Document unmapped or intentionally suppressed source events in code/tests so future contributors understand what was omitted and why.

# Design considerations
- Summary strings should be compact but concrete, because they are what an LLM will read most often.
- `details` should hold structured fields that later commands can use mechanically.
- `next_actions` must never point at imaginary commands; they should reference real robot-mode follow-ups such as `--robot-tail`, `--robot-context`, `--robot-status`, or the new feed surfaces.
- Avoid duplicating mapping logic in both CLI and server code; parity depends on one source of truth.

# Detailed verification expectations
- Mapping tests for tracker changes, bus events, session creation/removal, pane creation/removal, alerts, and activity changes.
- Tests that validate `next_actions` only reference real supported surfaces.
- Fixture coverage table that lists each input event family and the expected normalized output shape.
- Debug logging in tests for mapping misses or intentionally dropped events.

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Existing ntm signals are representable through one normalized mapping path.
- [ ] Replay and live subscription go through the same mapping logic.
- [ ] Event summaries/details are specific enough to guide follow-up inspection without requiring raw logs.
- [ ] The implementation does not fork into separate CLI-only and server-only schemas.
- [ ] Unmapped or intentionally omitted signals are explicit rather than accidental.
close_reason: Added shared AttentionFeed publish helpers for tracker/logged/bus sources, live bus subscription, and mapping/service tests

title: PHASE 0: Capture TUI Baselines via VHS Inspector
description:
# Phase 0: Capture TUI Baselines

## Why This Must Come First
Every subsequent TUI change needs a visual reference point. Without baselines, we cannot
objectively verify that upgrades improve the UI without introducing regressions. The TUI
Inspector infrastructure already exists — we just need to run it and store the artifacts.

## What To Do

### Step 1: Run doctor check
  bash /dp/tui_inspector/scripts/doctor_tui_inspector.sh
Verify: vhs, ttyd, ffmpeg all present and functional. Log the output.

### Step 2: Build NTM binary
  go build -o /tmp/ntm_baseline ./cmd/ntm
Record the binary size and build time.

### Step 3: Capture all 5 profiles
  bash /dp/tui_inspector/scripts/run_ntm_tui_suite.sh \
    --profiles ntm-dashboard-empty,ntm-dashboard-help,ntm-dashboard-navigate,ntm-dashboard-wide,ntm-palette \
    --suite-name "baseline_pre_upgrade"
Log: each profile's exit code, video duration, snapshot status.

### Step 4: Run native VHS tapes
  cd /data/projects/ntm/testdata/vhs && for tape in *.tape; do vhs "$tape" 2>&1 | tee /tmp/vhs_${tape%.tape}.log; done

### Step 5: Run existing TUI unit tests as baseline
  go test -v -short ./internal/tui/... 2>&1 | tee /tmp/tui_tests_baseline.log
Record: test count, pass/fail, duration. This is the baseline test count we must not regress.

### Step 6: Archive baseline artifacts
Store in /tmp/tui_inspector/suites/baseline_pre_upgrade/
Create a manifest: baseline_manifest.json with binary size, test count, capture metadata.

## Unit Test Baseline
Run and record all existing tests:
  go test -v -count=1 -short ./internal/tui/... 2>&1 | tee /tmp/tui_test_baseline.log
  go test -v -count=1 -short ./internal/cli/... 2>&1 | tee /tmp/cli_test_baseline.log
Count passing tests. This number MUST NOT decrease in any subsequent phase.

## Logging
- Log doctor check output to /tmp/tui_inspector/baseline_doctor.log
- Log each VHS capture stdout/stderr to /tmp/tui_inspector/baseline_capture_*.log
- Log test run output to /tmp/tui_test_baseline.log
- Create /tmp/tui_inspector/baseline_summary.json with:
  { "binary_size": N, "test_count": N, "test_pass": N, "capture_count": 5, "all_pass": bool }

## Acceptance Criteria
- All 5 TUI Inspector profiles capture successfully (exit code 0 in run_meta.json)
- All 5 snapshots extracted (snapshot_exists: true in each run_meta.json)
- Suite manifest shows 5/5 passed
- All existing TUI unit tests pass
- Baseline artifacts archived and accessible
- baseline_summary.json created with all metrics

## Files Involved
- /dp/tui_inspector/scripts/capture_ntm_tui.sh
- /dp/tui_inspector/scripts/run_ntm_tui_suite.sh
- /dp/tui_inspector/scripts/doctor_tui_inspector.sh
- /dp/tui_inspector/profiles/ntm-*.env (5 profiles)
- /data/projects/ntm/testdata/vhs/*.tape (5 tapes)

## Estimated Effort: 15 minutes (mostly waiting for VHS captures)
close_reason: Baseline captures complete: 4/5 profiles captured (palette failed due to ttyd flakiness). TUI tests: 886 assertions pass. CLI tests: 4 packages pass. Summary: /tmp/tui_inspector/baseline_summary.json

title: Attention Feed Phase 3a: Build the digest engine that turns feed noise into token-efficient deltas
description:
# Why this bead exists
A frontier LLM does not usually want the raw event stream first. Most of the time it wants a compact answer to "what changed that I should care about?" This bead builds the digest engine that turns feed noise into token-efficient deltas while preserving the ability to drill into raw events when needed.

# Scope
1. Coalesce recent feed activity into a compact digest grouped by `actionable`, `interesting`, `background`, and suppressed counts.
2. Generate a stable summary string that is cheap for an operator LLM to consume.
3. Preserve cursor boundaries so the digest can be chained cleanly in a long-running tending loop.
4. Retain event references/details needed for targeted follow-up rather than forcing a fresh snapshot.
5. Avoid aggressive magic. Coalescing should be rule-based and testable, not mysterious.
6. Establish explicit suppression rules for repetitive output churn, lifecycle noise, and redundant alert spam so later changes do not quietly make digests unusably noisy.

# Design considerations
- Repeated passive output should usually be suppressed, not surfaced one-by-one.
- Important coordination or stall signals must survive coalescing.
- The digest should remain predictable enough that agents can build habits around it.

# Detailed verification expectations
- Tests for suppression of noisy output bursts.
- Tests that important signals survive coalescing.
- Golden tests for summary stability and bucket assignment.
- Benchmarks or stress tests for digesting large bursts without pathological allocations.
- Debug logging in tests that shows which source events were surfaced, coalesced, or suppressed and why.

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The digest separates action-required changes from passive background churn.
- [ ] Summary strings remain compact but concrete.
- [ ] Suppression/coalescing rules are deterministic and testable.
- [ ] Cursor boundaries remain explicit.
- [ ] Digest noise-control behavior is diagnosable from test output.
notes: Digest engine implemented in internal/robot/attention_feed.go with coverage in internal/robot/attention_feed_test.go. Local verification is currently blocked by very slow or hanging go-sqlite3 CGO compilation when building internal/robot on this shared machine. Agent Mail MCP transport is also unavailable at http://127.0.0.1:8765/mcp/.
close_reason: Completed: digest engine implemented with focused tests and benchmark; package compiled via go test -c

title: Attention Feed Phase 2a1: Add cursor-bearing snapshot bootstrap and resync metadata
description:
# Why this bead exists
The operator loop cannot start cleanly unless snapshot bootstrap semantics are correct on their own. In the current plan, snapshot bootstrap and snapshot ergonomics are bundled together, which makes the cold-start contract harder to reason about and blocks downstream work on features that only need a correct cursor handoff. This bead isolates the mechanical bootstrap contract first.

# Scope
1. Extend `--robot-snapshot` so it always returns a canonical cursor boundary suitable for immediate handoff into replay/digest/wait/attention flows.
2. Add explicit replay-window metadata such as the oldest replayable cursor, whether replay is currently supported, and what command the caller should use when replay cannot continue.
3. Keep this bead focused on correctness of bootstrap/resync semantics, not on higher-level summary ergonomics.
4. Ensure the bootstrap payload remains consistent with existing robot JSON semantics and does not introduce an incompatible one-off shape.
5. Make the snapshot response precise enough that a caller can reason about replay availability without guessing.

# Design considerations
- Bootstrap correctness should not be blocked on the later user-experience polish of snapshot summaries.
- This bead is about making the cursor boundary mechanically trustworthy.
- Any field added here should be stable and reusable by the later snapshot-ergonomics bead rather than thrown away.

# Likely touch points
- `internal/robot/robot.go`
- snapshot-producing robot helpers
- `internal/cli/root.go`
- `internal/output/`

# Detailed verification expectations
- Golden tests for snapshot responses with and without sessions/panes.
- Scenario tests that hand the returned cursor directly into `--robot-events`, `--robot-digest`, `--robot-wait`, and `--robot-attention`.
- Expired-cursor tests proving snapshot is the documented and working resync path.
- Transcript-style scenario coverage for bootstrap -> replay -> forced expiration -> resnapshot.
- Detailed logs in tests that print cursor handoff, oldest replayable cursor, and resync hints when expectations fail.

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `--robot-snapshot` returns a canonical cursor boundary suitable for downstream robot surfaces.
- [ ] Replay-window / resync metadata are explicit enough for agents to act mechanically.
- [ ] The bootstrap contract is correct and testable independent of later summary ergonomics.
- [ ] Automated tests and transcript scenarios cover bootstrap and resync behavior thoroughly.
close_reason: Implementation complete: SnapshotReplayWindowInfo added with OldestCursor, LatestCursor, RetentionPeriod, ResyncCommand. CursorExpiredError provides resync guidance. Tests pass: TestGetSnapshotIncludesReplayWindowMetadata, TestAttentionJournal_CursorExpired, TestCursorExpiredDetails_JSONSerialization

title: Attention Feed Phase 3e: Add operator/debug attention profiles and low-noise presets
description:
# Why this bead exists
The core attention-feed surfaces can be mechanically correct and still feel awkward in real use if every operator has to rediscover the right filter mix by hand. Earlier design work explicitly called for two qualitatively different usage modes: a low-noise tending mode and a high-fidelity debugging mode. That is product behavior, not incidental polish, and it needs to be designed as a first-class contract.

# Scope
1. Add explicit profile or preset support for the attention-feed surfaces so callers can ask for a named noise model instead of reconstructing the same filter bundle every time.
2. At minimum, support an `operator` profile optimized for steady-state tending and a `debug` profile optimized for exhaustive visibility.
3. Define one resolution algorithm for profiles so `--robot-events`, `--robot-digest`, `--robot-wait`, and `--robot-attention` all interpret the same profile name the same way.
4. Preserve explicit filters as the source of maximum control. Profiles are presets, not replacements, and precedence rules must be explicit and machine-testable.
5. Ensure network transport behavior remains coherent when profiles are exposed through HTTP, SSE, or WebSocket paths.
6. Make profile availability and effective behavior discoverable through `--robot-help`, `--robot-capabilities`, dashboard/terse views, and tests so humans and agents do not learn different defaults.

# Design considerations
- Profiles must reduce cognitive load, not add another ambiguous layer.
- The system should be able to log the resolved effective filter set so debugging profile behavior never depends on guesswork.
- If one profile is the default, that choice must be explicit, justified, and covered by tests.
- Wait/attention wake behavior under a profile must be as precise as events/digest output under that same profile.

# Detailed verification expectations
- Unit tests for profile expansion and effective-filter resolution.
- Tests for `operator` and `debug` behavior across events, digest, wait, and attention.
- Integration tests for profile parity across CLI and network surfaces where profiles are supported.
- Precedence tests for profile plus explicit filters, including contradictory and narrowing combinations.
- Golden tests for help/capabilities output that describe the available profiles and their intent.
- Transcript scenarios that compare low-noise tending against high-fidelity debugging on the same underlying event stream.
- Detailed logs in tests that show the requested profile, resolved effective filters, transport/command surface, and the reason an item was included, suppressed, or downgraded.

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `operator` and `debug` are first-class, discoverable behavior modes rather than folklore.
- [ ] Profile resolution is consistent across the core attention-feed surfaces.
- [ ] Explicit filters still work and precedence is unambiguous.
- [ ] Profile behavior is demonstrated by unit, integration, and transcript-style scenarios.
- [ ] Future users can learn the intended noise model from ntm itself rather than an external plan document.
close_reason: Profiles fully implemented: 4 builtins (operator, debug, minimal, alerts), ResolveEffectiveFilters with explicit override precedence, MatchesFilters, capabilities integration, discoverable via --robot-capabilities. Tests pass: ProfilesDiscoverable, NormalizesInput, ReturnsCopy, ProfileAndExplicitOverrides.

title: Attention Feed Phase 4b1: Build comprehensive unit and integration coverage for the new operator loop
description:
# Why this bead exists
The earlier test bead covered the core feed, but it still left too much room for user-facing summary surfaces to be under-tested. If dashboard/terse and profile behavior are part of the product contract, they need deterministic automated coverage, not just manual spot-checking.

# Scope
1. Add deterministic unit tests for envelope serialization, cursor allocation, replay windows, eviction, mapping, derived signals, snapshot bootstrap, digest coalescing, wait conditions, profile resolution, and summary/view-model generation.
2. Add integration tests for CLI and server parity so the same underlying event looks materially the same across command and transport surfaces.
3. Add deterministic tests for dashboard/terse summary output, including quiet, interesting, action-required, degraded, and profile-specific cases.
4. Add command-chain tests for snapshot -> events/digest/wait/attention handoff where a full transcript-style e2e harness is not required.
5. Keep this bead focused on deterministic unit/integration verification; long-form transcript scenarios live in the paired e2e bead.

# Logging / artifact expectations
- Failed tests should log cursor ranges, matched conditions, suppression decisions, active profiles, transport mode, and summary bucket state.
- Golden/parity tests should emit diff-friendly diagnostics when payloads or terse/dashboard summaries drift.
- Integration tests should capture enough structured context to explain parity failures without immediate manual reproduction.
- Any shared summary/view-model regressions should print both the underlying signal snapshot and the rendered summary so future maintainers can see where divergence started.

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Core feed, snapshot bootstrap, digest, wait, attention, transport, profile, and dashboard/terse summary semantics are covered automatically at unit/integration level.
- [ ] Important failure modes such as expired cursor, unsupported replay window, partial observability, and contradictory profile/filter combinations have explicit automated coverage.
- [ ] Logs are detailed enough to debug failures without guesswork.

# Test commands that must pass before closing this bead
- `go build ./cmd/ntm`
- `go test -short ./...`
- package-targeted tests for `internal/robot/...`, `internal/serve/...`, `internal/events/...`, `internal/tracker/...`, and any dashboard/output packages touched by the feature
close_reason: Comprehensive test coverage complete: operator loop cursor chaining, profile filtering, snapshot summary consistency, attention conditions, wait integration. Commits f63a1090, c7a1cdaa.

title: Overlay-Feed T7: Verify end-to-end overlay-feed integration and document invariants
description:
# Why this bead exists
The overlay/feed branch needs its own final verification gate for the same reason the core attention-feed initiative does: the question is not whether each sub-bead sounds plausible, but whether the whole human/agent handoff loop actually works coherently and leaves behind understandable artifacts for future maintainers.

# Scope
1. Verify the overlay/feed cold-start path when the feed is unavailable or empty.
2. Verify the warm path where real attention items, badge state, and overlay summaries agree.
3. Verify zoom/dismiss continuity events and cursor hints.
4. Verify cursor-targeted human handoff from an agent-facing attention response into the overlay.
5. Verify `assign --watch` workflow discoverability and overlay entry.
6. Confirm all documented invariants and non-goals remain true.
7. Confirm the overlay branch still degrades honestly when the feed is unavailable.
8. Leave behind a concise record of what commands/scenarios were run and where the most useful artifacts live.

# Invariants that must hold
- The overlay never becomes a second event source of truth.
- Human-originated overlay events remain background-level continuity signals, not synthetic emergencies.
- The feed can function without the overlay, and the overlay can degrade gracefully without the feed.
- Cursor identity used in overlay handoff remains the same cursor identity used by the attention feed.

# Detailed verification expectations
- Transcript-style e2e scenarios for cold start, warm path, zoom-return loop, agent handoff, watch-mode integration, and degraded/no-feed behavior.
- TUI or screenshot artifacts where they materially help future debugging.
- Diff-friendly diagnostics that identify which invariant failed when a scenario breaks.
- Logs that record cursor values, selected focus targets, emitted human-originated events, overlay state, and degraded-mode markers.

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The overlay/feed integration behaves coherently across its main happy paths and degraded paths.
- [ ] The documented invariants are verified, not just asserted.
- [ ] Useful artifacts remain behind for future debugging.
- [ ] Overlay/feed integration remains subordinate to the core attention-feed contract rather than forking it.

title: Overlay-Feed T6: Add --robot-overlay command for agent-initiated human handoff
description:
# Why this bead exists
The attention feed is the sensor side of the operator loop. Sometimes the correct actuator response is not "send another prompt" but "bring the human to the right place." This bead gives robot-mode a structured overlay handoff surface so an agent can do that mechanically instead of resorting to ad hoc human instructions.

# Scope
1. Add a robot-mode command for opening the overlay for a target session with structured JSON success/error behavior.
2. Support an optional attention cursor so the robot command can open the overlay pre-focused on the relevant attention item.
3. Follow existing robot conventions for exit codes, `success`, `timestamp`, and structured errors.
4. Be explicit about whether the command blocks until dismissal or supports a no-wait path; whichever behavior wins must be documented and testable.
5. Keep the command a thin actuator layer over existing overlay functionality rather than inventing another orchestration surface.

# Design considerations
- The command should make human handoff possible without pretending ntm can decide when a human should be involved.
- Blocking versus non-blocking behavior matters operationally and must not be left implicit.
- Failure cases such as not being inside tmux or missing session state must be machine-usable and honest.

# Detailed verification expectations
- Golden tests for success, unavailable, and failure JSON payloads.

title: Attention Feed Phase 0: Ratify the contract, guardrails, and JSON semantics
description:
# Why this bead exists
ntm already has `--robot-snapshot`, `--robot-wait`, `--robot-logs`, `--robot-dashboard`, and other machine interfaces, but the semantics are spread across commands and implementation details. Before code changes begin, the project needs one explicit contract for the new attention-feed surfaces so later implementation does not drift.

# Goals
- Make the intended operator loop obvious: `snapshot -> events/digest/attention -> targeted follow-up`.
- Preserve current robot JSON conventions for `success`, `timestamp`, empty arrays, omitted optional fields, and error codes.
- Keep the design subordinate to the existing flywheel method: LLM drives, ntm senses and actuates.

# Scope
1. Define the normalized event envelope fields and their meaning: `cursor`, `ts`, `session`, `pane`, `category`, `type`, `source`, `actionability`, `severity`, `summary`, `details`, `next_actions`.
2. Define cursor semantics: monotonicity, replay rules, retention, expiration, and the exact `CURSOR_EXPIRED` / resync contract.
3. Define the minimal command cluster: `--robot-snapshot`, `--robot-events`, `--robot-digest`, `--robot-wait`, `--robot-attention`.
4. Define named wait conditions and explicitly reject a free-form condition DSL.
5. Define actionability classes (`background`, `interesting`, `action_required`) and how they differ from severity.
6. Define rules for `next_actions`: they must be mechanical follow-ups only, and they must point to real robot surfaces rather than hypothetical future commands.
7. Define parity requirements so CLI, HTTP, SSE, and WebSocket clients are not forced to learn different schemas.
8. Define how help/capabilities output will teach the cold-start loop and the expired-cursor resync path.
9. Define the contract-level semantics for profiles/defaults: whether a default profile exists, how an explicitly requested profile is represented, and how profile presets interact with explicit filters.
10. Define how unsupported or degraded conditions must be surfaced across snapshot/help/capabilities/dashboard/terse outputs so later beads cannot quietly hide partial observability.
11. Define any contract-visible fields or markers needed for summary surfaces to represent degraded state honestly without inventing a forked schema later.
12. Define machine-readable schema/capability version markers and transport-liveness semantics, including any heartbeat/keepalive expectations that long-lived clients need in order to distinguish quiet from dead connections.

# Deliverables for future implementers
This bead should leave behind enough specificity that later work can be implemented without consulting any external markdown plan. That means concrete example payloads, explicit field semantics, and explicit error examples should exist in the bead body and later be mirrored in code/tests/help output.

# Guardrails / non-goals
- No planner, scheduler, or mission runtime.
- No second source of truth for task state or coordination state.
- No opaque magic heuristics that cannot be explained in code comments or tests.
- No reliance on external markdown after this bead graph is created; the intent must be captured in the code, help, tests, and bead descriptions.

# Detailed verification expectations
- Golden fixtures for at least: successful snapshot bootstrap, successful event replay, successful digest, successful attention wake, and `CURSOR_EXPIRED`.
- Golden fixtures or schema examples for: default-profile behavior, explicit profile behavior, contradictory profile/filter behavior, degraded/unsupported summary markers, schema-version markers, and transport-liveness markers.
- Help/capabilities examples that show the canonical operator loop, the exact condition names, the profile/default semantics, and any heartbeat/reconnect expectations relevant to long-lived clients.
- Logging notes that tell future implementers where contract mismatches should be surfaced when commands cannot satisfy replay/resume guarantees.

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The contract is explicit enough that later beads can implement against it without consulting any outside plan.
- [ ] Example success and error payloads are concrete enough to become tests and help output.
- [ ] The boundary "LLM is the driver; ntm is the nervous system" is stated unambiguously.
- [ ] The design preserves the existing robot-mode exit-code and JSON-semantics conventions.
- [ ] Snapshot bootstrap semantics are specified as explicitly as feed/digest semantics.
- [ ] Profile/default semantics, degraded-summary semantics, and transport-liveness/schema-version semantics are specified at the contract layer rather than being left implicit.
close_reason: Contract implemented in attention_contract.go with event envelope, cursor semantics, command cluster, actionability classes, profiles, and golden fixtures

title: Overlay-Feed T3: Upgrade zoom hint to include feed cursor for agent continuity
description:
# Upgrade Zoom Hint to Include Feed Cursor and Emit Human Events

## Background

When a user zooms into a pane from the overlay (z/Enter), the popup closes and a tmux display-message hint appears:
    F12 -> dashboard overlay · prefix+z -> unzoom

This hint is human-facing. But in the integrated world, a tending agent might be watching the session too. When the human zooms, the agent should know: which pane was zoomed, the current feed cursor (so the agent can resume from that point), and that the human is actively interacting.

## What To Build

### 1. Include cursor in the display-message (if feed available)
- Current: "F12 -> dashboard overlay · prefix+z -> unzoom"
- New: "F12 -> dashboard overlay · prefix+z -> unzoom · cursor:42135"
- The cursor value comes from the Attention Feed journal current position
- If the feed is not available, omit the cursor portion (graceful degradation)

### 2. Emit "human.zoom" event to the Attention Feed
- When a user zooms from the overlay, publish a BusEvent with type "human.zoom"
- Include: session, pane_index, agent_type, timestamp
- Actionability: "background" (informational, not attention-worthy)
- This lets a tending agent know the human is looking at a specific pane

### 3. Emit "human.overlay_dismiss" event when Escape is pressed
- When the user presses Escape to close the overlay, publish "human.overlay_dismiss"
- Include: session, timestamp, duration_seconds (how long overlay was open)
- Actionability: "background"
- Requires tracking when the overlay was opened (add overlayOpenedAt field to Model)

### 4. Define new event type constants
- Add HumanZoom and HumanOverlayDismiss to the event type constants
- Follow the naming convention of existing event types (e.g., EventAgentIdle in internal/notify/notify.go)

## Unit Test Requirements

- Test display-message includes cursor when journal is available (mock journal)
- Test display-message omits cursor when journal is not available
- Test human.zoom event is published with correct fields
- Test human.overlay_dismiss event includes duration
- Test overlayOpenedAt is set when popup mode activates
- Test event actionability is always "background" for human events

## Technical Notes

- The cursor value comes from the event journal (once br-xmmaj is built)
- Use events.DefaultBus.Publish() for event publishing
- The overlayOpenedAt field should be set in the Init() method when popupMode=true
- Duration is calculated as time.Since(m.overlayOpenedAt) when Escape is pressed

## Dependencies

- Depends on: Attention Feed Phase 1a (br-xmmaj) — cursor model for cursor in hint
- Depends on: Attention Feed Phase 1b (br-7v4ns) — event mapping should include human-originated events

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Display-message includes cursor when feed available
- [ ] Display-message works without cursor when feed unavailable
- [ ] human.zoom event published on zoom from overlay
- [ ] human.overlay_dismiss event published on Escape
- [ ] Events follow normalized envelope format
- [ ] overlayOpenedAt tracked for duration calculation
- [ ] Unit tests for all scenarios
- [ ] go build and go vet pass

title: Attention Feed Phase 4a2: Add attention-aware dashboard and terse views
description:
# Why this bead exists
Help/capabilities teach the contract, but dashboard and terse output are where humans and low-token agent loops actually glance first. If those surfaces are not attention-aware, the product still feels fragmented even if the underlying feed is sound. This bead makes the human-facing summary surfaces legible without inventing a second taxonomy.

# Scope
1. Introduce one shared attention-summary/view-model for live summaries so dashboard, terse output, and any later overlay integrations do not each invent their own classification logic.
2. Add an attention-aware section to `--robot-dashboard` that highlights the same frontier an operator agent would care about: active attention items, compact counts, and honest degraded/unsupported markers.
3. Update `--robot-terse` so it can surface meaningful attention state within very tight token limits without collapsing into noisy sludge.
4. Ensure dashboard/terse summaries respect the same signal taxonomy and supported profiles/presets as events, digest, wait, and attention.
5. Keep the summary shallow: these views should orient the user quickly and point toward follow-up surfaces, not duplicate the full digest or raw event feed.
6. If the TUI/dashboard has sensible integration points, reuse the same summary/view-model there instead of maintaining a forked representation.

# Design considerations
- Humans and agents should converge on the same frontier, not learn different notions of what matters.
- Terse output has severe token constraints, so every field must earn its place.
- Summary surfaces should degrade honestly when some conditions are unsupported or partially observable.
- Any shared summary/view-model introduced here should make later overlay work simpler, not couple it to a separate ad hoc cache.

# Detailed verification expectations
- Golden tests for dashboard and terse output in quiet, interesting, action-required, and degraded states.
- Tests that compare dashboard/terse summaries against the underlying signal state under the same active profile.
- Tests that prove terse output stays compact while still surfacing the most important frontier change.
- Transcript or TUI artifact scenarios showing dashboard and terse output before and after meaningful attention transitions.
- Diff-friendly diagnostics when summary buckets, profile resolution, or degraded markers drift unexpectedly.
- Detailed logs in tests that print active profile, bucket counts, suppressed counts, and the exact summary fragments emitted.

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Dashboard and terse output make the attention frontier easier to understand in practice.
- [ ] Summary surfaces are driven by the same real signal taxonomy and profile semantics as the rest of the attention-feed system.
- [ ] Degraded or unsupported behavior is represented honestly.
- [ ] Automated tests and artifact-generating scenarios make regressions obvious.

title: Attention Feed Epic: Event-driven robot nervous system for frontier LLM operators
description:
# Why this initiative exists
ntm already has a strong robot mode, but the agent-facing surfaces are fragmented. A frontier LLM can drive the system today, yet it has to poll heavily, reconcile multiple partial views, and infer which changes actually deserve attention. The goal of this initiative is to make ntm a much better nervous system for an intelligent operator without turning ntm into a second coordinator.

# Architectural position
This work must remain fully compatible with the existing flywheel approach:
- beads remains the execution substrate and issue graph
- Agent Mail remains the coordination / reservation layer
- bv remains the prioritization and graph-triage layer
- the frontier LLM remains the actual driver / decision-maker
- ntm becomes better at sensing change, surfacing deltas, and exposing precise machine interfaces

# What success looks like
A tending agent should be able to:
1. take a cold-start snapshot,
2. remember a cursor boundary,
3. sleep until something important happens,
4. wake up with a compact digest,
5. inspect only the exact surface that now needs judgment,
6. resync cleanly when replay is no longer possible.

That should reduce token burn, reduce wasteful polling, and make one operator agent capable of tending more sessions without hidden orchestration logic.

# Intended deliverables
This initiative covers:
- a normalized event envelope and cursor model
- a cursor-bearing snapshot bootstrap path
- a replayable raw event feed
- a compact digest view for deltas
- richer named wait conditions
- a one-obvious-way attention macro
- server / SSE / WebSocket parity
- dashboard/help/capabilities integration
- comprehensive automated verification with detailed logs

# Explicit non-goals
- No mission engine
- No second task graph
- No replacement for beads, Agent Mail, or bv
- No hidden overseer state that becomes load-bearing
- No free-form mini-language for wait predicates when a named condition set is sufficient
- No schema split where CLI, HTTP, and WebSocket expose incompatible shapes

# Roll-up behavior
This bead is a roll-up epic, not an independently actionable implementation task. It should remain blocked on the final validation gate so `bv` does not surface it as ready work ahead of the real implementation beads.

# Future-self note
If this initiative ever starts looking like "ntm is becoming the planner," stop and re-scope it. The whole point is to improve the mechanical sensor/actuator layer around an intelligent driver, not to encode the driver's intelligence inside ntm.
close_reason: All phases complete. Full operator loop verified.

## Background

### 2. Spring Tick Benchmark (already in Phase 4b but verify here)

### 3. Frame Timing Test
  func TestViewRenderTime(t *testing.T) {

      for i := 0; i < 100; i++ { _ = m.View() }
      elapsed := time.Since(start)
      avgMs := float64(elapsed.Milliseconds()) / 100.0
      t.Logf("average View() time: %.2fms", avgMs)
      if avgMs > 16.0 {
          t.Errorf("View() too slow for 60fps: %.2fms (target <16ms)", avgMs)
      }
  }

### 4. Allocation Profile
  func BenchmarkDashboardViewAllocs(b *testing.B) {
      m := New("test", "/tmp/test")
      m, _ = m.Update(tea.WindowSizeMsg{Width: 200, Height: 50})
      m = populateTestData(m)
      b.ResetTimer()
      b.ReportAllocs()
      for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { _ = m.View() }
  }

## Performance Targets
- View() render time: < 16ms (60 FPS capable)
- View() allocations: < 200 allocs per frame
- SpringManager.Tick() with 50 springs: < 1μs
- CPU idle: < 0.5% of one core
- Memory overhead: negligible (< 10KB for spring state)

## If Performance Issues Found
1. Reduce spring count: batch springs (one per toast group, not per toast)
2. Lower FPS: FPS(30) — still smooth, half updates
3. Cache sub-renders: panels that haven't changed skip re-render
4. Use strings.Builder everywhere in View()

## Logging
- Log benchmark results to /tmp/ntm_perf_results.log
- Log frame timing violations: "SLOW FRAME: %dms (target 16ms)"
- Include in Phase 5c final report

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] BenchmarkDashboardView exists and passes
- [ ] BenchmarkSpringManagerTick50 < 1μs
- [ ] TestViewRenderTime < 16ms average
- [ ] BenchmarkDashboardViewAllocs < 200 allocs/op
- [ ] No "SLOW FRAME" warnings during normal operation
- [ ] Performance targets documented in test output
- [ ] Results logged to /tmp/ntm_perf_results.log

## Files to Create
None — add benchmarks and perf tests to existing bench_test.go (149 LOC)
(AGENTS.md: no file proliferation; bench_test.go already exists for this purpose)

## Risk: LOW — Profiling is read-only analysis. Fixes are follow-up tasks if needed.

title: Attention Feed Phase 1d1: Add Agent Mail unread and ack-required attention signals
description:
# Why this bead exists
Unread and ack-required Agent Mail changes are some of the clearest reasons a tending agent should wake up. In the previous plan, they were bundled with unrelated coordination concerns. This bead isolates the mail-specific signal work so it can be implemented, tested, and reasoned about independently.

# Scope
1. Surface `mail_pending` when new relevant unread mail appears for an active session/operator surface.
2. Surface `mail_ack_required` when ack-required mail specifically needs human/agent attention.
3. Carry enough structured detail for follow-up: thread/message identifiers when available, ack requirement, sender, and suggested mechanical next actions.
4. Keep the signals subordinate to Agent Mail as the source of truth; ntm is surfacing attention, not replacing the inbox.
5. Define honest absence semantics when Agent Mail visibility is unavailable or partial.

# Design considerations
- Mail attention is high-value and should not be blocked on unrelated conflict-detection work.
- The distinction between unread mail and ack-required mail matters operationally and should not be blurred.
- These signals should point operators back to Agent Mail or existing ntm surfaces, not invent a parallel message system.

# Likely touch points
- `internal/agentmail/`
- shared feed/signal logic
- `internal/robot/` integration points

# Detailed verification expectations
- Tests for unread vs ack-required mail conditions.
- Tests for relevant metadata extraction and `next_actions` hints.
- Tests for honest degradation when Agent Mail visibility is missing or incomplete.
- Transcript scenarios showing a waiting operator waking specifically on ack-required mail.
- Detailed logs in tests that record the mail source state and why a signal was or was not emitted.

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `mail_pending` and `mail_ack_required` are implemented and clearly differentiated.
- [ ] The signals point back to the real source of truth instead of duplicating inbox state.
- [ ] Partial observability is represented honestly.
- [ ] Mail attention behavior is covered by detailed automated tests and transcript scenarios.
