title: Overlay-Feed T4: Support --attention-cursor flag to open overlay pre-focused on specific event
description:
# Why this bead exists
A tending agent sometimes needs to bring a human directly to the attention item that triggered a wake-up. If the overlay can only open in a generic unfocused state, the human still has to hunt around and the handoff loses most of its value. This bead makes cursor-targeted overlay opening a first-class bridge between agent awareness and human awareness.

# Scope
1. Add an `--attention-cursor` path for opening the dashboard/overlay pre-focused on a specific attention item or the nearest surviving item.
2. Ensure the overlay focuses the attention panel and highlights the targeted item when it is still available.
3. Degrade honestly when the cursor is expired or no longer available by opening to the best current frontier rather than pretending exact continuity exists.
4. Provide a mechanical command shape that later robot-mode surfaces can emit directly as a suggested human-handoff action.
5. Keep cursor semantics aligned with the same namespace used by the attention feed and `--robot-attention` responses.

# Design considerations
- This feature is only useful if the cursor namespace is truly shared; any fork here would be a serious design bug.
- Focus/highlight behavior should make the handoff obvious without becoming visually obnoxious.
- Degraded behavior must be explicit so humans and agents do not infer false precision.

# Detailed verification expectations
- Unit tests for argument handling, focus selection, and cursor-found versus cursor-expired behavior.
- TUI snapshot/golden tests for focused/highlighted attention-panel rendering.
- Integration tests that prove robot attention responses can point to this surface mechanically.
- Transcript scenarios showing an agent wake, a suggested overlay command, and a human landing on the intended item or best-effort fallback.
- Detailed logs in tests that print requested cursor, located cursor, selected focus target, and degraded fallback choice.

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Cursor-targeted overlay opening exists and uses the same cursor namespace as the feed.
- [ ] The overlay focuses/highlights the intended attention item when possible.
- [ ] Expired or missing cursors degrade honestly and intelligibly.
- [ ] Automated tests and transcript artifacts make the handoff behavior easy to verify.

title: Attention Feed Phase 2b: Ship --robot-events as the raw replay/feed surface
description:
# Why this bead exists
Robot clients need one raw, replayable, machine-oriented surface that answers "what happened since cursor N?" without forcing a full snapshot every time. `--robot-events` should be that surface.

# Scope
1. Add a canonical `--robot-events` command in robot mode.
2. Support cursor-based replay, filtering, and an obvious streaming/follow mode when appropriate.
3. Follow existing robot conventions for exit codes, `success`, `timestamp`, and structured error payloads.
4. Return cursor metadata in a way that makes cursor chaining straightforward for agent consumers.
5. Keep the interface simple and enumerable. Prefer explicit filters (`--session`, `--panes`, `--type`, `--category`, `--actionability`, `--since-cursor`, `--limit`) over a clever DSL.
6. Ensure the command's cursor/filter semantics line up exactly with the snapshot bootstrap path and later digest/wait/attention surfaces.
7. Make follow-mode behavior explicit about how quiet periods are represented, including whether the command stays silent, emits periodic liveness markers, or delegates liveness expectations entirely to the caller.

# Design considerations
- This command should be useful both for one-shot replay and long-lived operator loops.
- If a cursor is expired, the response must say so clearly and tell the caller to resync via snapshot.
- The command should not require a consumer to understand server internals or websocket topics.
- Quiet follow-mode behavior must be documented well enough that agents do not mistake a healthy idle stream for a broken one.

# Detailed verification expectations
- CLI golden tests for replay, filter, streaming/follow mode, quiet-period behavior, and expired-cursor responses.
- Tests for parity with the underlying normalized feed service.
- Transcript-style Go scenario coverage showing: snapshot -> events replay -> additional follow-mode wake.
- Go-based e2e harness coverage that captures stdout/stderr/log artifacts for raw event replay, quiet follow-mode, and expiration handling.
- Detailed failure logging that shows requested cursor, delivered cursor range, filter set, quiet-period behavior, and resync hint when assertions fail.

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `--robot-events` exists as the raw replay/feed surface.
- [ ] Cursor chaining is obvious from the response shape.
- [ ] Structured filtering exists without introducing a bespoke query language.
- [ ] Error cases such as expired cursors or invalid filters are explicit and machine-actionable.
- [ ] Snapshot/bootstrap semantics and events replay semantics match exactly.
- [ ] Follow-mode quiet-period semantics are explicit enough that operators can distinguish healthy idleness from broken behavior.
close_reason: events.go implements --robot-events with cursor replay, filtering (session/pane/agent/category/actionability), hasMore detection, replay window metadata, cursor expiration handling with resync hints. Cleaned up duplicate declarations from concurrent agent work.

title: Overlay-Feed T5: Integrate F12 overlay toggle with assign --watch mode
description:
# Why this bead exists
`assign --watch` is one of the most likely places a human operator will sit while ntm is making decisions continuously. If overlay access is awkward there, one of the most important operational workflows remains disconnected from the new attention surfaces. This bead makes the watch workflow discover and use the overlay in a way that is actually useful, not just cosmetically bound.

# Scope
1. Detect when `assign --watch` is running inside the monitored tmux session and provide an explicit, one-time overlay hint in that context.
2. Ensure overlay binding/setup is present when the workflow can genuinely use it.
3. Make the hint and workflow point toward the attention-aware overlay experience rather than a generic dashboard detour.
4. Keep the behavior quiet and context-sensitive so remote/non-tmux usage does not get confusing noise.
5. Leave the watch loop semantics themselves unchanged; this is discoverability and ergonomics, not an assignment-engine rewrite.

# Design considerations
- This workflow should not advertise attention integration before the overlay attention panel exists.
- The hint should feel like a useful affordance, not nagware.
- Any auto-setup must stay consistent with the existing overlay binding logic rather than inventing a second path.

# Detailed verification expectations
- Unit tests for environment detection and hint emission/non-emission.
- Tests for overlay binding setup behavior when the binding already exists versus when it must be installed.
- Transcript scenarios showing `assign --watch` inside and outside the target tmux session.
- Detailed logs in tests that print session context, tmux detection result, whether the hint was emitted, and whether binding setup ran.

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `assign --watch` surfaces overlay access only in the contexts where it is genuinely useful.
- [ ] The workflow points users toward the attention-aware overlay rather than a generic dashboard path.
- [ ] Binding setup remains aligned with existing overlay behavior.
- [ ] Automated tests and transcript artifacts make regressions easy to diagnose.
notes: Implementation note: Part 1 (F12 hint + auto-setup) can be implemented immediately — it has no dependency on the Attention Feed and only touches existing overlay infrastructure. Parts 2 (event publishing) and 3 (watch progress badge) require the event envelope from Phase 1a. The br-xmmaj dep covers Parts 2-3. Implementers should ship Part 1 first as a quick win, then return for Parts 2-3 after the feed lands.

title: Attention Feed Phase 4b2: Build transcript-style e2e operator-loop scenarios and artifact logging
description:
# Why this bead exists
Transcript-style operator-loop scenarios are too important to leave implicit, and they now need to cover the human-facing summary surfaces as well as the raw robot loop. This bead exists to build the long-form scenario harnesses and artifact logging that prove the full user experience actually works end to end.

# Scope
1. Build Go-based e2e scenarios under `e2e/` for the canonical operator loop:
   - cold-start snapshot then cursor handoff
   - raw event replay after snapshot
   - wake on stalled pane
   - wake on ack-required mail
   - wake on reservation/file conflict
   - `--robot-attention` repeating cleanly across multiple wake cycles
   - resync behavior after expired cursor or process restart
2. Add transcript scenarios that explicitly compare low-noise operator mode versus high-fidelity debug mode on the same session state.
3. Add transcript scenarios for dashboard and terse output before and after meaningful attention changes so the human-facing frontier is validated too.
4. Ensure scenarios use the shared Go scenario/artifact harness instead of inventing separate fixture and logging conventions.
5. Ensure scenarios write detailed, stable artifacts to predictable locations under repo-controlled test artifact paths rather than ad hoc shell-script logs.
6. Make the Go harness verbose enough that a future maintainer can reconstruct what happened from the artifacts alone.
7. Keep scenarios honest about any partially supported or unsupported conditions, especially `bead_orphaned` if that remains unavailable.
8. Cover CLI and network-oriented paths where end-to-end user experience differs materially.
9. Use Go-based harness code as the primary test vehicle; do not rely on shell-script test runners as the canonical implementation.

# Logging / artifact expectations
- Transcript artifacts should record each command issued, key output excerpts, cursor values, wake reasons, active profiles, summary/view state, and resync transitions.
- Failures should leave behind step-by-step breadcrumbs rather than a single pass/fail line.
- Artifact locations should be explicit in the bead and in the eventual implementation/test output.
- The shared Go harness should support a retention/debug mode so artifacts can be kept when a test fails or when a maintainer explicitly asks for them.

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Go-based transcript-style e2e coverage exists for the canonical operator loop, its main failure/recovery paths, and the human-facing summary surfaces.
- [ ] The scenarios reuse the shared Go scenario/artifact harness rather than duplicating fixture plumbing.
- [ ] Operator-mode versus debug-mode behavior is exercised explicitly.
- [ ] Artifact logging is detailed enough to debug failures after the fact.
- [ ] The scenarios preserve all supported functionality and represent unsupported conditions honestly.
- [ ] The primary e2e harness lives in Go under the repo's normal test structure rather than shell scripts.
close_reason: Commit f63a1090: comprehensive e2e operator loop test coverage with transcript scenarios and artifact logging.

title: Phase 3a: Decompose dashboard.go (7017 LOC) into Logical Sub-Files
description:
# Decompose dashboard.go (7017 LOC) into Logical Sub-Files

## Background
7,017-line monolith — classic anti-pattern. All files stay in package dashboard.
ZERO LOGIC CHANGE — every function moves verbatim.

## Estimate: 120 minutes
This is a mechanical file-split. Each step is: cut code, paste to new file, add imports,
run go build. The Go compiler catches issues instantly. 7017 LOC ÷ ~800 LOC/file = ~9 files.
At ~12 min per file (cut, paste, fix imports, build) = ~108 min. Rounded to 120m.

## Target File Structure
  dashboard/
  ├── model.go         (~400)  Model struct, New(), constants, PostQuitAction
  ├── messages.go      (~200)  All custom message types
  ├── init_cmd.go      (~300)  Init(), initial fetch commands
  ├── update.go        (~1400) Update(), keyboard handling
  ├── update_data.go   (~1100) Data update handlers (accept*Msg)
  ├── view.go          (~800)  View(), header, footer
  ├── view_panels.go   (~1500) Content section, panel grid
  ├── helpers.go       (~800)  Formatting, utilities
  ├── run.go           (~220)  Run(), RunPopup(), RunWithOptions()

## AGENTS.md Compliance: No File Deletion
Per AGENTS.md RULE NUMBER 1: "NEVER delete a file without express permission."
After all code is extracted, dashboard.go should be reduced to a package-level comment:
  // Package dashboard — see model.go, update.go, view.go for implementation.
  // This file intentionally left as a redirect after decomposition.
  package dashboard
Do NOT delete dashboard.go without explicit user permission.

## CRITICAL: Zero Logic Changes
Every function moves verbatim. No renaming, restructuring, or improvements.
git diff should show only file additions and dashboard.go deletions.

## Implementation Steps
1. Create model.go → move Model struct, New(), constants → go build
2. Create messages.go → move all *Msg types → go build
3. Create init_cmd.go → move Init() → go build
4. Continue for each file (build after each move)
5. Reduce dashboard.go to redirect comment
6. go test -short ./internal/tui/dashboard/...

## Unit Tests (verify no regression)

### Pre/post test comparison protocol
  # Before:
  go test -v -count=1 ./internal/tui/dashboard/... > /tmp/dash_before.log 2>&1
  # After:
  go test -v -count=1 ./internal/tui/dashboard/... > /tmp/dash_after.log 2>&1
  # Compare (only timestamps should differ):
  diff <(grep '^---' /tmp/dash_before.log) <(grep '^---' /tmp/dash_after.log)

### New structural test: internal/tui/dashboard/structure_test.go
  func TestModelStructExists(t *testing.T) { var m Model; _ = m }
  func TestNewReturnsValidModel(t *testing.T) {
      m := New("test", "/tmp/test")
      if m.session != "test" { t.Error("session not set") }
  }
  func TestRunFunctionExists(t *testing.T) {
      var f func(string, string) (*PostQuitAction, error) = Run
      _ = f
  }

## E2E / VHS Verification
VHS captures MUST be pixel-identical to Phase 2 baselines.
Run all 5 profiles. Any visual difference = bug in the split.

## Logging
- No runtime logging changes (structural refactor only)
- Log decomposition completion: file count, LOC per file

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] dashboard.go reduced to redirect comment (not deleted)
- [ ] All code in logical sub-files (9 new files)
- [ ] go build ./cmd/ntm succeeds
- [ ] go vet ./internal/tui/dashboard/... clean
- [ ] All existing tests pass with identical results
- [ ] structure_test.go passes
- [ ] VHS captures pixel-identical to Phase 2
- [ ] No import cycles

## Files to Create
model.go, messages.go, init_cmd.go, update.go, update_data.go, view.go,
view_panels.go, helpers.go, run.go

Structural verification tests go in existing helpers_test.go — no new test file.
(AGENTS.md: no file proliferation)

## Risk: LOW — Mechanical split. Go compiler catches all issues.

title: Phase 1c: Replace Custom Spinner with bubbles/spinner
EPIC: TUI Glamour Upgrade — Leverage Full Charmbracelet Ecosystem
description:
# TUI Glamour Upgrade Epic

## Executive Summary
NTM's TUI (49,213 LOC) is a sophisticated Bubble Tea application with 22 dashboard panels,
3 Catppuccin themes, responsive 5-tier layout, and custom animations. However, it dramatically
underutilizes the Charmbracelet ecosystem it depends on. The `harmonica` spring physics library
is in go.mod with ZERO imports. `bubbles/table`, `bubbles/viewport`, `bubbles/progress`,
`bubbles/spinner`, `bubbles/help`, and `bubbles/list` are all available but replaced by
hand-rolled alternatives. Mouse support is never enabled. The `huh` forms library is absent.

This epic systematically upgrades the TUI to leverage these battle-tested components, adds
spring-based physics animations via Harmonica, enables mouse interaction, and decomposes the
7,017-line dashboard.go monolith — all verified at every step via the TUI Inspector VHS
capture-and-compare loop.

## Architecture Context
- Entry: `cmd/ntm/main.go` → `cli.Execute()` → Cobra commands
- Dashboard: `internal/tui/dashboard/dashboard.go` (7,017 LOC monolith)
- Components: `internal/tui/components/` (15 files, ~3,300 LOC)
- Styling: `internal/tui/styles/` + `internal/tui/theme/` (~3,000 LOC)
- Layout: `internal/tui/layout/layout.go` (5 responsive tiers with hysteresis)
- Panels: `internal/tui/dashboard/panels/` (22 implementations)
- TUI programs: dashboard, palette (cli/palette.go), tutorial (cli/tutorial.go), init_wizard

## Key Dependencies Already in go.mod
- charmbracelet/bubbletea v1.3.10
- charmbracelet/bubbles v1.0.0 (table, list, viewport, progress, spinner, help — all unused)
- charmbracelet/lipgloss v1.1.1-0.20250404203927-76690c660834
- charmbracelet/harmonica v0.2.0 (ZERO imports anywhere)
- charmbracelet/glamour v0.10.0
- charmbracelet/x/ansi v0.11.6

## Verification Infrastructure
- VHS installed at /home/ubuntu/go/bin/vhs
- 5 NTM-specific TUI Inspector profiles: ntm-dashboard-empty, ntm-dashboard-help,
  ntm-dashboard-navigate, ntm-dashboard-wide, ntm-palette
- Capture script: /dp/tui_inspector/scripts/capture_ntm_tui.sh
- Suite runner: /dp/tui_inspector/scripts/run_ntm_tui_suite.sh
- 5 native VHS tapes in testdata/vhs/ for unit-level visual regression

## Overarching Goals
1. Replace hand-rolled components with battle-tested Bubbles equivalents
2. Add spring-based physics animations via Harmonica (already a dependency!)
3. Enable mouse interaction for modern terminal UX
4. Decompose the dashboard.go monolith for maintainability
5. Add Huh forms for interactive workflows
6. Verify every change via TUI Inspector capture → compare → iterate loop
7. Maintain zero regressions in existing functionality

title: Phase 2b: Add bubbles/table to History and Timeline Panels
description:
# Add bubbles/table to History and Timeline Panels

## Background
panels/history.go (862 LOC) renders tabular data with manual string formatting AND has
3 filter systems: historyStatusFilter (all/ok/error), historyAgentFilter (all/claude/codex/
gemini), historyTimeFilter (all/1h/24h/7d). It also has cursor management, replay on Enter,
and keybindings for filter cycling.

panels/timeline.go (1,111 LOC) similarly renders events with agent colors.

bubbles/table provides column alignment, scrolling, selection, and mouse support — but we
must PRESERVE the existing filter systems and replay functionality.

## CRITICAL: Existing Filter Architecture
  historyStatusFilter: Cycle with 'f' key → all/ok/error
  historyAgentFilter: Cycle with 'a' key → all/claude/codex/gemini
  historyTimeFilter: Cycle with 't' key → all/1h/24h/7d
  applyFilters(): Combines all 3 filters → produces filtered entry list
  moveCursor(): Manages selection within filtered results

bubbles/table does NOT have built-in filtering. The filter logic STAYS in the panel.
Only the RENDERING of filtered results moves to bubbles/table.

## Implementation Plan — History Panel

### 1. Add table.Model to HistoryPanel struct
  type HistoryPanel struct {
      PanelBase
      table    table.Model        // NEW: replaces inline rendering
      entries  []history.Entry    // raw data
      filtered []history.Entry    // after filters applied
      // ... existing filter fields preserved
  }

### 2. Define columns (adaptive to tier)
  func historyColumns(width int) []table.Column {
      if width < 120 { return narrowColumns() }
      if width < 200 { return splitColumns() }
      return wideColumns()
  }

### 3. Convert filtered entries → table.Row on each filter change
  func (m *HistoryPanel) rebuildTableRows() {
      rows := make([]table.Row, len(m.filtered))
      for i, e := range m.filtered {
          rows[i] = table.Row{formatTime(e.Timestamp), e.Command, e.Target, statusBadge(e.Status)}
      }
      m.table.SetRows(rows)
  }

### 4. Filter cycling preserved — after filter change, call rebuildTableRows()
### 5. Replay on Enter — get selected row index, map back to filtered[index]
### 6. Style with Catppuccin theme
### 7. Route table.Update(msg) when panel focused

## Timeline Panel — Similar approach
  Columns: Time, Event Type, Agent, Description
  Agent column uses AgentBadge for color coding
  No filter system (simpler than history)

## Unit Tests (REQUIRED)

### Expand existing: panels/history_test.go (634 LOC)
  func TestHistoryTableColumns(t *testing.T) {
      p := NewHistoryPanel()
      p.SetSize(120, 20)
      p.SetEntries(testHistoryEntries(10), nil)
      view := p.View()
      if !strings.Contains(view, "Time") { t.Error("missing Time header") }
      if !strings.Contains(view, "Command") { t.Error("missing Command header") }
  }

  func TestHistoryTableNavigation(t *testing.T) {
      p := NewHistoryPanel()
      p.SetSize(120, 20)
      p.SetEntries(testHistoryEntries(5), nil)
      p.Focus()
      p.Update(tea.KeyMsg{Type: tea.KeyDown})
      sel, ok := p.selectedEntry()
      if !ok { t.Error("should have selection after down") }
      _ = sel
  }

  func TestHistoryTableFilterPreserved(t *testing.T) {
      p := NewHistoryPanel()
      p.SetSize(120, 20)
      p.SetEntries(testHistoryEntries(10), nil) // mix of ok and error
      // Apply status filter
      p.Update(tea.KeyMsg{Type: tea.KeyRunes, Runes: []rune{'f'}}) // cycle filter
      // Verify table rows reflect filter
      // Table should have fewer rows than total entries
  }

  func TestHistoryTableTierAdaptation(t *testing.T) {
      p := NewHistoryPanel()
      p.SetSize(100, 20) // Narrow

title: Attention Feed Phase 4a1: Document the operator loop in robot help and capabilities output
description:
# Why this bead exists
Help and capabilities output are the canonical contract surface for both human users and agent drivers. They should not be bundled with dashboard rendering concerns. This bead isolates the machine-readable and CLI-discoverability side of the work.

# Scope
1. Update `--robot-help` and `--robot-capabilities` so the attention-feed command cluster, condition taxonomy, cursor/resync behavior, and profile/preset system are explicitly documented.
2. Include concrete examples for the canonical operator loop: snapshot bootstrap, steady-state attention/digest, raw event replay, and expired-cursor resync.
3. Make unsupported or partially observable conditions explicit in capabilities output, especially for `bead_orphaned` if it remains unavailable.
4. Ensure examples and schema notes are accurate enough that future users do not need a separate markdown plan document.
5. Keep the output aligned with actual implementation rather than aspirational language.
6. Expose a machine-readable support matrix covering commands, conditions, profiles, transport features, degraded/unsupported reasons, and any schema/capability version markers needed by agent clients.
7. Document cursor-retention and transport-liveness expectations strongly enough that long-lived clients can adapt without trial and error.

# Design considerations
- Help/capabilities are part of the product surface, not an afterthought.
- Capability output should be precise enough for an agent to adapt automatically.
- The text should emphasize the one-obvious-way operator loop rather than listing an undifferentiated pile of commands.
- Machine-readable capability output should tell agents not just what exists, but which features are supported, degraded, or intentionally unavailable and why.

# Likely touch points
- `internal/cli/root.go`
- capability/help generation in robot-mode code
- `internal/output/`

# Detailed verification expectations
- Golden tests for help/capabilities output.
- Tests proving the documented conditions, profiles, commands, schema-version markers, and transport-feature support matrix match implementation reality.
- Diff-friendly diagnostics when examples or capability flags drift.
- Scenario checks that help/capabilities mention snapshot bootstrap, resync, retention hints, and transport-liveness expectations explicitly.

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Help and capabilities output accurately teach the operator loop.
- [ ] Conditions, profiles, transport features, and unsupported/degraded behavior are represented honestly.
- [ ] Capability output is machine-readable enough for agent clients to adapt automatically.
- [ ] The contract is discoverable from ntm itself without external documents.

title: Attention Feed Phase 3d: Add --robot-attention as the one obvious tending primitive
description:
# Why this bead exists
An agent-friendly system should have one obvious tending primitive, not five equally plausible loops. This bead adds `--robot-attention` as the recommended macro for operator agents: sleep until attention is needed, then wake with a compact digest.

# Scope
1. Implement `--robot-attention` as a transparent composition of wait + digest over the same cursor model.
2. Return the wake reason / matched condition alongside the digest so the operator knows why it woke up.
3. Preserve full transparency: no hidden planning, no hidden state machine, no magic side effects.
4. Make cursor handoff obvious so a tending loop can call the command repeatedly without bespoke bookkeeping.
5. Ensure the command works cleanly starting from a snapshot-provided cursor and after an expired-cursor resync.

# Design considerations
- This should be the one command a fungible tending agent can memorize first.
- The command should reduce token burn, not add ceremony.
- It must remain a convenience surface, not a new coordinator.

# Detailed verification expectations
- Tests for wake-on-attention behavior.
- Tests for cursor chaining across repeated calls.
- Golden tests for the combined response shape.
- Transcript-style looping scenario that runs snapshot -> attention -> targeted follow-up -> attention again, with a simulated replay-expiration/resync hop.
- Detailed logs for wake reason, returned digest summary, and next cursor when test expectations fail.

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `--robot-attention` exists and clearly behaves like wait-then-digest.
- [ ] Wake reason / matched condition is explicit in the response.
- [ ] Cursor chaining is obvious enough for a long-lived tending loop.
- [ ] The command introduces no hidden orchestration state.
- [ ] Snapshot/resync interactions are covered by automated scenario tests.

title: Attention Feed Phase 2c: Upgrade SSE, WebSocket, and HTTP transport to expose the same feed
description:
# Why this bead exists
The CLI cannot be the only way to consume the attention feed. ntm already has SSE, WebSocket, and HTTP surfaces, but they currently expose only a small subset of what an operator agent actually needs. This bead upgrades network transport so remote or embedded clients see the same feed contract instead of a watered-down variant.

# Scope
1. Upgrade the existing event streaming surfaces so they emit the normalized envelope rather than minimal type/timestamp/session stubs.
2. Add replay and filter support where appropriate so network clients can resume from a cursor instead of polling snapshots.
3. Preserve parity between CLI and network outputs; the same event should look materially the same regardless of transport.
4. Keep transport-specific wrappers thin. The feed contract should live in shared code, not in per-endpoint ad hoc shaping.
5. Make replay failure / cursor-expiration semantics as explicit over the network as they are in CLI mode.
6. Define explicit liveness behavior for long-lived transports: heartbeat/keepalive strategy, idle-period semantics, and reconnect guidance so clients can distinguish a quiet stream from a dead connection.
7. Ensure machine-readable capability/version output can tell remote clients which transport features are actually supported.

# Design considerations
- SSE and WebSocket differ operationally, but they should not invent different semantics.
- If replay/resume cannot be satisfied, the transport should return the same resync guidance the CLI gets.
- This bead should improve agent ergonomics for remote controllers without forcing them to shell out to the CLI.
- Heartbeats should be useful enough for liveness detection without creating pointless noise or a second event taxonomy.

# Detailed verification expectations
- Integration tests for SSE replay/subscribe semantics.
- Integration tests for WebSocket event shape, resume behavior, and idle-period/heartbeat behavior.
- Parity tests comparing CLI/network payload shape for the same underlying event.
- Go-based e2e scenarios that exercise HTTP/SSE/WebSocket flows and write detailed transcript logs for initial subscribe, replay, idle heartbeat, expiration, reconnect, and resync behavior.
- Failure logs that capture transport, cursor, filter set, liveness behavior, and payload summary when parity tests fail.

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Network clients can subscribe to the normalized feed with the same core fields and cursor semantics as CLI clients.
- [ ] Replay/resume behavior is explicit and consistent.
- [ ] Existing `/events` / WebSocket behavior is upgraded without creating a second schema family.
- [ ] Long-lived transport liveness/heartbeat semantics are explicit and tested.
- [ ] Network parity is demonstrated by automated tests and transcript logs.

title: Attention Feed Phase 1d2: Add reservation and file conflict attention signals
description:
# Why this bead exists
Reservation conflicts and file conflicts are a different class of coordination problem from mail. They are operational hazards, not conversation events. This bead isolates conflict-oriented coordination signals so they can be tuned and verified separately from mail behavior.

# Scope
1. Surface `reservation_conflict` when ntm can observe meaningful reservation contention that deserves operator review.
2. Surface `file_conflict` when file-level conflict or overlap conditions are observable through ntm's existing integrations and watchers.
3. Attach structured conflict details such as path/pattern, holder identity when available, and suggested next actions.
4. Keep absence semantics honest where observability is partial or integration-dependent.
5. Ensure these signals remain pointers to the real reservation/conflict source of truth rather than becoming a second coordination system.

# Design considerations
- Conflict signals have different urgency and remediation paths from mail and deserve separate tests and thresholds.
- `reservation_conflict` and `file_conflict` should not be collapsed into one generic problem bucket.
- If a conflict cannot be proven from observable data, the system should not emit it.

- Agent Mail reservation visibility where applicable

- Tests for reservation conflict emission and non-emission.

- Detailed logs in tests that capture the observed conflict inputs and the exact reason for emitting or suppressing a signal.

title: Epic: Overlay–Attention Feed Integration — Bridge human and agent control surfaces
description:
# Strategic context
ntm is gaining two complementary surfaces for tending sessions:
1. an agent-facing attention feed (`--robot-events`, `--robot-digest`, `--robot-wait`, `--robot-attention`), and
2. human-facing live summaries in the dashboard/overlay family.

If those surfaces evolve independently, the product will feel schizophrenic: the agent will react to one frontier while the human sees another. This epic exists to make the overlay family consume the same attention model rather than inventing its own.

# Architectural position
This epic is subordinate to the core attention-feed work. It must not:
- create a second event taxonomy,
- replace the feed contract,
- introduce a parallel coordination system,
- or make overlay-specific state load-bearing for robot-mode correctness.

It should:
- reuse the same attention-summary/view-model where possible,
- make human attention state visible in the overlay family,
- add thin handoff signals that help human and agent operators avoid stepping on each other,
- and leave behind transcript/TUI artifacts that make regressions diagnosable.

# Child work covered here
- T1: attention items panel in the overlay
- T2: attention-aware badge, stats bar, and navigation hints
- T3: cursor-aware zoom/dismiss continuity events and hints
- T4: open overlay pre-focused on a specific attention cursor
- T5: integrate assign/watch workflow with overlay discoverability
- T6: add a robot-mode overlay handoff surface
- T7: verify the whole overlay/feed integration and record invariants

# Success criteria
- The overlay family surfaces the same meaningful attention frontier the agent-facing system does.
- Human actions in the overlay can be surfaced back into the attention feed honestly and mechanically.
- No overlay integration bead is allowed to fork the core taxonomy or silently duplicate signal logic.
- Each child bead leaves behind good golden/TUI/transcript artifacts so future regressions are obvious.

# Roll-up behavior
This bead is a roll-up epic, not an independently actionable task. It should remain blocked on the final overlay verification gate so `bv` does not surface it as ready work ahead of the actual implementation beads.

title: Attention Feed Phase 1a: Build the normalized event envelope, cursor allocator, and replay journal
description:
# Why this bead exists
`internal/events/bus.go` and `internal/tracker/tracker.go` already contain pieces of an event system, but neither one currently gives robot-mode clients a single replayable, cursor-addressable, monotonic feed. The foundation of this initiative is a normalized envelope plus a bounded journal that can answer "what happened since cursor N?" reliably.

# Scope
1. Introduce a normalized robot-event envelope type that can represent current bus events, tracker deltas, and future derived signals without schema churn.
2. Add a monotonic cursor allocator for attention-feed events.
3. Add a bounded in-memory journal / replay buffer that retains recent envelopes for cursor-based replay.
4. Define retention behavior and expiration explicitly. In v1, process restart or journal expiry should require resync via snapshot, not a new persistent queue.
5. Expose a single internal service that can append, replay, and subscribe, rather than having each robot surface build its own one-off logic.
6. Preserve existing event flow where practical; this bead should compose with the current bus/tracker instead of replacing them wholesale.
7. Add explicit metrics or debug-visible counters for replay-window size, dropped/evicted events, and oldest available cursor so later operators can debug cursor-expiry behavior.

# Design considerations
- Ordering must be deterministic enough for agent consumers to reason about cursors.
- The journal must be bounded so this feature cannot quietly become an unbounded memory sink.
- Concurrency behavior matters: concurrent publishers must still yield strictly monotonic cursor assignment.
- Restart behavior must be honest. If replay is no longer possible, return a structured resync instruction instead of pretending continuity exists.

# Detailed verification expectations
- Unit tests for monotonic cursor assignment under concurrent publish.
- Unit tests for replay windows, retention eviction, and cursor-expiration handling.
- Golden tests for success/error envelope serialization.
- Benchmarks or stress tests that exercise high event churn so we can confirm the journal remains bounded and cursor assignment remains ordered.
- Diagnostic logging in tests that prints cursor ranges, replay windows, and eviction decisions when assertions fail.

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A normalized event envelope exists and is used by the new feed internals.
- [ ] Cursor assignment is monotonic and concurrency-safe.
- [ ] Replay since cursor works while the requested cursor remains in retention.
- [ ] Expired cursors produce a structured resync path instead of ambiguous empty output.
- [ ] The implementation remains bounded in memory and does not add a second durable store in v1.
- [ ] Replay-window visibility exists so cursor failures are diagnosable.

title: Phase 3b: Refactor Panel Focus Management with Proper Focus Ring
Implement rate limit backoff for agents
description:
Detect rate limit errors and notify users (do not auto-retry).

## What This Task Does

Detect when agents hit rate limits and notify users. This is simpler
and safer than auto-retry, which can cause more problems than it solves.

## Why Detection Only (No Auto-Retry)

Auto-retry is complex and error-prone:
- Can't reliably capture the 'last command' to replay
- Agent state may be corrupted after rate limit
- Infinite retry loops are possible
- Users should decide if/when to retry

Instead: Detect, notify, let user handle it.

## Detection

Rate limit patterns in agent output:
- 'rate limit exceeded'
- 'too many requests'
- '429'
- 'quota exceeded'
- 'try again in X seconds'

## Response

When rate limit detected:
1. Mark agent as 'rate_limited' in health status
2. Fire notification event (desktop, webhook, shell)
3. Include wait time if parseable from error
4. Show in 'ntm health' output with clear indicator

Example notification:
'Agent cc_1 hit rate limit. Suggested wait: 60s'

## Integration

- Uses health check infrastructure (ntm-239) for detection
- Uses notification system (ntm-gcv) for alerts
- Shows in 'ntm status' with rate_limited indicator

## Configuration

[resilience.rate_limit]
detect = true
notify = true
patterns = ['rate limit', '429', 'too many requests']

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Rate limit patterns detected in pane output
- [ ] Notification fired when rate limit detected
- [ ] Wait time parsed when available
- [ ] Status shown in ntm health output
- [ ] No auto-retry (by design)

# Policy Engine (internal/policy/)

## Why This Is Critical
The .ntm/policy.yaml file is referenced by MULTIPLE features but there's no dedicated engine to parse and enforce it:
- Destructive Command Protection (blocked/allowed patterns)
- BD Daemon Mode (auto-push policy gate)
- File Reservation Lifecycle (force-release approval)
- SLB Safety Gates (approval_required operations)

Without a unified Policy Engine, each feature reimplements policy checking, leading to inconsistencies and bugs.

## Policy File Structure
```yaml
# .ntm/policy.yaml
version: 1

# Commands that are always blocked
blocked:
  - pattern: "git reset --hard"
    reason: "Hard reset loses commits"
  - pattern: "git checkout --"
    reason: "Discards uncommitted changes"

# Commands that require approval
approval_required:
  - pattern: "git push --force"
    reason: "Force push rewrites history"
    slb: true  # Requires SLB two-person rule
  - pattern: "force_release"
    reason: "Releases another agent's reservation"
    slb: false  # Just needs any approval

# Commands that bypass checks
allowed:
  - pattern: "git checkout -b"
    reason: "Create branch is safe"

# Automation settings
automation:
  auto_push: false
  auto_commit: true
  force_release: approval
```

## Implementation (internal/policy/engine.go)

### Policy Engine Interface
```go
type PolicyEngine struct {
    policyPath string
    policy     *Policy
    mu         sync.RWMutex
}

type Policy struct {
    Version          int              `yaml:"version"`
    Blocked          []PatternRule    `yaml:"blocked"`
    ApprovalRequired []PatternRule    `yaml:"approval_required"`
    Allowed          []PatternRule    `yaml:"allowed"`
    Automation       AutomationConfig `yaml:"automation"`
}

type PatternRule struct {
    Pattern    string   `yaml:"pattern"`
    Reason     string   `yaml:"reason"`
    SLB        bool     `yaml:"slb,omitempty"`
    Exceptions []string `yaml:"exceptions,omitempty"`
}
```

### Key Methods
```go
func (e *PolicyEngine) Load(path string) error
func (e *PolicyEngine) Reload() error  // Watch for file changes
func (e *PolicyEngine) IsBlocked(command string) (bool, string)
func (e *PolicyEngine) NeedsApproval(action string) (bool, *PatternRule)
func (e *PolicyEngine) IsAllowed(command string) bool
func (e *PolicyEngine) AutomationEnabled(feature string) bool
```

### File Watching
Policy file is watched for changes and automatically reloaded:
```go
func (e *PolicyEngine) StartWatcher(ctx context.Context) {
    watcher, _ := fsnotify.NewWatcher()
    watcher.Add(e.policyPath)
    // Reload on change
}
```

### Default Policy
If .ntm/policy.yaml doesn't exist, use sensible defaults (block dangerous patterns, require approval for force operations).

## Integration Points
- Destructive Command Protection: Uses IsBlocked(), IsAllowed()
- BD Daemon: Uses AutomationEnabled("auto_push")
- File Reservation: Uses NeedsApproval("force_release")
- SLB: Uses NeedsApproval() with SLB flag check

## New Commands
```bash
ntm policy show           # Display current policy
ntm policy validate       # Check policy file syntax
ntm policy reset          # Reset to defaults
ntm policy edit           # Open in editor
```

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Policy file parsed correctly
- [ ] Default policy used when file missing
- [ ] File watching with auto-reload
- [ ] IsBlocked/NeedsApproval/IsAllowed work
- [ ] AutomationEnabled checks work
- [ ] Validation command catches syntax errors
close_reason: Policy engine complete with: Policy struct (Version, Blocked, ApprovalRequired, Allowed, Automation), AutomationConfig (auto_commit, auto_push, force_release), SLB support, CLI commands (show, validate, reset, edit, automation), comprehensive tests. File watching deferred to future enhancement.

title: Integrate routing with Agent Mail file reservations
description:
When routing work, consider Agent Mail file reservations as a signal for task affinity.

RATIONALE:
If an agent has reserved files via Agent Mail, they're likely the best agent to handle work related to those files. This creates natural task affinity.

INTEGRATION POINTS:

1. RESERVATION QUERY:
   - Query Agent Mail for active reservations in project
   - Cache results (refresh every 30s or on routing request)
   - Map: pane_id -> []reserved_paths

2. AFFINITY SCORING:
   - Extract file paths from prompt (patterns like "src/auth.go", "internal/")
   - Check if any agent has matching reservations
   - Add affinity bonus (configurable, default 30) to matching agent

3. CONFLICT PREVENTION:
   - If prompt mentions file reserved by another agent:
     - Warning in response: "File reserved by {agent}"
     - Option: --respect-reservations to skip reserved files

CONFIGURATION:
```toml
[routing.agent_mail]
enabled = true
reservation_bonus = 30
respect_reservations = false  # warn only vs enforce
cache_ttl = "30s"
```

DEPENDENCY:
- Requires Agent Mail MCP to be available
- Graceful degradation if unavailable

LOCATION: internal/robot/routing.go (extend existing)

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA:
- File reservations queried from Agent Mail
- Matching reservations boost agent score
- Warning when sending to non-reserving agent
- Works gracefully without Agent Mail

title: Implement ntm mail send command
description:
# Implement ntm mail send Command

## Purpose

Allow users to send messages between agents in a session, or broadcast coordination messages.

## Command Syntax

```bash
# Send to specific agent panes
ntm mail send myproject --to cc_1 "Please review the API changes"

# Send to all agents of a type
ntm mail send myproject --cc "Stop current work and focus on tests"

# Send to all agents
ntm mail send myproject --all "Checkpoint: sync and report status"

# With options
ntm mail send myproject --to cc_1 --subject "API Review" --urgent --ack-required "Review needed ASAP"

# From file
ntm mail send myproject --to cc_1 --file ./message.md
```

## Flag Mapping

| Flag | Agent Mail Parameter |
|------|---------------------|
| --to | to[] (specific agent) |
| --cc | cc[] |
| --subject | subject |
| --urgent | importance="urgent" |
| --important | importance="high" |
| --ack-required | ack_required=true |
| --thread | thread_id |
| --file | body_md from file |

## Agent Resolution

The --to flag accepts:
1. **Pane identifiers**: cc_1, cod_2 → resolve to agent names
2. **Agent names**: GreenCastle → use directly
3. **Agent type filters**: --cc, --cod, --gmi → expand to all agents of type

Resolution requires querying both tmux (for pane names) and Agent Mail (for registered agents).

## Message Composition

If no message body provided:
1. Open $EDITOR with template
2. Parse subject from first line (# heading)
3. Validate non-empty before sending

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Can send to specific agents by pane ID or name
- [ ] Can broadcast to agent type groups
- [ ] Subject auto-derived or manually specified
- [ ] Importance and ack_required flags work
- [ ] Thread ID support for conversations
- [ ] File input for long messages
- [ ] Editor mode for composition

title: Implement ntm mail ack and read commands
description:
# Implement ntm mail ack and read Commands

## Purpose

Allow marking messages as read or acknowledged, which signals to senders that the message was received and processed.

## Command Syntax

```bash
# Mark message as read
ntm mail read myproject 42

# Mark message as acknowledged
ntm mail ack myproject 42

# Acknowledge all urgent messages
ntm mail ack myproject --urgent

# Acknowledge all from specific agent
ntm mail ack myproject --from cc_1
```

## Semantics

- **Read**: Message was seen but not necessarily acted upon
- **Acknowledged**: Message was seen AND the recipient has taken action or committed to action

Agent Mail tracks both timestamps separately:
- read_ts: When mark_message_read was called
- ack_ts: When acknowledge_message was called

## Batch Operations

```bash
# Mark multiple messages
ntm mail read myproject 42 43 44

# Mark all unread as read
ntm mail read myproject --all

# Acknowledge all pending
ntm mail ack myproject --all
```

## Output

```
✓ Message #42 marked as read
✓ Message #42 acknowledged (ack_ts: 2025-12-10T15:35:00Z)
```

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Single message read/ack by ID
- [ ] Batch operations by ID list
- [ ] Filter-based batch: --urgent, --from, --all
- [ ] Proper error handling for already-read/acked
- [ ] JSON output mode for scripts

[EPIC] Robot Command Reliability
description:
# Epic: Robot Command Reliability

## Goal
Make robot commands bulletproof for AI agent consumption. This is the CRITICAL PATH for AI coding agents using NTM programmatically.

## Background
NTM serves two user personas: human operators (TUI) and AI coding agents (robot commands). AI agents are programmatic consumers - they parse JSON, check exit codes, and make decisions based on command output. Any inconsistency or ambiguity causes bugs in agent workflows.

Currently, robot commands have several reliability issues:
1. **Timeout units are inconsistent** - spawn uses seconds, others use milliseconds
2. **Error output location varies** - some to stderr, some to stdout JSON
3. **Agent type naming differs** - cc vs claude vs claude_code
4. **Unimplemented features return errors** - breaks agent error handling

## Success Criteria
- AI agents can reliably parse ALL robot command output
- No ambiguity in timeout values, error locations, or agent naming
- Unimplemented features don't break agent workflows
- All changes are backwards compatible with deprecation warnings

## Beads in this Epic
- R1: Duration string support for timeouts
- R2: Standardized JSON error responses
- R3: Agent type aliasing
- R4: Graceful unimplemented feature handling

## Architecture Considerations
- Use Go's `time.ParseDuration` for flexible timeout parsing
- Define `RobotResponse` base struct for all JSON outputs
- Create `resolveAgentType()` helper for consistent normalization
- Define `error_code` enum for programmatic error handling

## Testing Strategy
- Unit tests for each fix
- Integration tests for common robot workflows
- Validate JSON against documented schema
close_reason: All epic beads complete: R1 (duration strings), R2 (standardized errors), R3 (type aliasing), R4 (unimplemented handling)

title: Fallback asset discovery for upgrade resilience
description:
# Fallback Asset Discovery for Upgrade Resilience

## Problem Statement
If the preferred asset name pattern doesn't match exactly, upgrade currently fails hard.
A more resilient approach would try progressively looser matching before giving up.

## Current Behavior
```go
// Try exact versioned archive
if asset.Name == archiveAssetName { ... }

// Try raw binary name
if asset.Name == binaryAssetName { ... }

// Try prefix matching as fallback
if strings.HasPrefix(name, binaryAssetName) { ... }

// Give up
return fmt.Errorf("no suitable release asset found...")
```

## Proposed Fallback Chain

### Strategy 1: Exact Archive Match (Current)
Pattern: `ntm_1.4.1_darwin_all.tar.gz`
Confidence: 100%

### Strategy 2: Exact Binary Match (Current)
Pattern: `ntm_darwin_all`
Confidence: 90%

### Strategy 3: Prefix Match (Current)
Pattern: `strings.HasPrefix(name, "ntm_darwin_all")`
Confidence: 70%

### Strategy 4: Fuzzy Same-OS Match (NEW)
For darwin/arm64, also try darwin/amd64, darwin/all
Confidence: 50%
Rationale: macOS Rosetta 2 can run amd64 binaries on arm64

### Strategy 5: Legacy Naming Patterns (NEW)
Try old dash-separator convention: `ntm-darwin-arm64`
Confidence: 30%
Rationale: Handle upgrades from very old versions

### Strategy 6: Smart Selection (NEW)
If multiple assets for same OS exist, pick most compatible
Confidence: Variable based on match quality

## Benefits
1. **Graceful Degradation**: Download SOMETHING rather than fail completely
2. **Forward Compatibility**: Handle future naming changes without code updates
3. **Backward Compatibility**: Handle upgrades from old releases with different naming
4. **Better UX**: Users less likely to hit dead ends

## Concerns & Mitigations

### Concern: Downloading Wrong Asset
**Risk**: Fuzzy match picks incompatible binary
**Mitigation**: 
- NEVER match cross-OS (linux asset won't be offered for darwin target)
- Warn loudly for cross-arch
- macOS arm64→amd64 is safe (Rosetta 2)
- Verify binary after download (run `ntm version`)

### Concern: Masking Real Problems
**Risk**: Fallback succeeds but hides naming issues from maintainers
**Mitigation**:
- Always log warning when using non-exact match
- CI tests use --strict mode (exact match only)
- Include fallback usage in upgrade success message
- Analytics/telemetry could track fallback usage (optional)

### Concern: Increased Complexity
**Risk**: More code paths = more potential bugs
**Mitigation**:
- Comprehensive test coverage for each strategy
- Clear logging of which path was taken
- --strict flag for CI and testing
- Fallback only in interactive mode by default

## User Experience Example
```
🔄 NTM Upgrade

  Current version: 1.3.0
  Platform: darwin/arm64

  Checking for updates... ✓
  Latest version:  1.4.1

  ⚠ Note: Using fallback asset discovery
    Expected: ntm_1.4.1_darwin_all.tar.gz
    Found:    ntm_1.4.1_darwin_amd64.tar.gz (via fuzzy_same_os)
    
    This binary should work via Rosetta 2.

  Download: ntm_1.4.1_darwin_amd64.tar.gz (8.2 MB)
  
  Upgrade to 1.4.1? [y/N]
```

## Priority: P3 (Low)
Medium user-experience value. Adds complexity.
Current strict matching + enhanced error messages may be sufficient.
Consider after P2 items are complete.
acceptance_criteria:
1. If exact asset name not found, tries progressively looser matching
2. Logs warning when using fallback (not silent)
3. Shows which matching strategy was used in output
4. --strict flag available to disable fallback for CI/testing
5. Fallback never downloads incompatible architecture (e.g., linux binary on mac)
6. Legacy naming patterns (pre-fix) are attempted as final fallback
7. User can see all attempted patterns in verbose/debug mode

## Purpose

1. Messages TO any agent in the project (GreenCastle, BlueLake, etc.)

3. Filtered by session agents if desired

This gives the user visibility into all agent-to-agent communication.

```bash
# Show all messages in project (across all agents)
ntm mail inbox myproject

# Filter to session's agents only
ntm mail inbox myproject --session-agents
```

title: Implement scrollback capture for checkpoints
description:
## Overview
Capture tmux pane scrollback as part of checkpoint for complete conversation history.

## Location
Create `internal/checkpoint/scrollback.go`

## Scrollback Capture
```go
type ScrollbackCapture struct {
    PaneID      string
    Lines       int
    Content     string
    Compressed  []byte
    Size        int64
}

func CaptureScrollback(session, paneID string, lines int) (*ScrollbackCapture, error) {
    // Use tmux capture-pane
    cmd := exec.Command("tmux", "capture-pane",
        "-t", fmt.Sprintf("%s:%s", session, paneID),
        "-p",      // Print to stdout
        "-S", fmt.Sprintf("-%d", lines), // Start N lines back
        "-E", "-1", // End at current line
    )
    
    output, err := cmd.Output()
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    
    // Compress with gzip
    compressed := gzipCompress(output)
    
    return &ScrollbackCapture{
        PaneID:     paneID,
        Lines:      lines,
        Content:    string(output),
        Compressed: compressed,
        Size:       int64(len(compressed)),
    }, nil
}
```

## Storage
```
checkpoint-dir/
  checkpoint.json
  scrollback/
    cc_1.txt.gz
    cc_2.txt.gz
    user_pane.txt.gz
```

## Configuration
```toml
[checkpoints]
scrollback_lines = 5000      # Default lines to capture
scrollback_compress = true   # Always gzip
scrollback_max_size_mb = 10  # Skip if too large
```

## Considerations
- Large scrollbacks can be slow to capture
- Compression is essential for storage
- Some panes may have very little scrollback
- Binary output (rare) should be handled

Implement file conflict detection
description:
Detect when multiple agents may have modified same files. Essential for parallel agent coordination.

DETECTION APPROACH:

1. GIT-BASED DETECTION:
   - Run `git status --porcelain` to get modified files
   - For each modified file, get modification time via `stat`
   - Correlate modification times with agent activity windows
   - If file modified during window when 2+ agents were GENERATING: flag as conflict

2. NEWLY CREATED FILES:
   - Track files created during session (not in initial git status)
   - If same file path touched by multiple agents: definite conflict
   - Use inotify/fsnotify for real-time tracking (optional enhancement)

3. AGENT MAIL INTEGRATION:
   - Query Agent Mail file reservations
   - If file reserved by Agent A but modified while Agent B active: flag
   - Confidence boost: reservation + activity = high confidence

CONFLICT CLASSIFICATION:
```go
type FileConflict struct {
    Path         string
    LikelyModifiers []string  // pane IDs
    GitStatus    string       // M, A, D, ??
    Confidence   float64      // 0.0-1.0
    Reason       string       // "concurrent_activity", "reservation_violation"
}
```

CONFIDENCE LEVELS:
- 0.9+: High confidence (reservation violation, overlapping edits)
- 0.7-0.9: Medium confidence (concurrent activity window)
- 0.5-0.7: Low confidence (possibly unrelated)

ACTIVITY WINDOW TRACKING:
- For each pane, track: last_activity_start, last_activity_end
- Activity = state was GENERATING for continuous period
- Overlap = two panes' windows intersect

LIMITATIONS:
- Cannot know exactly which agent wrote which bytes
- Best effort heuristic based on timing
- False positives possible with fast sequential edits

LOCATION: internal/robot/synthesis.go (new file)

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA:
- Git status correctly parsed
- File modification times captured
- Activity windows tracked per pane
- Conflicts flagged with confidence scores
- Agent Mail reservations considered
- Handles newly created files

# Task: Implement Health Monitoring

Add health check loop with exponential backoff restart.

## Files to Create/Update
- internal/supervisor/health.go

## Health Check Loop
```go
func (s *Supervisor) healthCheckLoop(ctx context.Context) {
    ticker := time.NewTicker(5 * time.Second)
    for {
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return
        case <-ticker.C:
            for _, d := range s.daemons {
                s.checkHealth(d)
            }
        }
    }
}
```

## Exponential Backoff
```go
func (d *ManagedDaemon) nextRestartDelay() time.Duration {
    base := 2 * time.Second
    delay := base * time.Duration(1<<d.restarts)
    if delay > 5*time.Minute {
        delay = 5 * time.Minute
    }
    return delay
}
```

## Health Check Method
- HTTP GET to daemon.spec.HealthURL
- Timeout: 2 seconds
- Mark unhealthy after 3 consecutive failures
- Trigger restart on unhealthy

- Test restart with backoff
- Test max backoff cap

title: T9: Standardized truncation using single-character ellipsis
description:
# T9: Standardized Truncation Using Single-Character Ellipsis

## Parent Epic
[EPIC] Dashboard Visual Polish (ntm-af32)

## Problem Statement
Truncation is inconsistent across the codebase:

\`\`\`go
// Some places use three periods:
title = title[:maxLen-3] + "..."

// Some use single ellipsis:
title = layout.TruncateRunes(title, maxLen, "…")

// Some use custom suffixes:
title = truncate(title, maxLen, ">>")
\`\`\`

This inconsistency:
- Looks unprofessional
- Uses different character counts (3 vs 1)
- Makes width calculations inconsistent

## Solution
Standardize on single-character ellipsis "…" everywhere:

- Unicode: U+2026 HORIZONTAL ELLIPSIS
- Takes 1 character width
- Looks cleaner than "..."
- More precise truncation

## Implementation Details

### Standard Truncation Function
\`\`\`go
// internal/tui/layout/truncate.go

// TruncateRunes truncates string to maxLen runes, adding suffix if truncated.
// Always use this function for truncation - never manual string slicing.
func TruncateRunes(s string, maxLen int, suffix string) string {
    runes := []rune(s)
    if len(runes) <= maxLen {
        return s
    }
    if maxLen <= len(suffix) {
        return suffix[:maxLen]
    }
    return string(runes[:maxLen-len([]rune(suffix))]) + suffix
}

// Truncate is a convenience wrapper using "…" suffix.
func Truncate(s string, maxLen int) string {
    return TruncateRunes(s, maxLen, "…")
}
\`\`\`

### Search and Replace Pattern
Find all instances of:
- \`+ "..."\`
- \`+ ">>"\`
- Manual truncation without TruncateRunes

Replace with:
\`\`\`go
layout.Truncate(text, maxLen)
// or if custom suffix needed:
layout.TruncateRunes(text, maxLen, "…")
\`\`\`

### Files to Audit
\`\`\`bash
rg '\.\.\."|>\">|\"\.\.\"' --type go
rg '\[:[0-9]+\].*\+.*"' --type go  # Manual slice + concat
\`\`\`

### Files to Modify
- All dashboard panels
- Layout helpers
- Robot output formatters (if any)
- Any file using manual truncation

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All truncation uses TruncateRunes or Truncate
- [ ] All truncation uses "…" (not "...")
- [ ] No manual string slicing for truncation
- [ ] Width calculations account for 1-char ellipsis
- [ ] Visual consistency across all panels

## Examples

### Before (Inconsistent)
\`\`\`
Files:  src/authentication/handlers/login...
Beads:  Implement user registration flow>>
CASS:   Previous discussion about auth…
\`\`\`

### After (Consistent)
\`\`\`
Files:  src/authentication/handlers/login…
Beads:  Implement user registration flow…
CASS:   Previous discussion about auth…
\`\`\`

## Testing Notes
1. Resize terminal to trigger truncation
2. Verify all truncated text uses "…"
3. Verify truncation happens at correct length
4. Test with Unicode text (emojis, CJK characters)
close_reason: Implemented standardized truncation with single-character ellipsis (…) across TUI

description:
# Implement ntm lock/unlock File Reservation Commands

## Purpose

Expose Agent Mail's file reservation system as NTM commands, allowing agents to declare intent before editing files and avoid conflicts.

## Command Syntax

```bash
# Reserve files for editing
ntm lock myproject "src/api/**" --reason "Implementing user endpoints"

# Reserve multiple patterns
ntm lock myproject "src/api/**" "tests/api/**"

# With TTL (default 1 hour)
ntm lock myproject "config/*.json" --ttl 2h

# Shared (read) vs exclusive (write) lock
ntm lock myproject "docs/**" --shared

# Release specific locks
ntm unlock myproject "src/api/**"

# Release all locks for session
ntm unlock myproject --all

# Show current locks
ntm locks myproject
ntm locks myproject --all-agents  # Include other sessions
```

## Lock Display Format

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ File Reservations: myproject                                │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 🔒 src/api/**                                               │
│   Agent: ntm_myproject │ Exclusive │ Expires in 45m        │
│   Reason: Implementing user endpoints                       │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 🔒 tests/api/**                                             │
│   Agent: ntm_myproject │ Exclusive │ Expires in 45m        │
│   Reason: Implementing user endpoints                       │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 📖 docs/** (shared)                                         │
│   Agent: GreenCastle │ Shared │ Expires in 1h30m           │
│   Reason: Updating API documentation                        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Conflict Detection

When attempting to lock:
```
⚠️ Conflict detected:
  Pattern: src/api/**
  Held by: GreenCastle (cc_1)
  Reason: Refactoring auth module
  Expires in: 25 minutes

Options:
  1. Wait for expiry
  2. Request release: ntm mail send myproject --to cc_1 "Need src/api/**"
  3. Force lock (dangerous): ntm lock myproject "src/api/**" --force
```

## Integration with spawn/add

When spawning agents:
```bash
# Check for conflicts before spawning
ntm spawn myproject --cc=2 --check-locks

# Auto-reserve working directory
ntm spawn myproject --cc=2 --reserve-cwd
```

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Lock patterns with glob support
- [ ] TTL specification (default 1h, max 24h)
- [ ] Exclusive vs shared locks
- [ ] Conflict detection with helpful messages
- [ ] ntm locks command shows current state
- [ ] --all-agents shows all project reservations
- [ ] Integration hooks for spawn command

description:
AI-assisted work assignment suggestions based on current state.

## Rationale
With N agents and M ready beads, optimal assignment is non-trivial. This flag analyzes current state and recommends which agent should work on what, considering:
- Agent types and their strengths
- Current workload balance  
- Bead dependencies and priorities
- Recent activity patterns

## Usage
```bash
ntm --robot-assign myproject
ntm --robot-assign myproject --beads=ntm-abc,ntm-def  # specific beads
ntm --robot-assign myproject --strategy=balanced      # or: speed, quality
```

```json
{
  "session": "myproject",
  "strategy": "balanced",
  "recommendations": [
    {
      "agent": "0.1",
      "agent_type": "claude",
      "assign_bead": "ntm-1rz",
      "confidence": 0.85,
      "reasoning": "Profiler task matches claude's code analysis strengths"
```

title: Implement pre/post command hooks
description:
Run user scripts before and after NTM commands.

## What This Task Does

Enable users to define hooks that run before or after specific
NTM commands. Hooks can log, notify, validate, or transform.

## Configuration

# ~/.config/ntm/config.toml

[hooks]
# Run before any send command
pre_send = "~/.config/ntm/hooks/log-prompt.sh"

# Run after spawn completes
post_spawn = "notify-send 'NTM' 'Session created'"

# Run before dangerous commands
pre_kill = "~/.config/ntm/hooks/confirm-kill.sh"

## Hook Interface

Hooks receive command context as JSON on stdin:
{
  "command": "send",
  "args": ["myproject", "--all", "hello"],
  "session": "myproject",
  "flags": {"all": true},
  "timestamp": "2025-12-10T10:00:00Z"
}

Post hooks also receive result:
{
  "command": "spawn",
  "result": "success",
  "session": "myproject",
  "panes_created": 4,
  "duration_ms": 1234
}

## Hook Execution

Pre hooks:
- Run synchronously before command
- Non-zero exit blocks the command
- Stdout captured but not displayed (log only)
- Stderr shown to user

Post hooks:
- Run asynchronously after command
- Exit code doesn't affect NTM
- Good for notifications, logging

## Disabling Hooks

For scripting or sensitive operations:
$ ntm send --no-hooks myproject 'message'

## Example Hooks

Log all prompts:
#\!/bin/bash

title: Implement ntm health command for agent status checking
description:
Create a command to check health status of all agents in a session.

## What This Task Does

Create 'ntm health' command that checks and reports agent health:
- Process status (running/exited)
- Activity level (active/idle/stale)
- Error detection (rate limits, crashes)
- Output summary with visual indicators

## Command Interface

$ ntm health myproject
Session: myproject
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Pane │ Agent   │ Status  │ Activity │ Issues  │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 0    │ cc_1    │ ✓ OK    │ active   │ -       │
│ 1    │ cc_2    │ ✓ OK    │ idle     │ -       │
│ 2    │ cod_1   │ ⚠ WARN  │ stale    │ no output 5m │
│ 3    │ gmi_1   │ ✗ ERROR │ crashed  │ exit 1  │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Overall: 2 healthy, 1 warning, 1 error

$ ntm health myproject --json
{
  "session": "myproject",
  "checked_at": "2025-12-10T10:00:00Z",
  "agents": [...],
  "summary": {"healthy": 2, "warning": 1, "error": 1}
}

## Health Detection Logic

Process status:
- Check if pane has running process (tmux list-panes -F '#{pane_pid}')
- Check process state via /proc or ps

Activity detection:
- Capture pane content, compare over time
- 'active': Content changed recently (< 30s)
- 'idle': No change, but process running (prompt visible)
- 'stale': No change for extended period (> 5m)

Error detection (regex patterns):
- Rate limit: 'rate limit', '429', 'too many requests'
- Auth error: 'authentication', 'unauthorized', '401'
- Crash: 'error', 'exception', 'panic', exit codes

## Implementation

1. Create internal/health package
2. Implement process status checker
3. Implement activity detector
4. Implement error pattern matcher
5. Create ntm health command with TUI output
6. Add --json support (depends on ntm-ws2)

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] ntm health shows all agents with status
- [ ] Process crashes are detected
- [ ] Rate limit patterns are detected
- [ ] Activity level shown (active/idle/stale)
- [ ] Exit code reflects overall health
- [ ] --json output supported

title: Implement stdin and --file support for ntm send
description:
Enable sending prompts from files and stdin pipes.

## What This Task Does

Extend ntm send to accept prompt content from:
1. --file flag: Read prompt from a file
2. stdin: When piped/redirected and no prompt argument given

## Use Cases

From file:
$ ntm send myproject --all --file prompts/review.md

From stdin (pipe):
$ cat error.log | ntm send myproject --cc 'Analyze this error:'
$ git diff | ntm send myproject --all 'Review these changes'

From stdin (redirect):
$ ntm send myproject --all < prompt.txt

Combined with prefix:
$ cat code.py | ntm send myproject --cc --prefix 'Review this code:\n'

## Technical Details

Detection logic:
1. If --file specified, read from file
2. Else if stdin is not a TTY, read from stdin
3. Else use positional prompt argument

Implementation:
func getPromptContent(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) (string, error) {
    if file != "" {
        content, err := os.ReadFile(file)
        return string(content), err
    }
    
    if !isatty.IsTerminal(os.Stdin.Fd()) {
        content, err := io.ReadAll(os.Stdin)
        return string(content), err
    }
    
    if len(args) > 1 {
        return args[1], nil
    }
    
    return "", errors.New("no prompt provided")
}

New flags:
--file, -f    Read prompt from file
--prefix      Text to prepend to file/stdin content
--suffix      Text to append to file/stdin content

## Edge Cases

- Empty file: Error with helpful message
- Binary file: Warning, but proceed if forced
- Very large file: Stream rather than load all into memory? (future)
- Encoding: Assume UTF-8

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] --file reads prompt from specified path
- [ ] Stdin detected and read when not TTY
- [ ] --prefix and --suffix work with file/stdin
- [ ] Clear error messages for missing file, empty content
- [ ] Existing behavior unchanged when neither used

title: CI upgrade compatibility check job
description:
# CI Upgrade Compatibility Check Job

## What This Accomplishes
Runs `ntm upgrade --check` on every push/PR to validate that the current code can successfully find assets from the latest published release.

## Implementation Details
**File**: .github/workflows/ci.yml:327-388 (68 lines added)
**Job Name**: upgrade-check
**Matrix**: ubuntu-latest, macos-latest

**Workflow**:
1. Checkout repository
2. Setup Go 1.25
3. Build ntm from current source
4. Run `ntm upgrade --check`
5. Check output for "no suitable release asset" error
6. If found → FAIL with prominent error message

## Why This Catches Bugs That Tests Don't
The contract tests validate the LOGIC is correct (naming convention matches expectations).
The CI check validates the logic WORKS against REAL published releases.

**Scenario this catches**:
1. Contract tests pass (logic matches expected convention)
2. But latest release used a DIFFERENT convention than expected
3. CI check fails because ntm can't find the actual asset

This happens when:
- GoReleaser config was changed without updating tests
- Previous release had manual naming overrides
- Edge cases in template rendering

## Error Display
```
╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║  ERROR: Asset naming mismatch detected!                        ║
║                                                                 ║
║  upgrade.go cannot find assets from the latest release.        ║
║  This likely means:                                             ║
║  1. upgrade.go naming logic was changed, OR                     ║
║  2. .goreleaser.yaml naming template was changed                ║
║                                                                 ║
║  Review: TestUpgradeAssetNamingContract in cli_test.go          ║
╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

## Graceful Handling
- "no releases found" is acceptable (dev builds, new forks)
- Only "no suitable release asset" is a hard failure
- Exit 0 if upgrade check passes OR no releases exist

## Dependency Chain
Added to ci-success job's needs array, making it a required check.

## Design Decision: Why Not Windows?
Windows is excluded because:
1. ntm requires tmux which is Unix-only
2. Windows users use WSL anyway
3. The naming contract is validated via contract tests for Windows

## Commit Reference
7c57a6c ci: add upgrade asset naming contract tests and verification
close_reason: Implemented in commit 7c57a6c - all tests passing

title: Add spawn order to agent context
description:
Communicate spawn position to each agent so they can self-coordinate if needed.

## Problem

Even with staggered prompts, agents may benefit from knowing their spawn order:
- Agent can adapt behavior (first agent explores more, later agents rely on prior work)
- Agent can self-stagger if prompt arrives simultaneously (network/timing variance)
- Agent can reference siblings ("I'm agent 2 of 4")

## Implementation Options

### Option A: Environment Variable (Recommended)

Set AGENT_SPAWN_ORDER before prompt:

```bash
export NTM_SPAWN_ORDER=2
export NTM_SPAWN_TOTAL=4
export NTM_SPAWN_BATCH_ID=spawn-abc123
```

Agent's shell inherits these, agent can read them.

Implementation in tmux:
```go
func (s *Spawner) setSpawnContext(pane Pane, order int, total int, batchID string) {
    s.tmux.SendKeys(pane.ID, fmt.Sprintf(
        "export NTM_SPAWN_ORDER=%d NTM_SPAWN_TOTAL=%d NTM_SPAWN_BATCH_ID=%s\n",
        order, total, batchID,
    ))
}
```

### Option B: Prompt Injection

Include spawn order in the prompt:

```
[NTM Context]
You are agent 2 of 4 in this spawn batch.
Batch ID: spawn-abc123
Stagger: 90s (your prompt was delayed by 90s)

[Your Task]
{original prompt}
```

Pros: Agent definitely sees it
Cons: Uses tokens, clutters prompt

### Option C: File-Based

Write spawn context to file agent can read:

```bash
# .ntm/spawn-context.json
{
  "batch_id": "spawn-abc123",
  "agents": [
    {"pane": "proj__cc_1", "order": 1, "prompt_at": "..."},
    {"pane": "proj__cc_2", "order": 2, "prompt_at": "..."}
  ]
}
```

Agent can cat this file to understand context.

## Recommended: Hybrid

1. Environment variables for programmatic access
2. Brief prompt note for agent awareness
3. File for detailed batch context

## Prompt Addition (Minimal)

When stagger is enabled, prepend to prompt:

```
[Spawn context: Agent 2/4, batch spawn-abc123]

{original prompt}
```

Just one line, minimal tokens.

## Use Cases for Agents

1. **Self-stagger backup**: If agent detects NTM_SPAWN_ORDER > 1, wait a bit extra before selecting work
2. **Work coordination**: "I'm agent 2, let me pick something different than agent 1 might have picked"
3. **Reporting**: "Agent 2 completed task X" in Agent Mail messages

## Location

internal/robot/spawn.go

## Depends On

- ntm-gnqg: Add --stagger flag to spawn command

## Acceptance Criteria

- Environment variables set for each agent
- Minimal prompt annotation when stagger enabled
- Batch ID unique per spawn invocation
- Context accessible to agents
- No regression when stagger disabled

title: Implement agent type detection from pane content
description:
Improve agent type detection beyond pane title parsing.

## Current State
detectAgentType() in robot.go only checks pane title. This is unreliable because:
- Pane titles may not be set
- Users may use custom titles
- Agent type may not be in title

## Improved Detection
1. **Pane Title**: Check for 'claude', 'codex', 'gemini', etc.
2. **Process Name**: Check running process (claude, codex-cli, etc.)
3. **Pane Content**: Look for characteristic prompts/output:
   - Claude: '>' prompt, 'Claude' mentions
   - Codex: 'codex>' prompt, OpenAI references
   - Gemini: Gemini-specific formatting
   - Cursor: Cursor AI patterns
   - Windsurf: Windsurf patterns
   - Aider: 'aider>' prompt
4. **Environment**: Check for agent-specific env vars

## Detection Priority
Process name > Pane content > Pane title > Unknown

## Caching
Cache detected type per pane to avoid repeated content parsing. Invalidate on session reload.

## Output
```go
type AgentDetection struct {
    Type       string  // claude, codex, etc.
    Confidence float64 // 0.0-1.0
    Method     string  // how detected: process, content, title
}
```

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text:
## Detection Strategies

### Priority Order
1. **Process-based** (highest confidence)
   - ps aux | grep for process names: claude, codex-cli, gemini-cli
   - Check /proc/{pid}/cmdline on Linux
   - Most reliable but requires shell execution

2. **Environment-based**
   - Check for CLAUDE_*, OPENAI_*, GOOGLE_* env vars in pane
   - Can infer agent type from env configuration

3. **Content-based**
   - Scan last N lines of pane output
   - Look for characteristic patterns:
     - Claude: '>' prompt, 'Claude' in output, tool use XML
     - Codex: 'codex>' prompt, OpenAI references
     - Gemini: 'gemini>' prompt
     - Aider: 'aider>' or '/help' in prompt
   
4. **Title-based** (lowest confidence)
   - Current implementation - fallback only

### Caching Strategy
```go
type AgentTypeCache struct {
    cache map[string]CachedDetection // key: session:pane
    ttl   time.Duration              // default 60s
    mu    sync.RWMutex
}

type CachedDetection struct {
    Type       string
    Confidence float64
    Method     string
    DetectedAt time.Time
}
```

### Confidence Scores
- Process match: 0.95
- Env match: 0.85
- Content match: 0.70
- Title match: 0.50
- Unknown: 0.0

## Implementation Details

\`\`\`go
type EmptyStateOptions struct {
    Icon        string  // Visual icon (◎, ○, ◇, etc.)
    Title       string  // Primary message
    Description string  // Explanatory text (optional)
    Action      string  // Suggested action (optional)
    Width       int     // Available width
    Centered    bool    // Center in container (default: true)
}

func RenderEmptyState(opts EmptyStateOptions) string {
    // Render centered, styled empty state
}
\`\`\`

### Icon Meanings
| Icon | Meaning | Use Case |
|------|---------|----------|
| ◎ | Waiting | Data not yet available |
| ○ | Empty | Checked, nothing found |
| ◇ | External | Needs external action |
| ✓ | Success | Empty is good (no errors) |
| ? | Unknown | Couldn't determine |

### Panel Updates
Each panel gets appropriate empty state:

| Panel | Icon | Title | Description |
|-------|------|-------|-------------|
| Metrics | ◎ | No metrics yet | Data appears when agents start |
| History | ○ | No command history | Send prompts to build history |
| Files | ○ | No recent changes | File changes will appear here |
| Beads | ◇ | Not initialized | Run 'bd init' to enable |
| CASS | ◎ | No context found | Relevant history will appear |
| Alerts | ✓ | All clear | No alerts to display |

- \`internal/tui/dashboard/panels/*.go\` - Use new empty states
